text:
President Donald Trump again attacked Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar on Tuesday, calling her a "terrible person" a day after federal authorities searched her Washington, D.C.-area residence.

The investigation into Omar -- a sitting member of Congress who is up for reelection in just three weeks -- relates to her immigration paperwork, sources told ABC News.

Omar, who was first elected to the House in 2018, is the first Somali American in Congress. Born in Somalia, Omar became a naturalized U.S. citizen in 2000.

Asked whether he wants to see Omar deported after the Homeland Security Investigation's search at her residence on Monday, Trump said he doesn't "take a position" on the matter. It's not clear whether deportation is on the table for Omar.

"I don't take a position. I think she's a terrible person. I think she's a terrible congresswoman. I don't think she loves our country at all, but I don't take a position," Trump said as he departed the White House Tuesday morning.

Omar has denied wrongdoing and has not been charged with a crime.

In recent history, the Justice Department's practice has been to advise prosecutors not to take any overt investigative steps against members of Congress or candidates within 60 days of an election.

Trump has targeted Omar in the past, saying in social media posts earlier this year that Omar "should be in jail" and "sent back to Somalia."

Omar released a statement on social media earlier on Monday, saying that the search at her residence is "an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement." She added, "I will not be silenced."

During a rally in Ohio on Monday night, Trump called Omar a "disaster."

"She comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military, where all they do is shoot each other. And she comes into our country, and she says, 'I have a constitutional right,'" Trump said of Omar, who is a naturalized American citizen from Somalia.

Trump later assailed Somalia and claimed that Somali immigrants at large "cheat on everything" without providing evidence.

Trump has repeatedly criticized Somali immigrants, describing them as "garbage" and saying during a December 2025 Cabinet meeting that he didn't want them in the United States; the comments sparked backlash at the time.

Vice President JD Vance told reporters on Tuesday that he didn't have any warning about the search of Omar's residence.

"I did not have advance notice that her home was being raided. Look, I never -- we try to run our Department of Justice in a fair and honest way. We try to let the law follow the facts rather than creating facts just to prosecute people we don't like. And because of that, I think the president and I largely try to stay out of Department of Justice investigations and other prosecutions," Vance said.

Vance added that "we're going to look into" allegations against Omar.

"If there's a real case there, we're going to follow the facts. If there's not a real case there, then we won't," Vance said.

Speaker Mike Johnson weighed in on the search of Omar residence during an interview on Fox News on Tuesday morning, saying "we have to reserve judgment and let the system play out as it does."

"Maybe the timing's unfortunate for her or others, but this is the legal system, and it operates independently of the political system. So, we do our jobs, and we let the people decide," Johnson said.

ABC News' Lauren Peller contributed to this report.

text:
A sweeping immigration penalty campaign has helped drive thousands of self-deportations, the Trump administration said Tuesday, as officials finalize rules making it easier and faster to issue fines against immigrants who ignore deportation orders or enter the United States illegally.

According to a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Federal Register filing, more than 175,000 immigration penalties have been issued since the administration revamped its enforcement approach in 2025, marking a significant increase over the 12,000 issued in the months before the rule change.

DHS has been urging immigrants without legal status to self-deport, with a stipend that has risen to $3,000 and a government-funded flight to their home country, as well as forgiveness of immigration-related fines. The administration has framed it as safer and easier than facing potential U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention.

Read More on Politics

“While other presidents failed to secure the border and remove criminal illegal aliens, President Trump is using every law available to put Americans first and secure our country," a DHS spokesperson told Newsweek, adding that more than $84 billion in fines had been issued.

“In President Trump’s first year back in office, more than 3 million illegal aliens have left the U.S. because of the Trump administration’s crackdown on illegal immigration including an estimated 2.2 million self-deportations. As of September, we have now deported nearly 1.1 million illegal aliens and arrested over 1.1 million illegal aliens."

What New Rule Does

The DHS filing Tuesday finalizes a 2025 interim rule that applies to immigrants who fail to leave the U.S. after deportation orders, as well as those caught entering the country illegally.

The policy introduced last year streamlined how DHS imposes fines that Congress authorized years ago, with the Trump administration having argued that the old process was cumbersome and made large-scale enforcement impractical.

Previously, DHS issued a notice of how it intended to fine a person, there was a longer review process and then the penalty could be imposed. Under the 2025 change, DHS can start with a penalty decision, the appeals stay within the department rather than going to the Department of Justice, and the appeals must be filed within 15 days.

For illegal entry, the fine can be between $100 and $500, while voluntary departure violations can reach nearly $10,000, and failure-to-depart penalties can be around $998 per day.

DHS Says Penalties Are Driving Departures

The department said in its filing that the 2025 policy was "working as intended," with a greater number of penalty notices able to be issued.

From March 26, 2025, through June 26, 2025, DHS said it issued 12,135 penalties. After June 27, 2025, when the new rule was implemented, through September 10, 2026, approximately 110,000 failure-to-depart fines were sent, while U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) issued 66,000 unlawful entry fines.

Before the rule change, DHS said it was issuing around 930 penalties per week, while afterward, the number rose to around 2,800 a week. DHS said that its "robust use of civil penalties" was pushing more immigrants without legal status to self-deport.

"DHS data indicates that over 82,000 aliens with removal orders and voluntary departures orders have self-departed from the United States since DHS began issuing civil penalties in March 2025 through September 14, 2026," the department wrote.

Before the rule was implemented, during the same period DHS outlined previously, 8,600 people had self-deported.

"This final rule follows key trends of other immigration policy changes made by this administration including a focus on increasing self-departures to increase the overall number of deportations and adding pressure or fear-factor for noncitizens who are unlawfully present or seeking to enter the country unlawfully," Colleen Putzel-Kavanaugh, an associate policy analyst at the Migration Policy Institute, told Newsweek.

"The final rule is also reminiscent of a common tactic used by this administration: reviving old laws and implementing them for deportation."

Critics Say Rules Make It Harder to Fight Fines

DHS received feedback on the initial 2025 proposal, including concerns that the rule was ill-intentioned.

The filing stated that "the Departments reject the claim that this rule is intended to dehumanize or punish people navigating the immigration system.

"DHS notes that these penalties generally are not imposed until after the aliens have completed immigration proceedings and received a determination that they are not authorized to remain in the United States," the filing said. "The IFR did not create new categories of violative conduct or expand the scope of existing penalties."

Critics argued in the comments that appeals were now harder to file and the window to challenge penalties is shorter. They also argued that large penalties could devastate families, especially if daily fines rack up to the $1 million stated as a possibility by DHS.

"The shortened time from notice to opportunity to appeal, the changed process of appeals, and the elimination of an option for an interview leaves less opportunity for a noncitizen to make their case against the penalty," Putzel-Kavanaugh said. "The new rule also permits the use of ordinary mail vs. personal delivery or certified mail which could raise issues, particularly if the individual’s address has changed."

DHS said in its responses that appeals are still available and the process still offers immigrants due process.

How This Fits Into Trump's Deportation Strategy

Trump has been under pressure from his core base to deliver on a promise of mass deportations, and while ICE has received significant funding boosts and deportations have risen, clear data on removals and departures remains difficult to determine.

DHS says the goal is to present immigrants with a choice: depart voluntarily, potentially with government assistance and forgiven penalties, or remain in the U.S. and face escalating financial and immigration consequences.

Under the Trump administration, CBP made major changes to its app, which had been used to make appointments at the border for new arrivals seeking legal status. Now, it is designed to aid those seeking to leave the U.S. to avoid ICE detention and large fines.

CBP Home allows immigrants to notify the government of their intention to depart, potentially receive financial assistance, then leave on a regular flight to their home country, rather than be deported, before confirming they have arrived through the app.

The government has repeatedly pushed this method of departure, including when asked by the media about those in ICE detention, describing it as "a choice" that could be avoided if a person self-deports.

text:
HOUSTON — Videos collected by local investigators make it “pretty obvious” that an ICE officer intentionally ran over Miguel Parra Hernandez during an immigration stop Saturday, which could lead to assault charges, the district attorney said Tuesday.

“This was an intentional striking and running over of the person by the vehicle, and in that case, that is an aggravated assault with a deadly weapon in Texas,” Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare told NBC News.

Teare said the federal government is not cooperating with the investigation conducted by his office and the Harris County Sheriff’s Office. He also said ICE may have allowed the erasure of critical data in the vehicle involved in striking Parra, who was on foot.

Teare said that in his seven years as a Harris County vehicular crimes division chief, he has reviewed video from a number of other auto-pedestrian collision cases. He said the video his investigators have gathered in Parra’s case “goes above” the video that was posted online and obtained by NBC affiliate KPRC of Houston.

“My viewing of it, and many other investigators that have viewed it, as well, it’s pretty obvious that this was an intentional striking and running over of the person by the vehicle, and in that case, that is an aggravated assault with a deadly weapon in Texas,” he said.

Parra, 48, was left with multiple breaks and fractures in his body, according to his attorney and an advocate who has been speaking on his behalf. He had surgery on one leg and faces multiple additional operations, said Cesar Espinosa, co-founder and executive director of FIEL, an immigrant civil rights group.

Video obtained by KPRC shows a white truck headed in the opposite direction of traffic on a busy roadway. It shows a vehicle jumping a yellow median and heading in the direction that Parra is running.

It then appears to show the vehicle, which is not marked, swerving left toward Parra’s path, in front of a truck stopped in a shopping center. The parked truck leaves, and a man can be seen on the pavement behind the ICE vehicle, the video shows.

An ICE spokesman said over the weekend that officers were pursuing the fleeing men and that “Miguel Parra Hernandez ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck.”

Teare, a Democrat, announced late Monday that his office had launched an independent investigation.

On Tuesday, an ICE spokesperson who was not identified said in a statement that “allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE. The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct.”

ICE said the allegations are “disgusting smears” that are “peddled by the media,” leading to more than a 1,600% increase in assaults and a 3,300% increase in vehicle attacks against its law enforcement officers. It did not offer data behind those numbers.

ICE has said that Parra was not the target of the attempted stop but that he was in the country illegally. Parra’s attorney and family have said he has no criminal record and was on his way to work applying stucco.

Teare said his office and the sheriff’s office determined that the vehicle that struck Parra was a Jeep Cherokee and that it potentially had evidence, including a data crash recorder. He said his office wanted to know whether the vehicle locked in information at the time of the collision that could be downloaded, such as speed, steering and braking. Teare said the way to preserve data from the car would have been to “put it on a flatbed trailer and you take it to forensically download it.”

But he said he believes any data on the recorder related to the incident could have been erased when ICE drove the car away.

He and the sheriff’s investigators told ICE the information needed to be downloaded, but ICE refused, Teare said.

ICE did not respond to questions about a data crash recorder, the erasing of any potential data or any refusal to download it.

“Our office began drafting a search warrant that we were in the process of drafting when the ICE agent in question, the one that had been driving, we believed, at the time of the collision, jumped back into the car and drove it away from the scene,” Teare said. “In my 20-year career, I’ve never heard of anything like that.”

Teare also said two people from “an entirely different operation” were in the back seat of the ICE vehicle when it struck Parra. Those two people are also in ICE custody, along with Parra. Teare said his office is working to ensure all three remain in the country as material witnesses.

“I’ve taught for years at the Houston Police Department Academy, Harris County Department Academy. I’ve worked with law enforcement for 20 years. There is not a single agency in the United States that would teach that once you put people in custody in your car, you then begin to pursue other people,” he said.

Doing so puts “every single person out there in danger again,” he said.

According to Teare, the ICE vehicle should have activated its emergency equipment, such as its lights and siren, as it jumped a median and crossed into oncoming traffic.

A senior official at the Department of Homeland Security told NBC News on Tuesday that multiple ICE officers on the scene at the time were wearing body cameras. ICE is reviewing video of the scene as part of an internal investigation, the official said.

Espinosa said Parra told him that he fled because it was unclear whether there were officials in the vehicles, which he said were unmarked, did not use sirens and had dark, tinted windows.

ICE has said it was targeting another man, Jose Mendoza Cervantes, who was in the country illegally and had committed several crimes. Espinoza and Parra’s attorney Kim Bruno said neither Parra nor the man who was with him when ICE stopped their vehicle has any association with Mendoza.

In previous encounters between ICE and targets of its arrests in vehicle stops, including some who have been killed, such as Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston, ICE has alleged the people it tried to arrest weaponized their vehicles.

Parra was struck less than two weeks after the Trump administration issued guidance setting tighter rules for vehicle stops.

The guidance says only agents who have completed specific training should make vehicle stops. The memo also says that vehicles used for traffic stops must have lights and sirens and that all officers on the scenes of vehicle stops must wear and activate their body cameras.

The Harris County District Attorney’s Office has been asking witnesses and people who may have photos or video of the incident to contact it. Teare said that there is a secure portal that goes directly to the district attorney’s office and that no one is asked about citizenship or immigration status.

“All we are interested in is getting the truth, and any shred of cellphone footage, anyone that saw something and really can point us in the right direction, it would be wonderful,” he said.

text:
Seven people detained previously by ICE filed a lawsuit on Tuesday against the agency, accusing it of illegally refusing to return their personal documents and belongings months after they were released from custody.

Items allegedly withheld include Social Security cards, employment authorization documents, and phones, which the seven individuals allege is a violation of the Fourth Amendment—and ICE’s own confiscation directive, which only permits officers to keep belongings for a clearly defined reason, such as relation to a criminal case.

The ACLU of the District of Columbia, one of the bodies representing the seven plaintiffs, pointed in part to a 2024 federal appeals court ruling in Washington, DC, that barred that city’s police from holding personal property they seize for what the court deemed an unreasonable length of time.

Withholding items like employment documents prevents immigrants from being able to keep their jobs, the suit contends—at least some of the plaintiffs attest that they have indeed lost their jobs—and makes them fear leaving their homes due to lack of documentation.

One plaintiff from Russia with a pending asylum case, Vladimir Izmailov, was “unable to get meaningful employment without his work authorization documents,” ACLU of DC wrote—the suit details that ICE hasn’t returned these documents, and other items including his wedding ring, for more than five months.

“Now, I’m struggling to provide for my family because ICE still has my documents that show I am authorized to work,” Izmailov stated; he said that he has been forced to borrow money to make rent and continue to house himself, his wife, and their two children.

The lawsuit comes following a series of reports of similar incidents. My colleague Julia Lurie wrote about cases in Minnesota in February: “It’s more the rule than the exception that people generally are not given their stuff back,” Graham Ojala-Barbour, a Minneapolis immigration attorney, said in an interview for that article. “As far as I can tell, it’s the practice of ICE to throw everybody’s documents into a black box and then lose it.”

As she reported at the time:

Federal law requires noncitizens to carry proof of their lawful status. “The government not returning these documents to folks is essentially forcing them to walk around without this document that the government itself says these folks are supposed to carry with them,” says Julia Decker, policy director of the Immigrant Law Center of Minnesota.

The plaintiffs are asking the court to order ICE to return their items—and to stop the agency from continuing to unlawfully retain property without just reason.

title: Amicus Brief in Support of Judicial Review of USCIS Delay in Deciding Green Card Applications
description:
This amicus brief argues that a federal district court may review a claim that USCIS has unreasonably delayed deciding applications to adjust status to lawful permanent resident (green card applications).
The district court dismissed the complaint because it concluded that a section of the Immigration and Nationality Act barred judicial review of a “decision or action” in the agency’s discretion as to green card applications.
The amicus brief argues that the district court also can review the applicants’ mandamus claim to compel USCIS to decide.
The amicus brief also argues that since jurisdiction exists, the appellate court should return the case to the district court for a decision as to the delay.
Partners The American Immigration Council filed this amicus brief with the American Immigration Lawyers Association.
text:
This amicus brief argues that a federal district court may review a claim that USCIS has unreasonably delayed deciding applications to adjust status to lawful permanent resident (green card applications). The district court dismissed the complaint because it concluded that a section of the Immigration and Nationality Act barred judicial review of a “decision or action” in the agency’s discretion as to green card applications. Seeking reversal, the amicus brief argues that the statute must be read as allowing review because the ordinary meaning of “decision or action” does not include failure to decide or act. The amicus brief also highlights that unlike this statute, Congress created a special definition of “agency action” in the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), which includes the failure to act, and provided a remedy. The amicus brief argues that the district court also can review the applicants’ mandamus claim to compel USCIS to decide. The amicus brief also argues that since jurisdiction exists, the appellate court should return the case to the district court for a decision as to the delay.

Partners

text:
The increasingly violent reality of the Trump administration’s mass deportation agenda came into sharp focus again last week when plainclothes ICE officers opened fire on a car in New York City within seconds of surrounding the vehicle, wounding 28-year-old Oscar Belgal while his terrified 5-year-old son sat in the back seat. This alarming use of force, echoing across the country as communities grapple with a sharp rise in immigration enforcement violence, provides context for a major legal battle unfolding in Minnesota.

Just days before the New York shooting, the family of Renée Good, a 37-year-old mother of three who was shot and killed by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer in Minneapolis earlier this year, filed two significant federal lawsuits against the U.S. government and top administration officials.

Good’s family and lawyers seek to use two distinct legal paths to force accountability through the U.S. federal courts, even though doctrines such as qualified and sovereign immunity usually protect federal law enforcement officers and the administration’s top political leaders from facing civil rights lawsuits. The twin lawsuits target both the officer that killed Good and the systemic policies that the lawsuit claims made her death inevitable and near-guaranteed impunity for the officer’s deadly use of force.

Minneapolis deadly encounter

On January 7, 2026, during a tense confrontation between protesters and federal immigration officers deployed to Minneapolis as a part of the administration’s “Operation Metro Surge,” ICE officer Jonathan Ross fired three shots into Good’s car as she attempted to drive away. One bullet struck her in the head, killing her.

While the Trump administration initially claimed that Good was a “domestic terrorist” trying to run over the officer, the lawsuit argues that video footage clearly shows Good steering her vehicle away and talking to the officers using deescalating language. Good was a U.S. citizen and had no criminal history. After Good’s death, the administration neither indicted nor fired Ross and he is still in the agency as an active ICE officer.

A double attack on impunity

To overcome the significant legal doctrines that protect ICE officers and the federal government from liability, the lawsuits — filed by Good’s partner and her brother — rely on a two-part approach primarily via two legal statutes.

Federal Tort Claims Act

The first claim uses the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) and names the United Sates as the sole defendant. It accuses the government of battery, assault, false imprisonment, negligence, and intentional infliction of emotional distress that directly caused Good’s wrongful death. By using the FTCA, Good’s family and attorneys seek to hold the Trump administration liable for torts committed by federal immigration officers acting within the scope of their federal employment.

Typically, sovereign immunity protects the U.S. government from lawsuits; but Congress’ enactment of the FTCA provides an exception giving victims injured by government actions a mechanism for filing a lawsuit to seek damages. In the Good lawsuit, the FTCA legal claim focuses primarily on the mechanics of the shooting itself and the immediate liability of the government.

Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871

Parallel to the FTCA claim is the second and more politically explosive lawsuit, which uses a provision of the Reconstruction-era Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871. Congress designed the law to protect citizens from organized and systemic civil rights violations. At that time, local and state authorities routinely refused to prosecute Ku Klux Klan members for violence they inflicted upon newly freed Black Americans. Congress responded by enacting this law to explicitly enforce the newly ratified Fourteenth Amendment and ensure protection of civil and voting rights.

The Good lawsuit brings claims under two provisions of the statute, 42 U.S.C. Section1985(3) and 1986, to allege a broad Trump administration conspiracy to violate civil rights, naming not only Officer Ross, but also senior administration officials including Stephen Miller, Tom Homan, and former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem.

The Section 1985(3) claim alleges that these officials conspired with private actors, including far-right online provocateurs whose allegations against the Somali community in Minnesota led directly to the administration’s Operation Metro Surge, as well as private corporations whose technology was used to target neighborhoods for enforcement and track observers and protestors. The Section 1986 claim arises from the officials’ failure to prevent the wrongs of the alleged conspiracy.

At the core of the Ku Klux Klan Act claim, Good’s lawyers argue that her death was not an isolated operational error, but the “predictable result” of an unconstitutional campaign driven by racial animus targeting Hispanic and Somali communities. The family alleges that Trump administration officials deliberately structured federal immigration crackdowns to encourage aggressive, hostile confrontations, while signaling to rank-and-file officers that they would never face legal consequences for using excessive force.

Bringing claims under Sections 1985 and 1986 avoids the strict legal limitations of “Bivens actions” which in the past allowed individuals to sue federal enforcement officers for Fourth Amendment violations but which the Supreme Court has heavily curtailed in recent decades.

Systemic reckoning or indefinite impunity?

By linking executive policy to field-level operations, the lawsuit seeks to provide an alternative route to challenge immunity for high-ranking political appointees. If the federal court moves the case forward, it could establish a major precedent for holding top level administration officials accountable for the actions of ICE field officers. If the court does not allow the lawsuit to proceed, then the only way to ensure individual officials’ accountability for unlawful immigration enforcement violence will be for Congress to make overdue changes to outdated immigration laws which for decades have permitted immigration agent officers and agencies to operate with significant impunity. Congress could pass a law that would create a clear cause of action so that victims of constitutional violations committed by federal law enforcement officers can sue in federal court. When local police officers violate the Constitution, they can be sued in federal court; but when federal law enforcement agents commit the same violations there is no parallel recourse.

While the Good family seeks unspecified compensatory damages, their primary focus is public accountability. At an emotional Minneapolis press conference, Renee Good’s partner Becca Good stated: “The whole world had to watch as our entire universe was destroyed. We were all robbed.”

Following so closely on the heels of the recent New York City ICE shooting, the Renee Good lawsuits will test whether the federal judiciary is willing to hold federal officers accountable or continue to allow them to operate with near impunity on American soil.

text:
Rep. Delia C. Ramirez (D-Illinois) has introduced a bill that would abolish not just ICE, but the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) altogether, repealing the 2002 law establishing the agency and replacing it with one focused on protecting civil and human rights.

The wide-ranging legislation, dubbed the Reimagining Safety Act, would repeal the Homeland Security Act. Signed by President George W. Bush as part of his administration’s post-9/11 “war on terror,” the transformational bill created DHS and led to the establishment of Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

The bill would abolish DHS, CBP, and ICE — going further than the progressive call to abolish ICE. Other offices currently housed within the department, like Transportation Security Administration (TSA), the Coast Guard, Citizenship and Immigration Services, and the customs functions of CBP would be broken off into different authorities.

“We know that DHS was intentionally established with an overbroad mission and unchecked power. The last two years have made it visible what so many communities have actually been saying for decades: That DHS, frankly, is the single greatest threat to our public safety today,” Ramirez said in a press conference previewing the legislation last month. “We must strip away every single tool they are using to terrorize us.”

In DHS’s place, Ramirez’s bill would create a cabinet-level “Department of Community Safety,” which would address community concerns ranging from gun violence to disaster relief, using a public health-based approach. All immigration detention centers would be shuttered.

The legislation comes as DHS has ballooned into one of the largest agencies in the U.S. government in just 24 years of existence, with its authorities having been expanded by every subsequent presidential administration since its establishment.

Now, it has become central in executing President Donald Trump’s agenda, carrying out his administration’s fascist campaign of mass deportation, surveillance, and suppression of communities across the U.S.

The legislation is cosponsored by Representatives Adelita Grijalva (D-Arizona), Jim McGovern (D-Massachusetts), and Rashida Tlaib (D-Michigan), as well as over 40 advocacy and progressive groups.

“From its inception, those in power have wielded DHS as a weapon. Widespread illegal and abusive detention of immigrants, violent racial profiling, and state overreach — including domestic surveillance, civil rights violations via the USA PATRIOT Act,” Ramirez said.

“The bottom line is this: From its establishment, DHS has always been empowered to violate our rights, under the pretense of securing our safety,” Ramirez said. “Enough is enough.”

The administration has targeted hundreds of thousands of immigrants with arrests, detention, and deportations, often openly defying court orders and even constitutional safeguards to wreak havoc and invoke fear. At least eight people have been killed on the streets by DHS agents since the beginning of Trump’s second term, at least 57 have died in immigration detention, and thousands have been “disappeared” within the shadowy detention network or to places abroad. Meanwhile, journalists, activists, elected officials, and more, have repeatedly been caught in DHS’s ever-expanding dragnet.

Ramirez’s new bill also seeks to defang numerous other post-9/11-era policies and actions. It calls for the closure of the Guantánamo Bay military detention center, which Trump has used to imprison Somali immigrants. President Joe Biden pledged to and failed to close the center that became a notorious symbol of torture and indefinite detention under Bush, who once declared that the Geneva Conventions did not apply to the U.S.’s detainees at Guantánamo Bay and other CIA black sites established by the U.S. as it waged war on Iraq.

The bill additionally targets two sections of the Immigration and Nationality Act aimed at prosecuting supposed “terrorism.” It sunsets Section 219 of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which directs the federal government to designate and sanction “foreign terrorist organizations.” And it repeals language in the bill establishing “the statutory grounds that render noncitizens inadmissible based on “terrorist” affiliations, which would stop people in the U.S. from being deported under these grounds, according to the bill’s summary.

text:
Local immigrant advocacy organizations say they are seeing an increase in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) activity across San Luis Obispo County.

805UndocuFund, a nonprofit that supports immigrant communities and tracks reported immigration enforcement activity, says it has received reports from multiple areas of the county in recent days.

“We’ve been receiving several reports from different cities in SLO County,” said Primitiva Hernandez, executive director of 805UndocuFund.

According to Hernandez, the organization has verified multiple ICE detentions since Friday in communities including San Miguel, Nipomo and Oceano. She said the nonprofit relies on eyewitness accounts and reports from community members to confirm incidents.

“It is an increase that we have seen this week, that we have not seen in many, many months prior,” Hernandez said.

Another local advocacy organization, Ice Out of SLO County, has also reported an increase in immigration enforcement activity in the area.

Both groups point to reports of a possible federal immigration enforcement effort known as “Operation Safe California.”

“There’s been widespread news of this, what is believed to be a 45-day operation known as Operation Safe California,” Hernandez said.

A report published by the Washington Examiner described the alleged operation as a month-and-a-half-long enforcement effort in which federal agents are directed to arrest undocumented immigrants they encounter, regardless of criminal history.

Gov. Gavin Newsom responded to the report by stating that California would stand up for its communities and hold federal agents accountable.

Hernandez said recent enforcement actions are having a significant impact on local families.

“They are taking everyday community members who are here trying to provide better life for their families. That is the reality,” she said.

KSBY reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for confirmation of the reported operation. In a statement, the agency said:

“For operational security and the safety of our officers, ICE will not disclose or discuss law enforcement operations.”

Department of Homeland Security

In a statement released Thursday, San Luis Obispo County Supervisor Dawn Ortiz-Legg also addressed reports of recent ICE activity. Ortiz-Legg cited reports that the parent of a local middle school student had been detained by ICE agents.

Ortiz-Legg said her office was not provided information about the specific circumstances surrounding the detention, writing that “the lack of transparency creates unnecessary fear and uncertainty for all our community.”

According to Ice Out of SLO County, 218 people had been taken into ICE custody in San Luis Obispo County since at least early 2025, as of Saturday. 805UndocuFund reports that 1,270 people have been taken into ICE custody in neighboring Santa Barbara County during the same period.

Advocacy groups are encouraging families who may be impacted by immigration enforcement activity to seek legal assistance and community resources.

text:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

October 13, 2026

MEDIA CONTACT

Spencer Tilger | media@refugeerights.org

Trump Administration Lays Groundwork for Mass Deportation of Resettled Refugees

New Regulation Makes it Harder To Challenge Attempts to Terminate Refugee Status

(New York, NY) – Today, the Trump administration posted a new interim final rule that will make it easier to strip resettled refugees living in the United States of their legal status without due process. The rule, which goes into effect once it is formally published in the Federal Register tomorrow, substantially reduces the period in which refugees can appeal the termination before they lose status from thirty days to ten.

Under this regulation, refugees will lose meaningful due process protections, making it nearly impossible for them to challenge unfair or false accusations before they lose their refugee status and with it their right to work. Until recently, it has been exceedingly rare for refugees to have their status terminated, and previously they had thirty days to respond to such a notice. In that already-limited time, refugees had more opportunity to find counsel, submit evidence debunking the government’s often-baseless accusations, and defend and maintain their status. Absent exceptional circumstances, the law requires agencies to seek public input before imposing significant changes in regulations, but U.S. Citizenship & Immigration Services (USCIS) has chosen to forego the required notice-and-comment period and impose its new rule immediately.

The International Refugee Assistance Project (IRAP) has been defending resettled refugees against unlawful efforts to arrest, detain, and strip them of their status through litigation and on an individual basis since the administration began targeting them earlier this year. This regulation represents another escalation against immigrants with lawful status and these tactics lay the groundwork for the mass de-documentation and deportation of refugees. IRAP calls on USCIS to rescind the rule immediately and for Congress to exercise its authority to prevent this injustice from being carried out.

Laurie Ball Cooper, IRAP Vice President of U.S. Legal Programs said:

“The Trump administration has been relentless in its efforts to strip immigrants, including refugees, of their legal status and enact its racist and xenophobic vision for America. For months, IRAP has worked to defend refugees facing a government witch-hunt seeking to strip them of status in the United States. Now, it will be impossible for refugees to even fully understand the allegations against them, much less find counsel and contest those allegations, before their status is terminated. The government is reducing this process to mere window-dressing for an effort to strip lawfully present, lawfully admitted refugees of their status and deport them to persecution or worse. Refugees are American community members who have already proven and won their cases for protection. Threatening the safety and stability of our refugee neighbors is an attack on the constitutional rights of every American.”

Background

Beginning in early 2026, the Trump administration started unlawfully arresting and detaining refugees solely because they had not yet received their green cards. IRAP, alongside partner organizations, secured court orders preventing the government from carrying out this policy in Minnesota and nationally. But even once detentions stopped, refugees continued to be called in for aggressive revetting interviews, receiving Notices of Intent to Terminate their refugee status on spurious grounds, and some have been placed in removal proceedings after having their status terminated.

Additional Information

Read the posted but unpublished regulation: HERE

Learn more about IRAP’s work challenging the arrest and detention of refugees: HERE

Read IRAP’s legal explainer about refugee revetting: HERE

Access Know Your Rights information for refugees living in the United States: HERE

The International Refugee Assistance Project (IRAP) is a global legal aid and advocacy organization working to create a world where refugees and all people seeking safety are empowered to claim their right to freedom of movement and a path to lasting refuge. Everyone should have a safe place to live and a safe way to get there.

The U.S. has built “deliberate” and “systematic” new procedures for deporting immigrants to 35 foreign nations, often putting the immigrants in danger while sidestepping U.S. law, according to a recent report (opens in a new tab) by the Berkeley Law Human Rights Center (opens in a new tab) Investigations Lab (opens in a new tab).

The system has evolved rapidly since the start of 2025, the report says, with the Trump administration striking previously unknown agreements to pay countries tens of millions of dollars to accept refugees and migrants who have been living in the U.S. Other countries have been threatened with the loss of aid if they refuse.

The result: More than 21,000 immigrants and refugees — many of them in the U.S. legally, with no criminal record — have been removed from the country and sent to third countries where they have no previous connection. Some have been falsely labelled as gang members or criminals and then imprisoned. Others, the investigators found, have been returned from the third country back to their home countries despite the risk of persecution, torture and death.

“We are witnessing one of the most horrendous attacks on immigrant communities in U.S. history,” the report says. “The Trump administration’s mass removal policies are systematic, pervasive and coordinated with maximum intent to terrorize immigrants. … This research outlines an architecture of cruelty, a scaffolding that is being used to construct a new regime in which refugees and migrants are treated as if they exist outside the rule of law.”

text:
New, widely-cited federal data points to a dramatic spike in Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests in Vermont during the summer, mirroring a national trend.

But that picture of ICE activity in Vermont appears to be misleading, according to a Vermont Public analysis of the same data.

Figures obtained by the Deportation Data Project at the University of California, Berkeley and UCLA — and cited by outlets such as the New York Times — suggest that ICE agents in Vermont scaled up their enforcement operations in the spring and summer. The agency logged 124 arrests in Vermont through July, more than triple those carried out during all of 2025. The New York Times has repeatedly highlighted the Vermont enforcement jump as one of the steepest in the nation.

A closer look at the data, however, reveals that many of the people included in the ICE data were actually apprehended by U.S. Customs and Border Protection while trying to sneak across the Canadian border and later transferred to ICE custody for deportation.

In those cases, their arrest is being counted twice — once when Border Patrol agents apprehend them, and again when ICE agents later assume custody.

In other words: Their arrests had nothing to do with the sort of interior enforcement that the Trump administration is trying to bolster and which critics have denounced.

Vermont Public identified more than 50 arrestees in the ICE data whose case details closely match those of border-crossers apprehended by Border Patrol agents as documented in court records and U.S. Customs and Border Protection data.

In a June press release, for instance, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Vermont touted its prosecution of a Senegalese woman born in 2002. Court records show that Border Patrol agents arrested the woman, along with a mother and four children, on June 20, several hours after they walked across the border near Highgate. Federal prosecutors charged the woman with illegally entering the country, a misdemeanor. She appeared in federal court in Burlington on June 24, pleaded guilty and was sentenced to time served.

That same day, ICE records show that the agency took custody in Burlington of a Senegalese woman born in 2002.

This double-counting of some Border Patrol apprehensions as ICE arrests in Vermont appears to have begun sometime this year. It’s unclear why. Vermont Public did not find obvious signs of a similar data issue in other border states.

An agency spokesperson declined to comment except to say that ICE does not review, audit or give “context” to the data it has released to the Deportation Data Project in response to public records litigation.

ICE has published separate data that indicates Border Patrol agents made the initial arrest in roughly 10% of its cases nationwide during the current fiscal year.

What the data does show

The lion’s share of ICE arrests in Vermont through July involved people who were in some form of law enforcement custody before ICE agents got involved — which, in most cases, appears to be U.S. Customs and Border Protection. (While the agencies can sometimes become conflated in public discourse, ICE and Customs and Border Protection have distinct roles.)

The agency also conducted 29 “at-large” arrests during that seven-month period, including the controversial March 11 detentions of three immigrants at their home in South Burlington.

ICE arrested 35 people this way in 2025.

So ICE does appear to be on track to increase its interior arrests in Vermont this year, even if not as dramatically as the federal data suggests.

The agency employs a small crew of removal officers in the state. But their efforts are supplemented by ICE agents from nearby states and those from Homeland Security Investigations and Border Patrol, who also have legal authority to conduct immigration enforcement beyond the border.

Together, federal agents have arrested immigrants at job sites, at their homes and through traffic stops. Many do not have criminal records, and some were arrested because of a chance encounter, rather than a targeted operation.

ICE has made a spate of arrests involving migrant workers since the latest ICE data was compiled. Seven Days identified at least 12 construction workers who were detained by ICE agents during enforcement actions in August and early September.

That would mark one of ICE agents’ most active periods of interior enforcement here in recent years, the data shows.

In one of those cases, an agent noticed a group of roofers working on a Cornwall residence, pulled over and arrested two of them, the newspaper reported.

text:
ICE is offering children as young as 5 years old $3,000 “incentives” to voluntarily depart the country, legal advocates have reported, as the Trump administration works to separate immigrant families under the hammer of their mass deportation machine.

Bloomberg Law first reported on the offers, citing attorneys and immigrant advocacy groups who say that the offers are sometimes given to children who lack legal representation. The offers, they say, are a method of forcing children to take a deal so that they drop their legal challenges before they have gone through their time in the court system.

Shaina Aber, executive director for the Acacia Center for Justice, told Bloomberg Law that the tactic is “part of a larger pattern of really trying to coerce children, bully children, intensify pressure on children so that they abandon their cases.”

“It’s part of this deport-at-all-costs policy that seems to be in particular targeting children,” Aber went on.

The offer is being made by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) attorneys as well as immigration judges. In some cases, judges are telling children that it is a one-time offer and giving them no time to consider it, forcing them to make a decision “on the spot” even though “they might not understand what the longer term consequences are down the line,” Aber said.

Another group, the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, said that it and similar groups have received the emails from ICE’s Office of the Principal Legal Advisor offering a “$3,000 incentive” for children. Michael Lukens, head of Amica, told Bloomberg Law that the latest offer came to his office this week for an 11-year-old.

The reporting shows that the Trump administration’s policies toward child deportations are even more extreme than previously thought. Last year, NBC reported that the Trump administration was offering children aged 14 and older $2,500 to self-deport or voluntarily leave the country, according to a Department of Health and Human Services memo.

Indeed, reports have since found that the Trump administration is carrying out this policy even in cases where the children were living with their families, in cases likened to President Donald Trump’s family separation policies from his first term.

The Department of Homeland Security didn’t confirm or deny the payments, saying that the administration is supposedly working to reunite children who come to the U.S. unaccompanied with their families.

text:
Editor’s Note: Amol Sinha is a civil rights attorney and the executive director at the ACLU of New Jersey where he oversees litigation and advocacy to advance the rights of all New Jerseyans. This post was originally published by USA Today Network New Jersey.

Immigration detention is cruel and inhumane. It’s also deadly.

Conditions in detention facilities are so egregious that the death rate of people in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody has more than doubled since the start of President Trump’s second term, reaching its highest level in over a decade. But despite overwhelming evidence, certain members of Congress have refused to acknowledge what is happening in front of our eyes and to our neighbors.

At a hearing about conditions at Delaney Hall in July, House Judiciary Subcommittee on Oversight Chairman Jeff Van Drew, along with witnesses he invited, argued that accounts of medical neglect, inedible food, unsanitary conditions, and abuse at the immigration detention facility were exaggerated or fabricated. He even praised the care available at the facility and questioned the legitimacy of a weeks-long hunger strike by detained people protesting their treatment. "They get 24-hour emergency care whenever and wherever it’s needed," he said.

When it was my turn to testify, I set the record straight. I described what we have documented for months: people denied life-sustaining medication, individuals forced to go without their wheelchair, detainees losing dramatic amounts of weight, and repeated reports of serious medical conditions being ignored. I also spoke the name of Jean Wilson Brutus, a 41-year-old Haitian man who died one day after arriving at Delaney Hall last December.

I warned that if immediate action was not taken, this would happen again and again. I am devastated that I was right. Two weeks after the hearing, two more people detained at Delaney Hall died, reportedly from inadequate medical care.

Edwin Jovanny Lopez Cornejo, a 39-year-old man who had lived in Plainfield, New Jersey for more than two decades, died after suffering a medical emergency. He was a construction worker, a father to a 12-year-old U.S. citizen daughter, and a beloved member of his community.

According to his family, Mr. Lopez Cornejo had managed diabetes, high blood pressure, and epilepsy with medication for years. His relatives now question whether he consistently received this medicine during the six weeks he spent at Delaney Hall. His brother recalled that even obtaining Tylenol required submitting paperwork and waiting several days.

Rep. Rob Menendez reported that when Lopez Cornejo suffered his medical emergency, he was seen by nurse practitioners because the facility’s lone physician was neither present nor on call. An ambulance eventually transported him to University Hospital, where he was pronounced dead on August 1st.

We now know that around the same time as the July hearing, Jose Chajon-Raxon, another man detained at Delaney Hall, experienced a seizure and was transported to the hospital. ICE granted him a temporary medical release before he died. Because he technically was no longer in a detention center, his death was not counted as death in ICE custody.

Congress must confront the truth of these stories. They deserve to be told. That’s why I sent a letter to Rep. Van Drew and the subcommittee to enter the stories of Lopez Cornejo and Chajon-Raxon into the official congressional record.

But the cases from Delaney Hall are not outliers. In July, 45-year-old Jesus Manuel Arenas Silvadied while in ICE custody in Georgia. His family says officers prevented him from bringing most of the medications he needed. Days later, 29-year-old Prisciliano Trejo died from acute leukemia after his family said detention officials delayed urgent medical treatment while he repeatedly complained of severe symptoms.

Taken together, these deaths — along with the almost 60 other deaths in ICE custody since the start of the second Trump administration in 2025 — expose a system in which medical care is inaccessible, opacity is the standard, and ICE evades any accountability.

That is why congressional oversight matters. When people repeatedly report ignored calls for medical help, stalled emergency care, withheld medication, rancid food, and deplorable conditions, the allegations deserve investigation. Instead of asking whether the abuse is real, Congress should be asking why these reports have remained so consistent across facilities.

The human cost of these failures extends far beyond the detention center walls.

“I don’t have a way of healing this deep pain,” Lopez Cornejo’s mother said after losing her son.

His 12-year-old daughter put it even more simply: "I’m going to grow up without a father."

No congressional hearing can change what happened to their family. But Congress can choose whether those deaths become another statistic or the catalyst for meaningful reform, so it doesn’t happen to another family.

Members of Congress should conduct bipartisan, unannounced, and uncensored inspections of Delaney Hall and other ICE detention facilities, as they are authorized to do. They should speak directly with detained people and those recently released. They should compel testimony from ICE officials and private prison executives responsible for operating these facilities. They should advance legislation, including the Dignity for Detained Immigrants Act, that phase out for-profit detention facilities like Delaney Hall.

There is indeed a “false narrative” about Delaney Hall — that it is humane. The tragic evidence shows that this facility is dangerously mismanaged and that the ICE coverup must end.

text:
A Texas man whose leg was broken in multiple places after being struck by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) vehicle during a weekend traffic stop has never met the person the federal agents were allegedly pursuing, according to his representatives.

Miguel Parra-Hernandez, 48, suffered serious injuries including a shattered ankle and hip when he was run over in Houston, Texas, on Saturday by an SUV driven by an officer chasing two men who ran from a pickup truck.

ICE, according to multiple media reports, said it was in pursuit of another man, Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, during an early-morning operation and attempted a vehicle stop before the occupants ran away. It said Parra-Hernandez was not its target – but he ran in front of the ICE vehicle and was struck.

Video of the incident aired by ABC News affiliate KTRK, however, shows a dark-colored, unmarked SUV following Parra-Hernandez and veering towards him as he ran across empty spaces in the shopping center parking lot in Harris county, whose seat is Houston.

Parra-Hernandez’s attorney, Kim Bruno, and Cesar Espinosa, executive director of the immigrant advocacy group FIEL Houston, told reporters at a news conference on Monday that Parra-Hernandez remained in ICE custody and faced more surgery as well as many weeks of recovery.

Espinosa said Parra-Hernandez was hit “in a violent and brutal fashion”. Bruno said he told her that he fled because he did not know who was in the dark-colored vehicle. Neither he nor the other person in the car, whom he had picked up for work, knew Mendoza-Cervantes, she said.

The ICE vehicle, she added, was not using a siren or displaying flashing lights.

Earlier in October, ICE adopted new rules for traffic stops, including ensuring that vehicles are equipped with lights and sirens to let the public know they are law enforcement vehicles, although it did not mandate their use.

The guidelines, in a memo written by Marcos Charles, executive associate director of ICE, and obtained by the Associated Press, state that ICE officers are no longer permitted to chase vehicles that refuse to stop. The memo came after a series of violent and fatal confrontations involving federal immigration officers over the summer.

Espinosa said he and Bruno were able to meet briefly with Parra-Hernandez at the hospital on Monday morning. But their visit ended after about 15 minutes when ICE agents entered the room and began recording their conversation, and they were made to leave.

“To add insult to injury, Mr Miguel is in the custody of the ICE agents who ran him down,” Espinosa said, as reported by NBC News.

“This is so disheartening and so angering that Miguel has to face the people that brutally attacked them every single day, 24 hours a day.”

The Guardian has contacted ICE for comment.

Espinosa said Parra-Hernandez sustained hip and leg injuries, including a shattered ankle. Doctors have said he cannot put weight on his leg for at least six weeks, and Parra must wait for swelling to recede before reconstructive surgery can take place, Espinosa said.

Parra was struck at about 7.30am on Saturday. Witnesses said he remained on the ground for at least seven minutes after he was struck.

Bruno said Parra-Hernandez told her that the other person in the car was not Mendoza-Cervantes, who ICE has identified as an illegal immigrant with multiple previous arrests and a judicially issued final order of removal from the US.

She said Parra-Hernandez had lived in the US for 34 years, having arrived at age 14, and has no criminal record.

The Harris county district attorney, Sean Teare, said on Monday his office was investigating the Parra-Hernandez case.

The Harris county sheriff’s office said in a statement that it was called by ICE after the crash, which occurred as the agency has been met with nationwide criticism throughout Donald Trump’s second presidency for its aggressive arrest, detention and deportation tactics.

description:

This service demonstrated the eerie, callous strategy of fear ICE uses to disrupt the lives of millions of Americans and American migrant communities.
Because as I stood looking over the shoulders of my esteemed clergy colleagues, hidden behind tinted windows, ICE was there.
ICE invaded cities such as Los Angeles and Minneapolis, but now the violence is behind tinted windows, and we become complacent.
Many Vermonters have never had to fear what lies beyond tinted windows.
text:
This commentary is by Devon Thomas, an ordained minister of the United Church of Christ.

On Monday, Oct. 5, I joined Vermont’s clergy in attending a funeral service at the doors of the Williston Immigration and Customs Enforcement office. This service of remembrance was to recognize 98 people who were killed by ICE or died in its custody, according to a bulletin given out at the service, and to highlight a system of cruelty our governing administration is using against our migrant neighbors and fellow citizens to win political power.

​In our time, we are seeing fellow human beings martyred in America’s culture war. The funeral service at the Williston surveillance center showed me how human atrocity can be permitted in a society such as our United States. It did not halt ICE activities, as it was made clear ICE was aware of and had prepared for our protest. Nor did it grant any meaningful sense of closure and comfort to the families and loved ones of victims.

This service demonstrated the eerie, callous strategy of fear ICE uses to disrupt the lives of millions of Americans and American migrant communities. Because as I stood looking over the shoulders of my esteemed clergy colleagues, hidden behind tinted windows, ICE was there.

As mourners laid down bricks etched with the victims’ names, ICE was there. As mourners wept on the streets, silently, ICE was there. As clergy nailed shut the coffin, ICE was there, apparently unremorseful. The system was ready to do its job. To burst from behind closed doors with crowbars and hammers to smash the painful memorial we put at their feet. They tore apart the coffin and threw the bricks bearing the names of the victims into the back of a pickup truck to be carted off as trash. That trash held the names of 98 people who died, directly or indirectly, because of ICE. The oldest was 85; the youngest was three.

​This funeral was a symbol, and as a person of faith, I believe symbols have meaning. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is part of us, as a people. It was created after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks because we, as a nation, were hurt and scared, and we wanted to protect ourselves. For a time, it seemed this fear brought us together, but it also, subtly, tore us apart. We turned a blind eye to how we treated those we saw as different and a threat. We treated people with different religions, skin tones and cultural backgrounds as dangerous to us, and we turned away when other Americans began to target and violate the sacred commandment to love those whom God loves, as described in Matthew 22:37-39. At first, the violence was open. ICE invaded cities such as Los Angeles and Minneapolis, but now the violence is behind tinted windows, and we become complacent.

​As I write, ICE is organizing surges into migrant communities across the United States. This surge is happening silently, avoiding headlines and the attention of American citizens. It is implementing new and cruel methods of deportation and detention, sending migrants to countries where they have no connections or resources to survive, or confining people far from home in underresourced detention facilities.

Many Vermonters have never had to fear what lies beyond tinted windows. We have trusted law enforcement to protect us. That sense of security was a privilege many of our neighbors were never afforded. Now it is being stealthily stolen from the rest of us.

title: ICE Immigration Courthouse Arrests Curtailed by Judge's Order with Nationwide Impact
description:

Soon after, we asked the court to temporarily block immigration courthouse arrests while the lawsuit played out.
But in a shocking revelation in March, the government admitted to the judge that the 2025 memorandum it used to justify its immigration court arrests in fact “does not and has never” authorized these arrests.
This was a huge victory for New York immigrants as well as their families and advocates.
The Court agreed with us and found the government’s mass immigration court arrest policy “arbitrary and capricious” under the Administrative Procedure Act.
text:
President Trump strode into his second term in office promising record immigration arrests, and it wasn’t long before the terror started to unfold.

In a cruel and unprecedented change to protocol, armed and masked ICE agents soon began abducting immigrants who dutifully showed up to their routine, required appointments in immigration court. Previously, agents generally avoided making arrests at courthouses on the grounds that doing so would discourage people from showing up for their court dates.

The Trump administration’s policy put immigrants in a devastating catch-22: They could stay home and give up on the chance to remain in the country legally, or show up to court and risk getting separated from their families and the lives they have built here.

The impacts of the policy change were visceral. Many of them were caught on camera. The NYCLU went to court to put an end to this chaos, along with our partners at the ACLU, Make the Road New York, and Emery Celli Brinckerhoff Abady Ward & Maazel. We filed a lawsuit on behalf of two organizations that provide legal services to immigrants, African Communities Together and The Door. We argued the administration’s immigration courthouse arrest policies violated the Administrative Procedure Act, a federal law that ensures transparency and accountability in how federal agencies create and enforce policies and regulations.

Soon after, we asked the court to temporarily block immigration courthouse arrests while the lawsuit played out. The court partly denied this request in September 2025, finding a 2025 Trump administration memorandum justified the change in policy.

But in a shocking revelation in March, the government admitted to the judge that the 2025 memorandum it used to justify its immigration court arrests in fact “does not and has never” authorized these arrests.

We immediately asked the court to reconsider its decision, and this time the judge granted the stay. We secured an order temporarily blocking courthouse arrests at federal immigration courts located in Manhattan. This was a huge victory for New York immigrants as well as their families and advocates.

Then on October 1, we achieved a monumental victory for immigrants across the nation. The Southern District Court of New York ruled that ICE officers cannot make arrests in or near immigration courthouses, except in rare circumstances, in New York and across the country.

The Court agreed with us and found the government’s mass immigration court arrest policy “arbitrary and capricious” under the Administrative Procedure Act.

Courthouses should be sites of justice, not places where armed and masked ICE officers rip crying children from their parents’ arms. The ruling protects immigrants’ right to seek asylum or pursue other channels to remain in the country legally – without fear of being detained by ICE.

This is not only a victory for people trapped in our maddeningly byzantine immigration system. It’s a win for all those who believe every person deserves their day in court.

text:
Supreme Court Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Neil Gorsuch joined forces to issue a statement highlighting the “constitutional absurdity” of an immigration case that the high court declined to take up Tuesday.

Sotomayor, an Obama appointee, and Gorsuch, a Trump appointee, hail from opposite ends of the Supreme Court’s ideological spectrum. But the pair, which agreed 62% of the time during the most recent term, has teamed up in the past to express their concerns about cases and call for the consideration of specific issues in future litigation.

The justices did agree with the Supreme Court’s decision to deny review for Jesus Herrera-Salazar’s case, a Mexican national convicted twice of being “found in” the U.S. without proper documentation. The pair concurred in part because Herrera-Salazar had already been removed from the country by the time his case reached the high court.

What Sotomayor and Gorsuch took specific issue with was lower courts’ disregard for the double jeopardy standard, which prevents an individual from being tried twice for the same crime.

Trending

Sotomayor and Gorsuch described the “serious constitutional problems that plague the Government’s treatment of Herrera-Salazar,” including a lower court’s 2020 indictment for Herrera-Salazar being “found” to be present in the U.S. after having received an order of removal and leaving the country years earlier.

After Herrera-Salazar pleaded guilty and served a 15-month prison sentence, authorities expressly instructed him not to leave the Eastern District of Oklahoma while serving on supervised release. He was later arrested and indicted under the same federal charge in 2022 — though he did not leave the country again and reenter unlawfully between his two convictions.

Herrera-Salazar appealed his case after the 10th Circuit Court of Appeals rejected his double jeopardy concerns by arguing that a separate reentry offense was not required to indict him in 2022.

By the appeals court’s logic, Sotomayor and Gorsuch asserted, Herrera-Salazar could have been charged with a separate violation “for each day that he was ‘found in’ prison while serving his sentence for the first conviction.”

“Absurd as that seems, it is a logical outgrowth of the Government’s contention” that Herrera-Salazar’s second conviction “poses no double jeopardy problem,” the justices wrote.

The justices also argued that the government had presented Herrera-Salazar with a Hobson’s choice — a seemingly free decision that only offers one real option — because “whether Herrera-Salazar remained in the Eastern District of Oklahoma or left the United States, he would be breaking the law.”

Sotomayor and Gorsuch encouraged the justice system to “give the Double Jeopardy Clause its full weight and meaning” if courts are tasked with reviewing cases similar to Herrera-Salazar’s.

title: Supreme Court questions Trump's bid to redefine birthright citizenship under 14th Amendment

text:
"Ask any American what our citizenship rule is, and they'll tell you, everyone born here is a citizen alike," ACLU attorney Cecilia Wang said during oral arguments in the Supreme Court's landmark birthright citizenship case Wednesday.

President Donald Trump is asking the justices to uphold his Day 1 executive order eliminating birthright citizenship under a novel interpretation of the 14th Amendment and requiring parents to prove their own legal status before citizenship is granted to their children.

Trump attended the start of the proceedings Wednesday morning, making him the first sitting president to attend the high court's arguments.

Wang, during her opening statement, arguing that the principle was enshrined in the Constitution to prevent government officials from stripping citizenship away.

"That rule was enshrined in the 14th Amendment to put it out of the reach of any government official to destroy," she said.

"If you credit the government's theory, the citizenship of millions of Americans past, present and future could be called into question," she said.

Solicitor General D. John Sauer got a somewhat frosty reception from at least two key Supreme Court Justices -- Chief Justice John Roberts and Associate Justice Neil Gorsuch -- during his arguments, in which he contended that the longstanding understanding of the 14th Amendment is incorrect.

'Very quirky arguments'

"The citizenship clause was adopted just after the Civil War to grant citizenship to the newly freed slaves and their children whose allegiance to the United States had been established by generations of domicile. Here, it did not grant citizenship to the children of temporary visitors or illegal aliens who have no such allegiance," he said.

Roberts noted that the Trump administration is relying on "very quirky" arguments, saying they are using "narrow exceptions" to claim that a much broader class of people should be ineligible for birthright citizenship.

"You know, children of ambassadors, children of enemies during a hostile invasion, children on warships, and then you expand it to the whole class of illegal aliens here in the country. I'm not quite sure how you can get to that big group from such tiny and sort of idiosyncratic examples," said Roberts.

Gorsuch also remarked that the Trump administration seems to be relying on outdated "Roman law sources" and court precedents that do not work in their favor.

"I'm not sure how much you want to rely on Wong Kim Ark," Gorsuch remarked about the landmark 1898 case that enshrined birthright citizenship.

Justice Elena Kagan similarly voiced concerns about the sources cited by the Trump administration.

"You're using some pretty obscure sources to get to this concept," she said.

'Illegal immigration'

Justice Samuel Alito initiated a discussion on "illegal immigration" by noting that it was "something that was basically unknown" at the time when the 14th amendment was adopted in the 1860s.

"What we're dealing with here is something that was basically unknown at the time when the 14th Amendment was adopted, which is illegal immigration," Alito said. "So how do we deal with that situation when we have a general rule?"

Sauer responded by agreeing with Alito, saying that "illegal immigration did not exist [ then ] ," and "the problem of temporary visitors didn't exist."

Sauer pointed to "commentators" from 1881 to 1922 who, he claimed, were "uniformly saying the children of temporary visitors are not included." He argued that this logic "naturally extends" to those who enter the country illegally.

Justice Elena Kagan challenged Sauer's argument on immigration, saying his arguments in his brief did not focus on "illegal immigration."

"Most of your brief is about people who are just temporarily in the country where there was quite clearly an experience of an understanding that there were going to be temporary inhabitants," Kagan said. "And your whole theory of the case is built on that group."

"You don't get to talking about undocumented persons until quite later, and at much lesser ... I think it's like 10 pages to three pages or something like that," she said.

When asked about how the Trump administration would apply their birthright citizenship executive order, pointed to a guidance document from the Social Security Administration issued last year.

"How does this work? Are you suggesting that when a baby is born, people have to have documents present in the delivery room?" Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson asked.

"I think that's directly addressing the SSA guidance that cited in our brief, what SSA says," Sauer responded.

Justice Jackson appeared skeptical of that response, pressing Sauer about the steps of the process and whether a parent could challenge a final decision.

"We'll give you a social security number, provided that there's the system [ that ] automatically checks the immigration status of the parents -- which there are robust databases for -- and then it appears no different to the vast majority of birthing parents," Sauer said.

Birth tourism

In his opening statements, Sauer laid out one of the Trump administration's key arguments about why birthright citizenship should not be extended to the children of undocumented immigrants, claiming that if it remains "unrestricted" it will continue to be a "pull factor for illegal immigration" and would "reward" immigrants who violate immigration laws.

"It has spawned a sprawling industry of birth tourism as uncounted thousands of foreigners from potentially hostile nations have flocked to give birth in the United States in recent decades, creating a whole generation of American citizens abroad with no meaningful ties to the United States," Sauer said.

The Trump administration has often claimed that birth tourism -- the idea that foreign nationals travel to the U.S. with the sole purpose of having a child here -- poses a national security risk and undermines birthright citizenship.

Justice Roberts pressed Sauer to explain how common the problem is, but Sauer was unable to give a clear answer.

"No one knows for sure. There's a March 9 letter from a number of members of Congress to DHS saying, 'Do we have any information about this?' The media reports indicate estimates could be over one million, or 1.5 million from the People's Republic of China alone. The congressional report that we cite in our brief talks about certain hotspots, like Russian elites coming to Miami through these birth tourism companies," Sauer said.

Sauer went on to claim that media reports indicate there are 500 "birth tourism companies" in China, prompting Justice Roberts to interject to ask if Sauer agreed that had "no impact on the legal analysis before us."

"We're in a new world now as Justice Alito pointed out, to where 8 billion people are one plane ride away from having a child who is a U.S. citizen," Sauer added later.

In a statement Wednesday morning, ACLU Executive Director Anthony D. Romero addressed Trump's attendance at the proceedings, saying Trump would "watch the ACLU school him in the meaning of the Constitution and birthright citizenship."

"Any effort to distract from the gravity and importance of this case will not succeed. The Supreme Court is up to the task of interpreting and defending the Constitution even under the glare of a sitting president a couple dozen feet away from them," he said.

Although the proceedings should provide a sense of how interested the judges are in Trump's reinterpretation of the 14th Amendment, a ruling in the case isn't expected until the end of June.

text:
Esmeralda Soria has seen immigration enforcement throughout her life. Born to immigrant farmworkers in the Central Valley, the state assemblymember has spent her entire life in California’s agricultural powerhouse. Yet even for her, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids that shook the valley last week took her by surprise.
