“I have never experienced anything like this,” Soria said in an SFGATE interview Sunday. “Just all of a sudden, now we’re seeing ICE go rogue.”

Federal agents have spent the past week sweeping the Central Valley, with local immigrant advocates reporting officers conducting widespread, warrantless detentions, targeting gas stations and Mexican bakeries as farmworkers start their day. People have reportedly been detained without any warrants for their arrest.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The chaos turned violent when an off-duty ICE officer allegedly passed out drunk and assaulted a Fresno homeowner only to get shot himself, according to police.

Communities across the valley, including the San Joaquin Valley in the region’s south, are now terrified of further detentions. Community groups have postponed public events, and schools have reported an increase in student absences. Fresno Mayor Jerry Dyer, a Republican, condemned the raids as “disturbing” and called out a video showing ICE agents arresting a man in front of his screaming children.

For local Democrats, the raids are an obvious attempt by the Trump administration to instill fear in the immigrant community and stop people from voting in this year’s midterm elections.

“They are trying to do anything they can to suppress the vote and rig the election,” Soria said.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Latino voters are being closely watched, as they will largely decide who wins the valley’s 22nd Congressional District, a battleground seat currently held by Republican Rep. David Valadao. It’s one of the most watched races in the country and central to either party’s control over Congress.

Conservative news outlets, including the Washington Examiner, have reported that unnamed ICE sources said they were aiming to arrest all people living in California without authorization, even if they did not have a criminal record, under “Operation Safe California,” which would last through mid-November. The Department of Homeland Security declined to answer SFGATE’s questions about the raids, including if the raids are aimed at suppressing Latino voters. An unnamed spokesperson said they would not disclose details about law enforcement operations.

Valadao, who voted for President Donald Trump’s massive increase in ICE funding, did not return multiple SFGATE requests for comment and declined to answer in-person questions from a reporter on Friday. He released a statement Thursday that said the raids are focused only on people with “active warrants and known criminal histories.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Local advocates have strongly disputed that characterization, saying that people without criminal records are being detained. Fresno city councilmember Miguel Arias told SFGATE Friday that one of his constituents, with no criminal history and a legal right to be in the United States, was detained while he was cutting his own lawn.

“They’re not serving search warrants with specific targets, it’s all random,” Arias said.

Valadao’s Democratic opponent, Randy Villegas, said in a phone interview with SFGATE Monday morning that the raids are clearly aimed at suppressing the vote.

“This is the most Latino district in California, and what we’re seeing right now is a blatant attempt to try to suppress the vote,” Villegas said.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Villegas pointed out that his Republican opponent said, “It is what it is,” when discussing in a debate last week the immigration raids in the valley.

“I think it’s pathetic and disgusting that Valadao claims to be a moderate on this issue when he voted to triple ICE’s budget and has remained silent while ICE terrorizes our communities,” Villegas said.

Nora Zaragoza-Yáñez, a manager at Faith in the Valley, a faith-based nonprofit that helps immigrant families entangled in the raids, agreed that ICE’s operation is aimed at discouraging voting. She called the raids the largest in years and said the officers are targeting anyone who looks Hispanic.

“I think it will backfire, that is what many of us are trying to mobilize our community,” Soria said.

text:
Washington, DC – Today, Congresswoman Delia C. Ramirez (IL-03), Ranking Member of a Committee on Homeland Security Subcommittee, introduced the Reimagining Safety Act, a legislation to dismantle the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and create the Department of Community Safety. The landmark community-led legislation would create a new human- and community-centered federal department that promotes collective safety, repeal the authorities that give DHS its power, and redirect DHS funds to programs that working families rely on.

The Reimagining Safety Act is a first-of-its-kind bill and the first time community stakeholders designed a cabinet-level department. The Reimagining Safety Act would:

Establish the Department of Community Safety

Dismantle DHS, preserving the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), the Transportation Security Administration (TSA), and Customs functions

Abolish ICE and Customs and Border Protection (CBP)

Reinvest funds in our communities

Limit government surveillance, rein in unlawful abuses of data, and curb militarized enforcement

Begin the process of establishing a separate civil immigration system

“Every person dead in detention, shot or killed by ICE and CBP, every neighbor deported to a third country, every family separated, every community FEMA failed, every miscarriage due to substandard care, every dissenter wrongfully branded, targeted, and persecuted as ‘terrorist,’ and every threat against our elections by Trump, Markwayne, and Miller is a reason DHS must be dismantled and something new must take its place. There are more than a million reasons to take action today,” said Congresswoman Ramirez. “DHS was founded out of a profound national trauma, established to violate our rights under the pretense of securing our safety. But we cannot add new pains to old ones.”

The introduction follows a community press action on September 23, when Congresswoman Ramirez stood with Illinois public officials, civil society, and community members to announce the Reimagining Safety Act.

“Instead of the weapon DHS has proven to be, we need a department built on the best parts of who we are and can be, and the best examples of how we can take care of each other in hard times. I am proud to have led that work with the organizations in my district and nationally,” added Ramirez. “Building something new, creating in a time of destruction, is a revolutionary act. It is proof of our hope and belief in what is possible even in dark times. A different world is possible because the people have the power to reshape our government and reimagine how we cultivate safety and collective well-being.”

The legislation’s original cosponsors include Congressmembers Rashida Tlaib (MI-12), Adelita Grijalva (AZ-07), and Jim McGovern (MA-02). The bill is endorsed by a coalition of more than 40 national and local cross-issue organizations, including Muslims for Just Futures, Casa DuPage Workers Center, Latino Union of Chicago, Muslim Civic Coalition, Organized Communities Against Deportations, La Casita de ut ac, Albergue Tochan Nuestra Casa, Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights, AL OTRO LADO, League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC), Free Speech for People, Immigration Advocacy Law Group, Decolonize Sudan, The Right to Immigration Institute/Dignidad, American Friends Service Committee, Servicio Internacional para la Paz, Global Exchange, Immigrant Welcome Network of Johnson County, Council on American-Islamic Relations Chicago (CAIR-Chicago), US Campaign for Palestinian Rights Action, Center for Constitutional Rights, Alliance of South Asians Taking Action Power (ASTA Power), Women Cross DMZ, Haitian Bridge Alliance, Arise Chicago, Palenque LSNA, Zero Hour, MADRE, Mijente, Indivisible Chicago Alliance, Grassroots Collaborative, Warehouse Workers for Justice, Jewish Council on Urban Affairs (JCUA), Rising Majority Action Front, IL Poor People’s Campaign, Sustainable Economies Law Center, National Nurses United, Immigrant Legal Resource Center (ILRC), Defending Rights & Dissent, Bend the Arc: Jewish Action, DREAM of Detroit, and United States Solidarity Economy Network, Charity and Security Network, Muslim Advocates, IMEU Policy Project, and Detention Watch Network.

title: State-Level Criminal Justice Progress in 2026 | Vera Institute
description:
Despite headwinds and continued setbacks, criminal justice reform remains a popular and personal issue in the United States.
Oklahoma and other Republican-led states are defying the stereotype that criminal justice is a partisan issue Many perceive criminal justice reform as a “liberal” or “progressive” issue, especially as some Republican-led states, like Louisiana, have turned away from past progress.
Even as criminal justice reform advances, many states continue to undermine it with outdated “tough-on-crime” measures like sentencing enhancements.
Conclusion The 2026 sessions continue to challenge the narrative that the country has lost its appetite for criminal justice and immigration reform.
Criminal justice reform no longer commands the attention it did in 2020, but it is advancing, quietly and unevenly, out of the spotlight.
text:
Over the past six years, a popular narrative has taken hold that progress on criminal justice reform in the United States is stalled, or even dead. This narrative suggests that after landmark victories in the 2010s, the pendulum swung back against reform amid a backlash to the racial justice movement of 2020 and a pandemic-era rise in crime. This may be true at the federal level, where virtually every major issue remains gridlocked. But at the state level, criminal justice reform continued to thrive as a bipartisan issue in 2026, demonstrating that it has weathered a period during which the country turned toward a punitive politics of fear. As politics and public opinion continue to shift in favor of justice and immigrant rights while “tough-on-crime” fearmongering loses its potency amid a historic drop in crime, the reform movement is positioned to accelerate in 2027 and beyond.

Various criminal justice experts have observed this trend in recent years. Princeton University’s Udi Ofer and the Council on Criminal Justice’s Marc Levin have written about the persistence of state-level progress. As Ofer wrote in The Atlantic in 2024, “The reform movement has entered a new era of quiet pragmatism, which focuses on practical solutions and consensus-building rather than ideological purity.” Yet ill-informed critics, including the president, continue to fearmonger against popular, evidence-backed reforms, feeding the backlash narrative that the facts don’t support.

In 2026, states passed 425 criminal justice reform and immigration laws across 45 states, plus Washington, DC, that held legislative sessions, from 76 laws in reentry to 52 in sentencing reform and 54 in law enforcement accountability. The movement remains bipartisan: Republican-led (trifecta) states account for 28 percent of all laws, Democratic-led states account for 58 percent, and divided states account for 14 percent. Many of these reforms are incremental, while some mark real breakthroughs. Maryland became the fourth state to pass a Fair Chance Housing Act to eliminate barriers to housing access for people returning from incarceration. Missouri became the 14th state to pass a Clean Slate law. Six states now have policies allowing people to sue federal agents for violating their constitutional rights.

Despite headwinds and continued setbacks, criminal justice reform remains a popular and personal issue in the United States. Nearly one in two adults has had an immediate family member incarcerated, and roughly one in three have some kind of conviction history. In 2024, FWD.us polling found that 81 percent of likely voters support justice reform, with strong support across battleground states, racial groups, and political parties. Vera Action research shows that voters consistently choose proven solutions that prevent crime and break its cycle, not simply more police and prisons. The political conditions that fueled the backlash are also changing. The pandemic-era rise in crime that drove much of the retreat has solidly reversed. Historic-low crime rates have weakened the case for punitive responses.

This report unpacks state-level legislative progress in 2026 to help lawmakers and advocates prepare for the coming legislative sessions. Because several sessions are still in progress and some bills await governors’ signatures, Vera is releasing it now to aid 2027 planning, and an addendum will follow in January. This kind of review relies on subjective criteria, as detailed at the end of the report, and thus should be read as informative rather than as an exact account.

Importantly, state legislation is only part of the story. Reform is also advancing through local governments, state budgets, courts, and other system actors. In 2026, for example, New York City and Chicago established violence-prevention offices; Pennsylvania invested in a new Medicaid reentry program; district attorneys fought to hold federal agents accountable; and a California court recently ruled that bail must be affordable, while a Pennsylvania court struck down mandatory life without parole for second-degree murder. States also made real headway funding deportation defense: State and local investments have climbed from approximately $260 million in 2025 to more than $500 million committed nationwide for 2027, helping ensure that the rising number of immigrants in detention can access their basic rights to due process.

As we enter 2027, mass incarceration still remains deeply entrenched, with many states enacting policies that worsen the problem and the federal government rapidly expanding immigrant detention, including using space in state and local jails and prisons to hold people in civil immigration custody. Yet the progress on reform has not retreated. This report shows how, in the face of rollbacks and a hostile federal government, states are still leading the charge toward a system grounded in evidence and focused on delivering safety, justice, and accountability.

Maryland continued to lead the way among Democratic-led states advancing justice reform

In 2025, Maryland took major strides forward for justice reform, including a Second Look Act and geriatric and medical parole reform, showing how states can move significant legislation even in the face of “tough-on-crime” headwinds.

Rather than resting on that record, Maryland enacted 24 more laws this year. It became the fourth state (after New Jersey, Colorado, and Oregon) to pass a Fair Chance Housing Act, which limits the use of criminal background checks in rental applications. This is a critical step toward giving formerly incarcerated Marylanders a fairer chance to secure housing, one of the most important elements of successful reentry. Maryland also took on juvenile justice, despite a climate of concern over youth crime and major opposition. It passed the Youth Charging Reform Act to end automatically charging kids as adults for certain offenses and to prohibit children from being placed in adult jails. The state also enacted a significant parole reform law, restored the right of people with most convictions to serve on a jury, and allowed volunteers into prisons to help prepare people for release.

Neighboring Virginia also saw a successful legislative session, marking a departure from a period of hostility to reform under previous governor Glenn Youngkin. This year, the state expanded earned time credits, limited the amount of time young people spend in their room or cell, and established a literacy program for incarcerated people reading below an eighth-grade level. Colorado was similarly active, passing measures to increase state oversight of correctional facilities and expanding opportunities for sentence reduction. However, in both states, governors undercut progress by vetoing important reforms.

New Jersey, long a leader in justice reform, had a productive 2026 as well. The Garden State followed in the steps of states like Oklahoma and Georgia in passing a Survivor Justice Act, allowing courts to consider shorter sentences (and resentencing) for survivors of abuse. Additionally, the Incarcerated Women’s Protection Act provides new services for incarcerated women, including pre-release counseling and doula services for pregnant women, and a new Division of Women’s Services under the Department of Corrections.

Oklahoma and other Republican-led states are defying the stereotype that criminal justice is a partisan issue

Many perceive criminal justice reform as a “liberal” or “progressive” issue, especially as some Republican-led states, like Louisiana, have turned away from past progress. But Oklahoma has remained committed to reforms addressing its astronomically high incarceration rate and racial disparities. In recent years, the state has passed a Clean Slate law, the Oklahoma Survivors’ Act, and a law to eliminate many criminal justice fees.

This year, Oklahoma continued to reform the use of fines and fees, requiring courts to assess a defendant’s ability to pay fines, costs, and fees before imposing them and preventing incarcerating people solely for fines or costs they can’t afford to pay. It also removed barriers to expungement (including automating the Clean Slate process), restored voting rights for people who have completed incarceration and probation for a felony offense, and established a mentoring program for children of incarcerated parents.

Oklahoma is not alone: in Nebraska, the Youth Reentry and Transitional Support Act improves reentry support for youth, and another law improves education and vocational training behind bars. South Carolina expanded a diversion program for people charged with a first offense, allowing them to participate again if enough time has passed. Tennessee passed a law establishing human trafficking as a justification for self-defense, and Indiana established a 988 crisis response center and mobile crisis team. Even Louisiana enacted some modest legislation, like establishing a new reentry program for women and a requirement to provide people leaving state prisons with identification. These laws will not offset Louisiana’s return to failed punitive approaches, but they show that even in a challenging environment, advocates can still find openings that make a real difference in people’s lives.

Many states took action to protect immigrant communities from overreach by federal law enforcement

As federal immigration enforcement has grown vastly more aggressive under the Trump administration, state legislatures have responded with bills limiting local entanglement with ICE and attempting to safeguard the rights of people at risk of detention and deportation. Some states already had such laws, like Maine’s 1989 Civil Rights Act and New York’s 2019 Protect Our Courts Act. This year brought a renewed push, with states and localities building on one another’s work.

Many of the new laws answer accountability demands that federal Democrats attempted to win during the shutdown this year: Seven states have banned masked enforcement, nine have required judicial warrants for certain civil immigration arrests, six have created civil remedies for agents who violate constitutional rights, and 11 have declared schools, hospitals, and other sensitive locations off-limits to ICE arrests. Four have also banned 287(g) agreements, bringing the total number of states banning cooperation between local and federal law enforcement to 10. Maryland’s Community Trust Act and No Kings Act, New Jersey and Virginia’s mask bans and ICE limits, and California’s ban on electric shock gloves are among the measures in this wave.

Connecticut’s bipartisan omnibus bill, SB 397, was one of the most sweeping responses: in addition to the above measures, it allows residents and the attorney general to sue ICE for constitutional violations, empowers the state inspector general to probe federal use-of-force incidents, protects the right to record enforcement actions, and ensures that all peace officers, including federal agents, meet Connecticut's basic police training requirements. Other states targeted ICE’s dangerous and deadly detention facilities, with Delaware, Maryland, and New Mexico largely banning private detention contracts.

Nevertheless, states are running up against ICE’s apparent impunity. Even in states with 287(g) bans, local police and jail staff have continued to informally collaborate with federal agents, and ICE has already flouted its constitutional obligation to obtain judicial warrants. Even the most consequential reforms face an uncertain future: Colorado’s law mandating annual health and safety inspections of detention facilities was partially blocked after a lawsuit from detention contractor GEO Group, and the DOJ is suing Maryland over its Community Trust Act, among a litany of other suits against blue states.

These laws establish a vital line of defense, but they cannot end the harm: immigrants across the country continue to face the violence, chaos, and lethal consequences of enforcement. No state law can match the breadth of federal enforcement. And in much of the country, people have no protections at all: in July 2026, 39 percent of people detained by ICE were held in Republican-dominated Texas and Louisiana, and ICE arrests are climbing fastest in Republican-led jurisdictions. Meanwhile, significant legislation that would bring fairness and dignity into the immigration system remains stalled—like New York’s Access to Representation Act and California’s AB 2600, which would guarantee legal representation for anyone facing deportation. Next year, lawmakers at every level, including in Congress, can continue to learn from one another and find new ways to rein in ICE, safeguard due process, and establish accountability, rather than rest on these 2026 victories.

Progress also means defeating harmful bills

Despite such broad progress, states are still passing laws that lengthen sentences, undermine police accountability, and criminalize homelessness, among many other harmful actions. That makes stopping harmful bills a central part of any honest account of progress. These wins are worth recognizing, and they often demand as much work as passing new laws.

In California, dedicated advocates flock to Sacramento every year to help lawmakers understand how criminal justice bills that may appear sensible will actually cause real damage. This year, one such bill would have enhanced sentences for domestic violence. As advocate and survivor Claudia Gonzalez testified, “AB 292 is framed as a measure to prevent domestic violence and hold people accountable. It will do neither. Instead, AB 292 will expand punishment that risks deepening the criminalization of domestic violence survivors who are often arrested for acts connected to self-defense or survival.” The bill passed the assembly but failed to make it out of the Senate Public Safety Committee, ensuring its demise.

Another important win came in Arizona, where Governor Katie Hobbs vetoed SB 1061. This bill, which the governor also vetoed in 2025, would have reduced the threshold for mandatory minimums for fentanyl possession with intent to sell from 200 grams to just nine grams. Advocates argued that the state should invest in treatment instead and that harsher punishment wouldn’t deter people from using drugs. In her veto letter, Hobbs touted her administration’s actions to fight the overdose crisis and explained that this bill “does not effectively target the high-level drug dealers and cartels who are responsible for pushing poison on our streets.”

Somewhat similarly, in Wisconsin, Governor Tony Evers vetoed a sentencing enhancement for distributing drugs in or near a shelter, explaining, “Wisconsin should be taking an evidence-based, data-driven approach to corrections and justice reform—this can help make our communities safer and reduce the likelihood that someone might reoffend when they are released.”

Progress has come alongside significant rollbacks

While this progress should be celebrated, it shouldn’t distract from the parallel rollbacks that hit red and blue states alike. Even as criminal justice reform advances, many states continue to undermine it with outdated “tough-on-crime” measures like sentencing enhancements.

At least three states passed major packages this year that will fill their prisons—and drain their budgets—for years to come. A Missouri law increased mandatory minimums for prison sentences, with the law’s fiscal note stating that it will require the construction of a new $825 million maximum security prison. An Iowa law creates a “three-strikes” rule for “habitual offenders,” while Kansas similarly passed a law effectively instituting a “two-strikes” rule for juveniles—threatening to unwind decades of past successful juvenile justice reforms in the state.

In the wake of the Supreme Court’s 2024 Grants Pass decision allowing cities to punish people for sleeping outside, states like Indiana and Louisiana also continue to pass laws criminalizing public camping that punish people experiencing homelessness. Louisiana’s law even authorizes courts to order unhoused people into unpaid labor programs if they cannot afford treatment.

This year, several red states walked in lockstep with the president’s agenda. Kansas lawmakers overrode Democratic Governor Laura Kelly’s veto to let county jails hold people without charges pending ICE transfer. In advance of Trump’s Model Cities Initiative that seeks to enlist local governments under a unified federal enforcement agenda, numerous states, including Indiana and Mississippi, passed anti-sanctuary laws requiring police to collaborate with ICE. Idaho and Tennessee, meanwhile, created new state crimes tied to violations of federal immigration law. And in the wake of the Trump administration’s memo pushing states to expand capital punishment, Alabama, Mississippi, and Tennessee all moved to make child sex crimes death-eligible, effectively inviting a challenge against Supreme Court precedent.

In some blue states, governors remain an obstacle to progress. Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger, despite leading a Democratic trifecta, vetoed bills that would have banned ICE courthouse arrests and created a regulated legal cannabis market, among others. In Democratic-controlled Colorado, Governor Jared Polis vetoed a bill to let residents sue federal immigration agents for civil rights violations. And in purple Maine, Governor Janet Mills vetoed the bipartisan Clean Slate bill.

Blue states also actively advanced legislation harmful to criminal justice: California’s AB 46 makes it easier for judges to deny diversion for defendants who otherwise qualify for community mental-health treatment. California, Maryland, Oregon, and Rhode Island enhanced criminal penalties for metal theft, responding to (and in some cases amplifying) public anxiety over visible property crime.

These setbacks will take years to undo, and they show how fragile progress can be. Even as evidence continues to favor reform, many lawmakers remain convinced that “tough-on-crime” policy is the only answer, and others lack the courage to defend sensible policy. That is why this moment of resilience matters—reform does not advance in a straight line, and every gain must be defended.

Conclusion

The 2026 sessions continue to challenge the narrative that the country has lost its appetite for criminal justice and immigration reform. Criminal justice reform no longer commands the attention it did in 2020, but it is advancing, quietly and unevenly, out of the spotlight. This remains a bipartisan issue that can improve safety and community stability, while in many cases saving significant taxpayer money. Lawmakers, advocates, funders, and voters all have good reason to be encouraged, and no one should write off red states as having abandoned the issue.

Still, the familiar obstacles remain, including powerful lobbies, politicians, and pundits who fearmonger to score political points. The president continues to use the bully pulpit to rail against U.S. cities and advocate for policies like harsher bail laws and more capital punishment, while advancing his own false narrative that unchecked immigration enforcement and federal deployments are making the country safer. Already, states like Texas are planning to advance “tough” policies in 2027.

The present moment offers both peril and opportunity. Many states whose leaders are allied with the president will likely keep pursuing “tough-on-crime” policies that serve his agenda, and resisting such efforts will sap energy that could otherwise go toward progress. But slowly, the ground is shifting. Many states are channeling their opposition to the administration into action, and that energy can carry into criminal justice—for example, by turning public concern about federal law enforcement into renewed demand for police accountability. Voters are also increasingly noticing that crime is at record lows, and majorities already back a long list of reforms. The fear that drove the last six years of backlash is losing its hold. Lawmakers who champion reforms will be on solid ground.

The lesson of 2026 is one of persistence. Reform has not run its course; advocates this year have maintained a steady drumbeat of progress—some victories sweeping, some incremental but meaningful nonetheless—even amid a national turn toward a punitive politics of fear. Now, with the political winds shifting again, they are well positioned to seize the moment and accelerate the reform agenda in 2027 and beyond, in city halls, statehouses, and Congress.

title: San Antonio takes DHS, ICE to court over planned Eastside detention facility
authors: Diego Medel, Ken Rodriguez, TPR Staff

The city is asking a federal judge to prevent DHS and ICE from moving forward with development until the required environmental review is completed.

text:
San Antonio filed a federal lawsuit Tuesday seeking to halt development of a planned immigration detention facility on the East Side until federal authorities comply with environmental review requirements.

The lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement seeks to stop the conversion of a nearly 640,000-square-foot warehouse acquired by ICE in January on Southeast Loop 410 into an immigration detention and processing facility capable of holding up to 1,500 people.

City Attorney Andy Segovia announced the legal action Tuesday morning alongside Mayor Gina Ortiz Jones and several City Council members, marking the city’s most significant effort yet to challenge the proposed facility.

The lawsuit centers on the National Environmental Policy Act, or NEPA, which requires federal agencies to assess the potential environmental effects of major projects before proceeding. The city is asking a federal judge to prevent DHS and ICE from moving forward with development until the required environmental review is completed.

Segovia said those reviews go beyond assessing air and water quality to consider how a project could affect the surrounding community, including its economy, history and culture.

“With a facility of this size and scope, within the core urban core of San Antonio, these sorts of reviews are even more critical,” Segovia said. “It’s very clear to see that there will be these impacts, and the law is there to make sure that those impacts are mitigated.”

The lawsuit follows months of unsuccessful attempts by city officials to obtain information about the conversion, development plans and potential environmental impacts of the facility.

Since February, city officials have sent five letters to DHS and ICE seeking details about the proposed facility, including environmental reviews, permitting requirements and opportunities for public input.

Federal officials responded to one letter in June, promising to coordinate with the city, seek community feedback and share engineering and design reports before beginning work.

But Jones said the city has received none of that information, even as ICE awarded a $17.3 million contract to GardaWorld Federal Services, a contractor involved in Florida’s controversial “Alligator Alcatraz” detention facility, to renovate the warehouse.

“We have been very patient with the federal authorities, in particular DHS and ICE, on this issue,” Jones said. “San Antonio is done waiting.”

What could the lawsuit accomplish?

While the lawsuit may not permanently stop ICE from opening the facility, city leaders hope the environmental review process will create enough obstacles for federal authorities to reconsider the project altogether.

“So while the legal action is to delay, our hope is that looking at the significant impact that facility may have, that the department makes their independent decision based on that information they obtain to do something different,” Segovia said.

Segovia said he expects the preliminary environmental assessment of the warehouse’s conversion to find significant impacts, potentially triggering a more extensive environmental impact study that could take months to complete.

District 2 Councilman Jalen McKee-Rodriguez, who represents the district where the proposed facility is located, pointed to other cities where concerns raised by local governments have prompted federal authorities to reconsider or cancel plans for immigration detention centers altogether.

“It has become clear, DHS has no intention of doing its due diligence,” McKee-Rodriguez said.

He said a review of the proposed facility would likely identify problems with its proximity to schools, parks and community centers, as well as the infrastructure needed to accommodate up to 1,500 people.

Those concerns have already prompted additional scrutiny from City Council.

Last week, council members directed city departments and local utilities to conduct independent assessments of how the facility could affect water, wastewater, electricity and emergency services in the surrounding area.

The studies could provide additional information to support the city’s legal challenge. Similar concerns about local water and power capacity have reportedly led ICE to abandon plans to convert two warehouses into processing facilities in Pennsylvania.

While most City Council members have supported the legal challenge, council members Marc Whyte (D10) and Misty Spears (D9) have criticized it as an expensive effort that will do little more than delay the facility.

“This is political theater, nothing more than political theater that, unfortunately, my colleagues and the mayor want to engage in,” Whyte said in an interview following the announcement.

Whyte disputed the likelihood that the lawsuit would lead ICE to abandon the facility, arguing that similar legal challenges elsewhere have merely delayed federal projects.

“That is what I anticipate is going to happen here. Sure, the federal government could decide that they don’t want to be in San Antonio,” Whyte said. “But it’s not going to be because of this lawsuit.”

Spears questioned why the city was raising environmental concerns about the ICE facility when it had not raised similar objections to the city’s former Migrant Resource Center.

“The double standard is glaring,” Spears said. “Suing the federal government for enforcing our nation’s immigration laws is political theater at taxpayers’ expense.”

Whyte estimated the lawsuit could cost the city $500,000 or more, arguing that money would be better spent on public safety and infrastructure.

Segovia declined to provide an estimated cost for the suit Tuesday, saying the city had shared preliminary figures with council members but that the final expense would depend on the federal government’s response and how far the litigation proceeds.

Jones defended the decision to pursue legal action despite the potential cost, arguing that the community deserves answers about the facility and its possible long-term economic effects.

“To the point of wasted money, you tell me what is the price tag for respect?” she said. “You’ve got to respect this community. Our community deserves to understand what is happening at that facility.”

DHS and ICE did not respond to a request for comment at the time of publication.

text:
SILVER SPRING, Md. —HIAS denounces the outrageous new policy published today by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) that will make it easier for the Trump administration to terminate the legal status of people who were resettled through the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program (USRAP), and ultimately quickly remove them from the United States, potentially sending them right back into harm’s way. The new policy will reduce the number of days that someone has to challenge the effort to terminate their refugee status from 30 days to just 10 days, making it essentially impossible for someone to obtain legal counsel and state their case for why their refugee status should not be terminated. The new policy also reaffirms that US Citizenship and Immigration Service (USCIS) may place someone who was admitted as a refugee directly in removal proceedings, without a formal termination of refugee status. Together, these policies put vulnerable people at risk, and fundamentally alter the decades-old system established to protect people fleeing persecution.

“The release of this new policy marks a new low, in a parade of lows, in this administration’s ongoing effort to make permanent protection for refugees in this country a thing of the past,” said Naomi Steinberg, HIAS Vice President, Refugee, Immigration Policy and Advocacy. “First, the administration shuttered refugee admissions. Now, they are trying to upend the core principle that refugee resettlement represents permanent protection. If this policy is allowed to go into effect, America can no longer claim to be the place of refuge and hope that it once was.”

What makes this new policy particularly egregious is the people it will harm. Refugees who arrived through USRAP were vetted, approved, and welcomed into the United States with the promise that they finally found permanent safety.

“Stripping away the security promised to refugees, and with little to no procedural safeguards, shatters our promise to them and sends a devastating message to both refugees and their persecutors alike: that even the most lawful and carefully vetted path to protection in the United States can be arbitrarily revoked,” continued Steinberg.

The consequences of this policy could be immediate and devastating. Refugees who have already endured violence, persecution, and displacement will now be at greater risk of being sent to countries where they face significant harm, persecution, or torture. HIAS is deeply concerned for the safety of our clients and for resettled refugees throughout the country who do not yet have their green cards.

HIAS stands in solidarity with the many thousands of refugees that we have resettled, and will never stop advocating for the dignity, fairness, and humanity they deserve.

For press inquiries, please contact media@hias.org.

—

HIAS is a 145-year-old international Jewish humanitarian organization dedicated to transforming the lives of refugees, asylum seekers, and immigrants. With a sharpened focus, we deliver vital support through protection services, mental health care, economic empowerment, Jewish community engagement, and robust advocacy—defending the rights of all displaced people to rebuild their lives and creating a world of welcome, safety, and opportunity.

text:
SAN ANTONIO - The City of San Antonio filed a federal lawsuit Tuesday morning against the Department of Homeland Security, seeking to stop work on a proposed ICE detention facility on the East Side until federal environmental requirements are met.

City Attorney Andy Segovia said the lawsuit seeks to enforce the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), which requires federal agencies, including DHS, to conduct environmental reviews before moving forward with major projects.

The proposed facility would convert an existing warehouse measuring more than 640,000 square feet into an immigration detention center capable of holding up to 1,500 people.

Segovia said city officials have repeatedly attempted to obtain information about the project, sending five letters to federal authorities since February, with the most recent dated Sept. 9.

According to Segovia, DHS responded to one of those letters in June, assuring the city that federal officials would coordinate with local leaders, consider community input and share design and engineering reports before beginning work. However, Segovia said the city has received no further communication about those commitments since early summer.

The lawsuit asks a federal judge to invalidate the federal government's purchase of the property, cancel the contract to convert the warehouse into a detention center and halt work until DHS and ICE comply with NEPA requirements.

Segovia emphasized that the required environmental review goes beyond traditional concerns about air and water quality. It must also consider the project's potential socioeconomic effects on surrounding neighborhoods, including impacts on the area's appearance, history and cultural character.

City officials argue that federal coordination and a comprehensive environmental review are necessary to protect residents and ensure the potential consequences of the detention center are fully evaluated before the project moves forward.

Archbishop Gustavo García-Siller is voicing his support for the City of San Antonio's federal lawsuit challenging a proposed ICE detention facility on the East Side, raising concerns about public health, safety and the treatment of immigrants.

In a statement, the archbishop praised city leaders for taking legal action against the proposed conversion of a 640,000-square-foot warehouse into a detention center capable of holding up to 1,500 people. García-Siller also criticized the federal government's handling of the project and called for greater protections for immigrants and their families.

Here is his full statement:

I applaud the efforts of the City of San Antonio in taking legal action against the proposed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) processing facility on the city’s east side, as the federal government has refused to supply information and repeatedly ignored compliance with obtaining environmental assessments or receiving local permits.

The 640,000 square-foot warehouse could contain as many as 1,500 beds and has elicited concerns that it will negatively impact the city’s sewage and water systems, along with raising concerns for the impacts on the public health, safety, and the provision of emergency services.

The proposed facility has also elicited public protests in addition to this recent lawsuit.

As the city states in its civil complaint against the Department of Homeland Security and ICE, the warehouse was designed for the storage and transloading of commercial goods – not for any human residence.

“Defendants are purchasing warehouses nationwide to retrofit them into immigration detention and processing centers capable of holding tens of thousands of immigrants to facilitate ICE’s stated goal of running deportation operations ‘like [Amazon] Prime, but with human beings,” reads the city’s civil action.

“The thought of holding thousands of families in massive warehouses should challenge the conscience of every American,” said Bishop Brendan J. Cahill of Victoria, chairman of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops (USCCB) Committee on Migration. “Whatever their immigration status, these are human beings created in the image and likeness of God, and this is a moral inflection point for our country.”

At least eight facilities in Georgia, Maryland, Pennsylvania and three in Texas — including the building on the east side of San Antonio -- have already been acquired.

The “mega centers” would each be capable of detaining 7,000 to 10,000 people, with the estimated cost for the ICE’s “new detention center model” being $38.3 billion.

Bishop Cahill noted, “Aside from the internment camps used to incarcerate Japanese Americans in the 1940s, such facilities have no precedent in American history.”

“The federal government does not have a positive track record when it comes to detaining large numbers of people, especially families, and the proposed scale of these facilities is difficult to comprehend,” he said.

In their legal filing seeking relief from the courts, the city of San Antonio writes, “In their rush to convert warehouses into Amazon-life store-and-ship facilities for immigrants, Defendants have trampled over federal law designed to protect the city and other stakeholders’ interests.”

ICE detention centers have been cited for unsanitary conditions, lack of basic care, and instances of violence and death, as well as denial of pastoral visits and access to legal counsel. In just the past few months, two separate ICE facilities in Montana and Texas had measles outbreaks. Incidents such as these endanger public health and would require a response by city health officials.

American prelates have expressed alarm over reports of pregnant mothers not getting medical care they need while in immigration detention, tragically resulting in miscarriage in some cases, as well as reports of nursing mothers being separated from their babies when detained by ICE.

The Archdiocese of St. Louis recently filed a lawsuit against the federal government over a policy it said prohibits priests from distributing Communion and hearing confessions to ICE detainees. The lawsuit said a no-contact policy at a detention center ICE uses for migrants awaiting deportation proceedings has refused to accommodate clergy seeking to provide sacraments to migrants held there. In a statement, the archdiocese said it “steadfastly supports the right of all Catholics and the priests who serve them to practice their Catholic faith.”

In 2025, 32 people died while in ICE detention — the largest number in over two decades, according to a report by The Guardian.

The Church reaffirms the centrality of the understanding of human dignity, as the Incarnation itself “tells us who God is and where He chooses to dwell.” Christ unmistakably identifies Himself with the displaced in Matthew 25:35: “I was a stranger and you welcomed me.”

Earlier this year, I and other bishops of border states echoed comments from the USCCB that plans to convert warehouses into mass detention centers is “deeply troubling.” In our view, the use of detention should be minimized, not expanded, and alternatives to detention be pursued.

As the bishops and many across the country have advocated for decades, Congress should repair the U.S. immigration system by placing hard-working immigrants and their families on a path to citizenship and by improving access to the legal immigration system.

As always, we stand ready to work to create an immigration system which ensures public safety, protects human rights, encourages economic growth and justice, and upholds our heritage as a nation of immigrants.

I applaud and support the city’s initiative to ensure that proper procedures are being followed for the protection of all involved, especially our migrant brothers and sisters in Christ.

title: Unreported in FBI Hate Crimes Data: Immigrant Purges Leave Communities At Risk
description:
In August, the FBI released its 2025 Hate Crimes statistics, which showed a decrease in the overall number of reported hate crimes.
The true picture of hate crimes in America is hidden by this report in a number of ways: 1) Unreliable Data We know that the data in this report is historically unreliable.
Among the cities that did report hate crimes, we know that many additional crimes and incidents may yet be unreported because the police who responded did not classify them as hate crimes or chose not to share accurate data with the FBI.
Finally, many programs that have helped communities build resilience to hate crimes have been completely cut and abandoned.
If we want to see a true decrease in hate crimes, we must:
text:
Following the release of the FBI’s 2025 Hate Crimes Data, UnidosUS has joined Asian Americans Advancing Justice, Jewish Council for Public Affairs, Human Rights Campaign, Muslim Public Affairs Council, National Urban League and Sikh Coalition to warn that the data is incomplete and potentially misleading for failing to capture the way mass deportations, the normalization of extremism, cuts to vital programs and more have created unreliable data, increased threats, and less security for our communities.

In August, the FBI released its 2025 Hate Crimes statistics, which showed a decrease in the overall number of reported hate crimes. A decline from an historic peak, however, is not synonymous with safety. Instead of settling into complacency or believing the work is done, we, as organizations representing a range of religious, ethnic, and other vulnerable communities, are warning that the data released by the FBI is incomplete and fails to capture the real risks to our communities.

While any reported decrease in threats is welcome, these numbers remain historically high, especially compared to pre-pandemic totals. And, because of a number of deliberate policy choices being made by the current administration—particularly the increase in aggressive immigration enforcement, dramatic funding cuts, and continued extremist rhetoric— we are concerned that the reporting is becoming less reliable even as threats are increasing.

The true picture of hate crimes in America is hidden by this report in a number of ways:

1) Unreliable Data

We know that the data in this report is historically unreliable. Even according to the FBI’s own 2025 data, thousands of law enforcement agencies, serving populations that total approximately 17 million people, refused to report any hate crimes statistics at all.

Among the cities that did report hate crimes, we know that many additional crimes and incidents may yet be unreported because the police who responded did not classify them as hate crimes or chose not to share accurate data with the FBI. Grants and other programs that were created to help prevent hate crimes and report incidents have been abruptly terminated by the Trump Administration and Department of Justice, despite bipartisan support for such measures.

We also know that still other crimes were not reported at all by communities due to even greater mistrust and lack of confidence in law enforcement. The influx of violent, masked, and poorly trained immigration enforcement agents into our communities has created fear and confusion about the role and reliability of law enforcement more broadly. Community members are afraid to report crimes because they are afraid of retaliation, deportation (despite traditionally being eligible for a U-Visa as a victim or witness), or otherwise exposing their community to the public safety risk of violent and oppressive immigration enforcement.

2) Increasing Threats

Despite persistent underreporting, hate and violence continue to rise. While some communities did see a decrease, Sikh, Hindu, and Buddhist communities have documented increases in hate crimes, and the prevalence of anti-immigrant, Islamophobic anti-Arab, anti-Hispanic and Latino, anti-Black, anti-LGBTQ+, and antisemitic rhetoric and action are still creating new threats daily. Moreover, political leaders have normalized conspiracy theories and hateful rhetoric that were once relegated to the fringe, leaving all communities at risk. Hate speech online, which is known to lead to violence, is spreading unchecked. This includes large and growing platforms such as social media, video games, and streaming that shape the minds of so many.

From targeting houses of worship and congregants under the guise of protesting political differences, to the use of bigoted conspiracy theories like the debunked “Great Replacement” theory, to justify dehumanizing policies, extremism is on the rise—and without a reliable hate crimes report and comprehensive prevention programs, we will not be able to understand and respond to the reality of hate impacting all our communities.

3) Less Security

At a time of growing threats to communities, the Department of Justice’s Civil Rights Division has not only failed to prioritize our protection but has also ceased meaningful engagement with many of the organizations that represent those most frequently targeted by hate. In neglecting its core mission, the Division has redirected its resources toward interpretations of civil rights law that legitimize and risk emboldening actors who traffic in hate, exclusion, and intolerance. And in some cases, like of white supremacist violence or the numerous Black bodies found hanging from trees across the country, necessary hate crimes investigations have not even been initiated, while others have been granted pardons. The FBI has similarly pulled back from engagement with civil rights and community partners that have long served as trusted intermediaries for reporting hate crimes, identifying patterns of violence, and raising community concerns. At the same time, the Administration and the partisan majority in the 119th Congress have targeted leading anti-hate organizations, including groups that have historically monitored extremist activity and supported vulnerable communities.

At the same time, policies aimed at maximizing deportations have exacerbated these problems and left our communities at risk, as Department of Justice staff and FBI agents have been reassigned to focus on immigration enforcement. Finally, many programs that have helped communities build resilience to hate crimes have been completely cut and abandoned. In 2025, the DOJ moved to rescind or terminate $46 million in grant funding intended for hate crime prevention and response initiatives. Other programs, like the Nonprofit Security Grant Program, have been laden with mismanagement as well as new terms and conditions based on politics, not security, that make these grants less accessible to many of the communities that feel the greatest threat. As a result, communities facing rising threats are being left more vulnerable by the very institutions charged with protecting them. The erosion of education, federal partnerships, prevention programs, and civil rights enforcement has not merely reduced support, it has compounded the risks facing communities already targeted by hate and violence.

Recommendations

The FBI’s statistics do not exist in a vacuum. They are being released at a moment when community trust is being undermined by immigration enforcement policies, bigotry and violence as responses to political differences are being mainstreamed, anti-hate organizations are being targeted and sidelined, federal resources are being shifted away from preventing and responding to hate crimes, and critical programs that help vulnerable communities protect themselves are being curtailed.

Taken together, these actions weaken our nation’s ability to monitor hate, support victims, prevent violence, and keep communities safe. Policymakers should not mistake lower reported numbers for evidence of progress when many of the very mechanisms designed to confront hate are themselves being dismantled.

text:
SAN ANTONIO – UPDATE 10:30 A.M.: The City of San Antonio has filed a lawsuit over the immigration detention facility on the East Side.

In a news conference Tuesday, City Attorney Andy Segovia said the lawsuit was filed in federal court against the U.S. Department of Homeland Security Tuesday morning.

Watch the full press conference below:

A majority of the San Antonio City Council has been critical of the planned 1,500-person processing facility, which U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has said could open early next year.

Segovia said the suit is to ensure compliance by DHS with the requirements of the National Environmental Policy Act, NEPA.

Segovia said the city is requesting the federal court to do the following:

Vacate the purchase of the facility

Vacate the contract that they have issued to start the work in converting the warehouse into a detention facility

Halt all activity until DHS and ICE have fully complied with the requirements of NEPA

The city will also seek a temporary injunction to pause the project. If there are visible signs that work has started at the site, the city will request an emergency hearing to stop it.

“We have been very patient with the federal authorities, in particular DHS and ICE on this issue,” San Antonio Mayor Gina Ortiz Jones said. “This lawsuit today is directly related to the federal government, DHS, and ICE in particular, failing to uphold their obligations to the people of San Antonio.”

Last week, City Council voted 9-2 to ask the city-owned utilities, San Antonio Water System and CPS Energy, as well as certain city departments, to assess the potential impacts of the facility.

ICE bought the 640,000 square-foot warehouse off Loop 410 for $66.1 million earlier this year.

In late August, it awarded a $17.3 million contract to GardaWorld Federal Services LLC to renovate the East Side warehouse into a processing and detention facility and provide wraparound services to operate it.

Federal contract records show the contract has since grown to $61.8 million.

Segovia said the city wrote to DHS and ICE five times beginning in February, most recently on Sept. 9, seeking information about the project. The agencies responded once, in June, promising to coordinate with the city, accept community input and share design and engineering reports before any work began.

The city said it has not heard from them since early this summer.

In a statement sent to KSAT Tuesday morning, DHS said the lawsuit is not about the environment and accused the city of trying to stop President Donald Trump “making America safe again.”

“Let’s be honest about this. This isn’t about the environment. It’s about trying to stop President Trump from making America safe again. The left didn’t care about the mountains of litter that illegal aliens dumped on ranches and riverbeds during Biden’s border crisis. They’re feigning concern now because they want those same illegal aliens to stay forever—and vote here as well.

“From day one, DHS has remained singularly focused on removing the worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens from the United States and is always evaluating the best methods to do so. These heinous criminals, once arrested, should be removed at lightning speed, not housed on American soil at the taxpayer’s expense. DHS is moving swiftly to utilize EXISTING detention space with our state and county partners.”

DHS spokesperson

KSAT has also reached out to ICE and GardaWorld for comment.

text:
Published on October 13, 2026

SAN ANTONIO (October 13, 2026) – The City of San Antonio today filed legal action in federal court regarding the proposed federal immigration detention facility planned for San Antonio’s East Side. The City is asking the Department of Homeland Security to comply with the National Environment Policy Act (NEPA) by conducting an Environmental Review of the proposed ICE Detention Center in San Antonio before work is started on the current warehouse.

The City has raised concerns regarding compliance with federal law, including environmental reviews and other applicable requirements associated with the proposed facility and has sought additional information and coordination regarding its development and operation. Despite assurance from ICE that they would keep the City informed and coordinate efforts they have remained silent since June on compliance with the law and have reportedly signed an agreement with GardaWorld to have work started.

The NEPA requirement for an Environmental Assessment calls for more than just looking at impacts on air and water but also looking at the socio-economic impacts of the project. This is especially important given the location is within the urban core of San Antonio. The City is asking the court to enjoin DHS/ICE from proceeding with any development of the property until ICE complies with the required environmental assessment process.

“This action is focused on ensuring that applicable legal requirements are followed and that the community’s interests are protected,” said City Attorney Andy Segovia.

The lawsuit is specific to the proposed facility and the processes associated with its development and operation. It does not challenge the federal government’s authority to enforce federal immigration laws.

The City will continue to monitor developments related to the proposed facility and will provide additional information as appropriate as the case moves through the legal process.
