title: Attacks on Immigrants Threaten Access to Sexual and Reproductive Health Care
description:
They have also had profound negative impacts on the health of immigrants and their families, including on their sexual and reproductive health and well-being.
Everyone, regardless of immigration status or income, deserves access to comprehensive health care, including sexual and reproductive health services, and the ability to make decisions about their bodies and families.
Medicaid has been critical for people’s, including many immigrants’, access to contraceptive care and other reproductive health services.
While many immigrants do receive Medicaid coverage, certain groups of immigrants—including those who are undocumented—are ineligible for federal Medicaid coverage.
Policymakers should ensure access to comprehensive sexual and reproductive health care for all, regardless of immigration status.
text:
The Trump administration’s militant anti-immigrant agenda has wreaked havoc in the United States immigration system, exacerbating challenges that immigrants have faced for decades by imposing and escalating a set of policies designed to intimidate and persecute them. These policies have disrupted and endangered people’s lives and the consequences have been deadly. They have also had profound negative impacts on the health of immigrants and their families, including on their sexual and reproductive health and well-being. Particularly harmful policies and practices include targeting immigrants at hospitals and other health care facilities, detaining and mistreating pregnant and postpartum people in ICE custody, and accessing personal health data for the purpose of immigration enforcement, as well as new restrictions on access to publicly funded health insurance coverage and care, including abortion and contraception.

The punitive and broken immigration system in the United States has ruined many lives and forced many to live in fear and in the shadows for decades. It is administered by a complex and often unaccountable web of agencies housed within the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP). Rather than try to reform the system, the Trump administration has displayed open hostility to immigrant communities, aggressively profiling, detaining and deporting people without due process, often blatantly ignoring the rule of law and court orders, while holding immigrants in substandard facilities (including some outside the United States), where many have reported evidence of physical abuse, overcrowding and medical neglect. More than fifty people have died in immigration detention in the last 18 months. At the same time, the administration has, despite court challenges, terminated Temporary Protected Status protections for hundreds of thousands of people who fled to the United States from dangerous situations in Haiti, Venezuela, Syria, South Sudan and other countries.

As of June 2025, there were an estimated 51.9 million immigrants residing in the United States. These include naturalized citizens, lawful permanent residents and temporary lawful residents, as well as those who are “unauthorized” or “undocumented,” terms which can cover people living in the United States with a range of “impermanent, precarious statuses.” An analysis of 2023 Census data estimated that there were 14 million such unauthorized immigrants in the United States.* Millions of households contain people with various citizenship and immigration statuses, with one in four children in the United States having at least one immigrant parent.

While US immigration policies have long had negative effects on the health and well-being of immigrants and their families, the scale and intensity of the administration’s anti-immigrant campaign has imposed new restrictions on immigrants’ bodily autonomy and access to health care. These policies have overlapping and compounding effects in immigrants’ lives, reducing their access to a wide range of public services and spaces while often prompting them to delay or avoid visits to health care facilities. Everyone, regardless of immigration status or income, deserves access to comprehensive health care, including sexual and reproductive health services, and the ability to make decisions about their bodies and families.

This fact sheet details some of the Trump administration’s policies and attacks on immigrants and the impact that has on their reproductive health and well-being.

ICE Enforcement at Hospitals and Health Care Facilities

The threat of immigration enforcement at hospitals and other health care facilities has been shown to have a “chilling effect” on immigrants and their families accessing health care services out of fear for themselves or their family members being arrested and deported.

In January 2025, the Trump administration rescinded guidance that had limited immigration enforcement at “sensitive locations” such as hospitals, at or near schools, places of worship, and courthouses. Agents are now permitted to enter public spaces, such as waiting rooms and lobbies, with a judicial warrant.

Since then, there have been increased reports of ICE agents showing up to engage in enforcement activities and detain immigrants at or near hospitals and clinics across the country.

Nearly half (48%) of likely undocumented immigrant adults and 14% of immigrant adults overall say they or a family member have avoided seeking medical care since January 2025 due to immigration-related concerns.

Additionally, one in five pregnant women in an online survey reported that ICE activity has prevented them from seeking prenatal care.

Mistreatment of Pregnant, Postpartum and Nursing Immigrants in ICE Detention

Pregnant, postpartum and nursing immigrant women have suffered severe mistreatment and medical neglect while in detention facilities in violation of longstanding ICE guidelines. These conditions seriously jeopardize the health of parents and their children.

While medical mistreatment in detention facilities is not unique to pregnant people and has been a problem for decades, reporting has shown that the problem has intensified under the second Trump administration. Investigations reveal that since January 2025, pregnant women have experienced substandard care and medical neglect in detention, including being shackled while experiencing a miscarriage, being placed in solitary confinement, being denied prenatal care, being denied medical care while bleeding, and experiencing serious life-threatening pregnancy complications while in detention.

According to information from DHS in response to a Senate inquiry, 363 pregnant, postpartum and nursing immigrants were deported in the period between January 1, 2025 and February 16, 2026. DHS also reported that 16 miscarriages had occurred in its detention facilities in the first nine months of 2025, but have no information on miscarriages since October of that year.

Young pregnant immigrants are especially at risk. Since July 2025, ICE has been detaining all pregnant unaccompanied minors in a facility in South Texas, a shift from previous longstanding practice where they were placed in Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR) shelters or specifically designated foster homes. The Texas facility is several hours away from specialized obstetric care, aggravating health risks for these detainees, some of whom are as young as 13 and half of whom became pregnant as a result of rape. The Texas detentions also run counter to ORR rules, which say that priority placement for all pregnant youth should be in states without abortion bans and which prohibit federal officials from impeding pregnant unaccompanied minors’ access to abortion care.

Exacerbating Immigrants’ Barriers to Medicaid Coverage

Medicaid is one of the largest sources of health insurance coverage for people with low incomes and is provided via federal‒state partnerships. Medicaid has been critical for people’s, including many immigrants’, access to contraceptive care and other reproductive health services.

Medicaid eligibility rules are complicated for immigrants and often depend on policies in their state. While many immigrants do receive Medicaid coverage, certain groups of immigrants—including those who are undocumented—are ineligible for federal Medicaid coverage. Even those with qualified immigration status, such as individuals with green cards, are barred from accessing Medicaid for the first five years after their entry or status change. (This policy is known as the “five year bar.”) At the same time, some states have used their state funds to provide health care coverage for some or all undocumented immigrant residents.

HR 1, the so-called “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” signed into law in July 2025, enacted severe cuts to Medicaid and other federal health programs, many of which impacted immigrants. For example, the law now includes refugees and asylum seekers in the categories of immigrants denied Medicaid coverage, adding to the high numbers of non-citizens already excluded from coverage.

At the same time, the law is expected to limit many non-citizens’ access to marketplace plans under the Affordable Care Act (ACA). New, stricter eligibility limits on the subsidies that make coverage affordable will likely prevent as many as one million lawfully present immigrants from enrolling in marketplace plans, denying many low-income immigrants any pathway to affordable health coverage.

Additionally, HR 1 instituted strict work requirements for adults aged 19‒64 who are enrolled in Medicaid. Guttmacher Institute analysis projects that this policy could cause over 2 million women of reproductive age to lose Medicaid coverage, including many who are immigrants.

Losing insurance has been associated with decreases in the likely use of SRH care and access to person-centered care—evidenced by an increase in the likelihood of experiencing barriers to obtaining one's preferred method of contraception.

Barriers to Accessing Abortion

At least 1.9 million undocumented immigrant women live in states with total abortion bans or bans before 18 weeks gestation. There are 13 states with total abortion bans and seven additional states ban abortion at or before 18 weeks.

Millions more immigrants live in states with other medically unnecessary policies, including mandatory waiting periods and multiple required visits, all of which make abortion hard to access.

For noncitizens, the myriad of state laws restricting abortion are particularly challenging to navigate, especially alongside restrictive immigration policies. In states with abortion bans, many people seeking an abortion must travel to receive care, forcing them to cross state lines and potentially go through immigration checkpoints or airports. For those who are able to overcome the financial and logistical burdens of travel, these options place immigrants at increased risk of surveillance and detention. Yet others who choose to access abortion care via telehealth, online websites or community networks also face risks. The current context of abortion stigma and criminalization of pregnancy outcomes is compounded for immigrants who may have additional concerns about being tracked or surveilled in their online activity or in potential interactions with the health care or criminal justice systems.

Affordability is also a challenge that abortion patients, including immigrants, must overcome. Due to the Hyde Amendment and related coverage restrictions, individuals who are insured through federally funded health care programs, like Medicaid, Medicare and CHIP, and those in federal detention—including immigration detention—are restricted from accessing abortion except in cases of life endangerment, rape or incest. While 21 states use state funds to cover abortion care through Medicaid, the Hyde Amendment disproportionately impacts people already facing systemic barriers to health care, including Black and Brown, indigenous and immigrant communities, and people with low incomes.

Medicaid Sharing Data with ICE

Serious data privacy concerns have emerged for many individuals enrolled in Medicaid, who did so believing that their information would not be shared for immigration enforcement purposes.

In 2025, it was reported that the Trump administration had started sharing with ICE the personal and health data of noncitizen Medicaid enrollees in several states. Subsequently, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) and ICE established an “information exchange agreement,” reversing earlier policies in which CMS had committed to not sharing health coverage eligibility information for the purposes of immigration enforcement. Despite several states securing a preliminary injunction that blocked such data sharing in those states, CMS proceeded to share their residents’ health data with ICE.

ICE’s new ability to access Medicaid records has created a further chilling effect on health care access for immigrant families, including those who may be citizens or have protected status but live in mixed status households.

In California, for example, where state funds help provide health coverage for immigrants of any status, many immigrants have disenrolled from the state’s Medicaid program due to fears that their personal information is being shared with ICE.

Public Charge Rule Chilling Access to Care

Public charge is a concept that has been in US law for decades and which asserts that some people can be denied admission into the country through a visa or denied legal permanent resident status, also known as a green card, if they will likely depend primarily on government support now or in the future.

In September 2026, a new public charge rule went into effect that expands and distorts the definition of public charge. It gives DHS more discretion to deny status based on any use of income-based public services by an immigrant or their family members. While this expansion now allows programs such as Medicaid and Title X family planning services to be considered federal benefits, the new rule also makes the policy more ambiguous and gives more power to the US Citizenship and Immigration Service, leaving the interpretation of public charge to the discretion of individual officers in each case.

The ambiguity of this new rule—especially when considered alongside immigration enforcement at hospitals and the sharing of insurance information with ICE—will likely have additional chilling effects on health care access by immigrants. For example, some families with US citizen children may fear using the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) if other family members are still seeking authorized status, and studies suggest some citizens with undocumented family members are already forgoing health screenings and checkups for fear of retaliation.

In addition to reducing health care access, the new rule could also aggravate patterns of immigrants forgoing other social services such as childcare, housing, and food support, losses which can impact the long-term health and well-being of families and communities.

Attacks on Title X and Defunding Family Planning Programs and Clinics

Publicly supported family planning clinics serve as the primary entry point to the health care system for many people, including immigrants, and are sometimes one of the only ways that people can access sexual and reproductive health care.

Title X is the nation’s only federal program dedicated to providing people with low incomes, particularly those who are under- or uninsured, with access to comprehensive family planning and contraceptive services, as well as to preventative health care such as screenings for sexually transmitted infections and cancer. This program serves many immigrants, including those with undocumented status. (Federal law does not disqualify such immigrants, although eligibility may vary by state and clinic.)

In July 2025, the Department of Health and Human Services issued a notice that dramatically expanded the number of federal programs, including Title X, that are deemed inaccessible to certain segments of the immigrant population. While under litigation and not yet in effect, this new policy threatens to push reproductive health services and other supports even further out of reach for immigrants and others who need them most.

For several months in 2025, the Trump administration froze millions of dollars designated for some Title X program providers. These funds had still not been released by July, when HR 1 included a provision defunding some family planning clinics, including Planned Parenthood health centers, by denying them federal Medicaid reimbursement for one year. (That provision expired July 2026.) Attacks like these, in concert with changes to the public charge rule, make affordable contraceptive care and related services less available, thereby undermining health equity and exacerbating health risks for immigrant communities.

Congress Must Act to End the Assault on Immigrants’ Access to Care

Policymakers at all levels of government have a responsibility to do all they can to support immigrants in their communities. Ideally, this would include proactive work to pass policies that ensure their legal protection and access to health care, including addressing practical challenges many immigrants face, such as language barriers, limited access to culturally responsive care, and overly complex systems of applying for and accessing services. It is equally important that policymakers hold the administration and anti-immigrant lawmakers accountable for defying existing laws and policies that provide people due process and civil rights.

Congress especially has a strong role to play. Unfortunately, in 2026, they passed legislation along party lines to massively fund ICE and the CBP for the next three years. As 80 gender justice organizations (including Guttmacher) wrote in an open letter earlier this year, Congress should halt funds to those agencies “until enforceable restrictions conditioned on compliance with civil rights, medical standards and due process are in place.” Not only must Congress take measures to ensure that ICE and CBP stop abuse on the ground, it needs to restore limits on immigration enforcement in sensitive locations, including health care settings, protect health care data and insurance coverage information from immigration authorities, and end the mistreatment and detention of pregnant, postpartum and nursing people.

Congress should also pass the HEAL For Immigrant Families Act which would remove discriminatory legal barriers to health coverage that were imposed in federal law thirty years ago and would help to ensure that immigrants can receive reproductive health care services. The bill would restore eligibility for full-benefit Medicaid and the Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) to all lawfully present immigrants who are otherwise eligible, eliminate the long-standing “five-year bar” that delays lawful permanent residents from accessing Medicaid and Medicare benefits, and end the exclusion of undocumented immigrants from the Affordable Care Act's health insurance exchanges. Congress should also pass the Lifting Immigrant Families Through Benefits Access Restoration (Lift the Bar) Act, which would restore access to federal public benefits for lawfully present immigrants and similarly remove the five-year bar to programs such as Medicaid and the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP).

While a better and more just immigration system requires an end to the abuse and terror that immigrant families are experiencing, it also requires a proactive approach that guarantees full respect for people’s human rights and supports access to services that meet people’s basic needs. Policymakers should ensure access to comprehensive sexual and reproductive health care for all, regardless of immigration status.

text:
A Chicago man who has been a U.S. citizen for 15 years could lose his citizenship after the Justice Department accused him of concealing an abandoned green card, a previous identity, and an immigration exclusion order dating back more than three decades.

Federal prosecutors filed a civil lawsuit against Emmanuel Tayo Akinkunmi on October 7, 2026, seeking to revoke the citizenship he obtained in June 2011. The government alleges that the Nigerian-born man concealed his immigration history to secure a second green card and later become a naturalized American.

The dispute traces back to 1993, when Akinkunmi allegedly abandoned his lawful permanent resident status under the name Ezekiel Aremu Adetayo. According to the government's allegations, he later became subject to an immigration exclusion order, which the Board of Immigration Appeals upheld in 1997.

Despite that ruling, Akinkunmi allegedly obtained another green card in 2000 under his current name. Prosecutors claim he concealed his earlier identity and denied having been subject to exclusion proceedings, allowing him to obtain permanent residency without officials knowing his full immigration history.

He applied for U.S. citizenship in 2010 and allegedly repeated those denials, failing to disclose the previous identity and exclusion order. Immigration authorities approved his application, and he took the Oath of Allegiance on June 8, 2011.

More than 15 years later, prosecutors are seeking to undo that naturalization, arguing that the information Akinkunmi withheld would have affected his eligibility to become an American citizen.

Under the Immigration and Nationality Act, the government can seek to revoke citizenship obtained unlawfully or through the deliberate concealment of material facts. Although abandoning a green card does not itself justify denaturalization, prosecutors contend that Akinkunmi's alleged misrepresentations allowed him to obtain permanent residency and citizenship without meeting the legal requirements.

The government must prove its allegations in federal court through clear, unequivocal and convincing evidence, a demanding standard that applies to civil denaturalization cases. Akinkunmi remains a U.S. citizen while the lawsuit proceeds unless a court orders otherwise.

His case comes amid an expansion of denaturalization proceedings under the Trump administration. On October 5, the Justice Department announced that it had filed 40 lawsuits seeking to revoke naturalized citizenship between August 21 and October 2. The filings involve allegations of concealed criminal histories, false identities, and other misrepresentations, as federal prosecutors revisit citizenship applications approved years or decades earlier.

In its 2017 decision in Maslenjak v. United States, the Supreme Court held that an unlawful act must have contributed to obtaining citizenship to support a criminal conviction for unlawful naturalization. Akinkunmi's lawsuit is a civil action governed by separate legal standards.

The Justice Department is seeking a court order revoking his naturalization and canceling his certificate of citizenship. If prosecutors succeed, he could face separate immigration proceedings and possible removal from the United States.

text:
Supreme Court Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Neil Gorsuch joined forces to highlight what they called an “absurd” criminal case, in the latest pairing of the Obama and Trump appointees on what they have both seen as government abuses — even when their colleagues have stayed silent.

The most recent example came Tuesday in the case of Jesus Herrera-Salazar. Like most people who petition the justices to review their cases, he was rejected on the court’s latest order list. But Sotomayor nonetheless felt the need to speak out about the “constitutional absurdity that occurred” in his case, and Gorsuch joined her.

Herrera-Salazar was charged with being “found in” the United States following his removal. After he pleaded guilty and served prison time, he was ordered not to leave the Eastern District of Oklahoma while on supervised release. But he was then pulled over in a traffic stop and charged with the same crime again. He was convicted by a jury and sentenced to new terms of imprisonment and supervised release.

“Because I hope the facts of this case are anomalous and because Herrera-Salazar has since been removed from the United States, I concur in the Court’s decision not to grant review in this case,” Sotomayor wrote, joined by Gorsuch, in the statement that appeared on the court’s order list announcing the latest action on pending petitions.

But she explained that she wrote “to underscore the serious constitutional problems that plague the Government’s treatment of Herrera-Salazar.”

More articles

She called his second prosecution “difficult to square” with the Constitution’s double jeopardy protections, while noting that a federal appeals court disagreed with her. But under the appeals court’s rationale, the justice observed, “a person in Herrera-Salazar’s shoes can be subjected to repeated, limitless ‘found in’ charges without offending the Constitution.”

By that logic, she went on, the government could have charged him with a new crime “for each day that he was ‘found in’ prison while serving his sentence for the first conviction.” Though that seems “absurd,” Sotomayor wrote, she said it’s a “logical outgrowth” of the government’s position.

Joined by Gorsuch, the justice concluded that, if a situation like this arises again, courts should “avoid the constitutional absurdity that occurred here and give the Double Jeopardy Clause its full weight and meaning.”

The statement marks the second week in a row that Sotomayor has spoken out on the order list as the justices start their new term. On the first day of the term last week, she issued a solo statement in a death penalty case that she similarly thought warranted spotlighting even if it didn’t warrant Supreme Court review.

text:
Rep. Delia Ramirez is expected to introduce a bill to abolish the Department of Homeland Security and eliminate all immigrant detention in the United States on Tuesday, the Illinois Democrat shared exclusively with The Intercept.

The Reimagining Safety Act would repeal “duplicative and overreaching terrorism laws,” according to the bill summary and text, and curtail the widespread surveillance state that emerged in the wake of 9/11 terror attacks.

It comes the day after agents from Homeland Security Investigations searched the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., in what the Department of Justice has described as an opaque “federal criminal investigation.” HSI is a component of Immigrations and Customs Enforcement, the agency at the center of mounting concerns about the violent weaponization of DHS against immigrants and the Trump administration’s perceived political enemies.

The sweeping legislation faces long odds in Congress, but Ramirez argues that strictly limiting the government’s immigration enforcement apparatus is critical for public safety in the wake of yet another shooting by federal immigration agents.

Last Thursday, an ICE agent shot 28-year-old Oscar Belgal in the neck by firing into his car, where Belgal’s 5-year-old child was in the backseat, in New York City. Belgal was the latest of at least 25 people shot by federal immigration agents in the past year; six of those shootings were fatal. Deaths in detention are also surging under Trump. As of early October, at least 28 people have reportedly died in ICE custody this year, according to the National Immigration Project.

“Just this week, our communities were reminded that DHS is a weapon: pointed at a father shot in front of his 5-year-old and at Congresswoman Omar, who is using her voice to demand an end to fascism,” wrote Ramirez in a statement to The Intercept. “It is clear that now is the time to reimagine our safety, dismantle DHS, abolish ICE, and end the use of broad authorities to circumvent our rights and due process.”

Ramirez’s bill seeks to replace DHS with a new agency called the Department of Community Safety, which would oversee the Federal Emergency Management Agency. The new department would also fund new public safety measures like providing support to community violence intervention programs and public health-backed approaches to gun violence. And it would implement a new program where social workers, medical professionals, and interpreters aid asylum-seekers who arrive at the border.

Other DHS functions would be transferred to existing agencies. The DOJ would take over immigration enforcement authority; the Department of Transportation would assume the functions of the Transportation Security Administration and the Coast Guard; and the Department of the Treasury would conduct customs enforcement.

The Department of Homeland Security has only existed since George W. Bush established it in 2003, ushering in a new era of broad federal surveillance and policing powers that the new legislation now seeks to roll back.

For example, the bill would prevent the federal government from placing people on the “no-fly list” without a criminal conviction or warrant. Civil liberties advocates have frequently criticized the database that restricts people from air travel, arguing it’s arbitrary, secretive, and racially biased.

The legislation would also terminate the ability of the secretary of state to declare “foreign terrorist” organizations, arguing that the arbitrary list has been weaponized against protesters and civil liberties groups.

In 2025, Trump’s State Department attempted to revoke the visas of several students who had protested or spoken out against Palestine under the guise that their support for Palestinians amounted to “material support” for Hamas, making them immediately deportable. The Treasury Department, meanwhile, in August sanctioned Palestine Action, a U.K.-based group that opposes Israel’s genocide in Gaza, as a foreign terrorist organization, allowing the federal government to freeze all the group’s U.S. assets, impose travel restrictions, and ban U.S. companies from conducting business with the organization.

The raid on Omar’s home, Ramirez said, is just the latest example to underscore how the Trump administration has weaponized DHS in particular. President Donald Trump and his allies have routinely and without evidence accused Omar, who became a U.S. citizen in 2000, of immigration fraud and threatened to deport her back to Somalia.

In a statement to The Intercept, Omar spokesperson Jackie Rogers called the raid “an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies.”

Ramirez said the search was an example of DHS “acting as designed.”

“DHS is not rogue,” wrote the congresswoman. “For 23 years, since its inception, DHS has been utilized by the government to target and persecute those they consider the public enemy — whether it is Muslim-Americans, Haitians escaping violence, Latinos yearning for a better life, or dissenting voices demanding an end to the genocide in Palestine and the kidnapping of our neighbors.”

Congress is currently in recess until after the November elections to give members a chance to campaign, which means the bill won’t get a vote until November 9 at the earliest. The legislation is highly unlikely to pass this session. Republicans maintain the majority, and only a handful of Democratic members have called for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Still fewer have called for abolishing the Department of Homeland Security.

But Ramirez said she hopes this bill shows what is legislatively possible if lawmakers want to unravel the surveillance and carceral state that has arisen in the last two decades.

“Every person dead in detention, everyone shot or killed by ICE and CBP, every neighbor deported to a third country, every family separated, every community FEMA failed,” wrote Ramirez, “every miscarriage due to substandard care, every dissenter wrongfully branded, targeted, and persecuted as ‘terrorist,’ and every threat against our elections by Trump, Markwayne [Mullin], and [Stephen] Miller is a reason DHS must be dismantled and something new must take its place.”

text:
United States federal agents have searched the Washington, DC home of Democratic Congresswoman Ilhan Omar, a Muslim and a prominent critic of President Donald Trump, as part of an investigation that one source said was linked to alleged immigration fraud.

The predawn raid on Monday came three weeks before the US midterm elections on November 3, in which Omar is seeking a fifth term representing Minnesota’s 5th congressional district.

Recommended Stories

list of 3 items

list 1 of 3US Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home searched by immigration agents

list 2 of 3Trump insists energy ceasefire holds as Ukraine reports new Russian strikes

list 3 of 3Despite long history with Netanyahu, Trump hedges as Israel vote nears

end of list

Omar called the raid an attempt to “weaponise federal law enforcement”, while top Democrats said the timing raised “serious questions”.

So why has the search caused such alarm? Here’s what we know:

What happened?

Agents from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), part of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), executed what the US Department of Justice called a “judicially authorised search warrant”.

The department said only that it was part of “an ongoing federal investigation”.

The street around Omar’s home was blocked off on Monday morning, and agents were seen removing boxes labelled “Seized Property Evidence”.

Hours later, Trump told reporters he had “nothing to do” with the search, saying it was “really up to the DOJ [Justice Department]”.

What is Omar under investigation for?

Officially, it is unclear.

However, a person described as familiar with the investigation told the Reuters news agency that it relates to alleged immigration fraud, and that part of it concerns paperwork filled out by Omar’s late father when she was a child.

Omar fled Somalia’s civil war with her family when she was aged eight.

According to her House biography, the family spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya before moving to the United States in the 1990s. She became a citizen in 2000.

Conservative websites have for years alleged that she “married her brother” to commit immigration fraud, claims Omar has dismissed as “disgusting lies”.

US Vice President JD Vance said in March, without offering evidence, that the administration believed Omar “definitely committed immigration fraud”. Her office called the claim fabricated and defamatory.

Last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told conservative podcaster Benny Johnson that “something’s going to happen” in the case.

“If we can prove that you shouldn’t have been here in the first place, we’ll deport you,” he said.

Why is the raid’s timing controversial?

Justice Department policy usually avoids taking any action whose timing would appear to affect an election or benefit a candidate or party. In practice, therefore, the department has historically avoided overt investigative steps against candidates within about 60 days of a vote.

Randall Eliason, a law professor at George Washington University and former federal public corruption prosecutor, said the raid appeared to break with that practice, though there is no way to enforce the policy.

“The idea is to avoid even the appearance of any kind of interference by the Department of Justice with the political process,” he said.

The norm’s most famous test came in 2016. On October 28, 11 days before the presidential election, then-FBI Director James Comey told Congress that the bureau was examining newly discovered emails linked to its investigation into Hillary Clinton’s private email server.

Clinton has blamed this, in part, for her defeat. A 2018 review by the Justice Department’s inspector general found Comey’s conduct “extraordinary and insubordinate”.

Electorally, little appears to hang on the outcome. Omar represents a very safe Democratic seat covering Minneapolis, which she won in 2024 by 50 percentage points.

On November 3, she faces Republican Dalia al-Aqidi, an Iraq-born former journalist who has called Omar “pro-Hamas”, in a rematch of the 2024 race.

The search fits a wider pattern, however. During Trump’s second term, the Justice Department has charged several of his perceived political enemies, including Comey himself, New York Attorney General Letitia James and former National Security Adviser John Bolton.

What has Omar said?

She claims she is being targeted as one of Trump’s “political enemies”.

“For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns,” she wrote on X. “This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced.”

Omar has previously described Trump’s focus on her as an “unhealthy and creepy obsession”, and says she and her family have received death threats that she blames on his rhetoric.

In early December last year, Trump took aim at the Somali community in Minnesota and called Somali immigrants “garbage“. “We’re going to go the wrong way if we keep taking in garbage into our country. Ilhan Omar is garbage. She’s garbage. Her friends are garbage.”

In January, a man sprayed her with vinegar at a town hall in Minneapolis. Anthony James Kazmierczak, who admitted attacking her because he disagreed with her progressive views, was sentenced last month to 14 months in prison.

Trump, meanwhile, returned to Omar’s origins at a rally in Youngstown, Ohio, on Monday this week.

“She comes from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet,” he said, as the crowd chanted: “Deport.”

What are Democrats and other critics saying?

That the raid on Omar’s home is an abuse of power.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, joined by Representatives Katherine Clark and Pete Aguilar, called the raid “deeply disturbing”.

Trump’s “mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family”, they said, promising to “deliver full accountability”.

Minnesota Governor Tim Walz said Trump was “abusing his power to go after political opponents weeks before an election”.

Few Republicans have commented publicly. One who did, Representative Nancy Mace, wrote that if fraud was proven, Omar “should be denaturalised and removed from this country”.

Questions have also been raised about internal checks. A person familiar with the investigation told Reuters the department consulted its Public Integrity Section, which has historically approved investigations of members of Congress, before the search.

The Trump administration has cut the Public Integrity Section to about two lawyers as part of the sweeping government cuts he introduced after taking office in January 2025. Before that, the unit had 35 to 40 full-time lawyers.

text:
U.S. authorities conducted a predawn raid on Monday on the Washington, D.C., home of Democratic U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, an outspoken critic of Donald Trump who has been the target of political insults by the Republican president, as part of an ongoing investigation, the Justice Department said.

A person familiar with the investigation said it is related to alleged immigration fraud, and part of the probe concerns the Somali-born lawmaker’s immigration paperwork filled out by her late father when she was a child.

Omar wrote on social media that the U.S. government is being weaponized to target a political enemy of the president.

“For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns,” Omar said. “This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced.”

Other Democrats accused Trump and his administration of abuse of power. Omar, 44, is seeking a fifth two-year term in the U.S. House of Representatives in the midterm elections on Nov. 3.

Campaigning in Youngstown, Ohio, Trump quickly turned to Omar, who was born in Somalia and became a U.S. citizen in 2000, settling in Minnesota, home to a large community of Somalis.

“She comes from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet,” Trump said. “What a mess they have done — Somalia.”

The crowd chanted: “Deport, deport.”

He urged supporters to vote Republican “if ⁠you want to stop Ohio from being plundered, ransacked and destroyed like Minnesota’s being destroyed.”

In announcing the raid, a Justice Department spokesperson said: “Today in the Washington, DC area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice. This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation.”

Homeland Security Investigations is part of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE.

Trump administration border czar Tom Homan told Fox Business Network that the Justice Department is leading the investigation with the Department of Homeland Security. Homan declined to address the specifics of an ongoing criminal investigation.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, a Trump appointee, said last month that “something’s gonna happen” in the investigation into Omar’s family’s entry into the United States.

“If we can prove that you shouldn’t have been here in the first place, we’ll deport you,” Mullin told conservative podcaster Benny Johnson at the time.

Monday’s raid occurred a little more than three weeks before the midterms, with Trump’s party seeking to retain control of Congress. Omar, a prominent progressive, represents a safe Democratic district. She won reelection in 2024 by a margin of 50 percentage points.

In a statement, U.S. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries and other members of the party’s leadership in the chamber said the raid was “deeply disturbing and raises serious questions” about the weaponization of the federal government against Trump’s enemies.

Republicans have “relentlessly targeted” Omar, said Jeffries, joined by Reps. Katherine Clark and Pete Aguilar. Trump’s “mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family,” they added, and they vowed to “deliver full accountability” for a “rogue abuse of power.”

Minnesota Democrats also condemned the raid.

“Americans see this for what it is,” Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz wrote on social media. “President Trump is abusing his power to go after political opponents weeks before an election.”

Few Republican lawmakers publicly commented. One who did, Representative Nancy Mace, wrote online: “If the fraud is proven, she should be denaturalized and removed from this country. NO ONE is above the law.”

Justice Department policy bars federal prosecutors and agents from timing any action to affect an election’s outcome or benefit a candidate or party. It historically has avoided taking investigative steps against political candidates within about 60 days of an election.

George Washington University law professor Randall Eliason, a former U.S. public corruption prosecutor, said the raid appears to be a break with past Justice Department practice of avoiding investigative steps likely to become public close to Election Day. But Eliason noted there is no way of enforcing the policy.

“The idea is to avoid even the appearance of any kind of interference by the Department of Justice with the political process,” Eliason said. “It’s not surprising that they wouldn’t really care about violating this policy because they’ve shown they don’t really care about politicizing the Justice Department in many other ways.”

A person familiar with the investigation said the Justice Department consulted with its Public Integrity Section, a unit that has historically advised and approved investigations of members of Congress, and acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter prior to the search. The Trump administration has reduced the Public Integrity Section to about two lawyers and curtailed much of its authority.

The Justice Department during Trump’s second term in office has investigated and brought charges against a range of Trump’s perceived political enemies.

It has charged former FBI Director James Comey, New York state Attorney General Letitia James and Trump’s former national security adviser turned critic John Bolton. It also has investigated Democratic lawmakers who urged the U.S. military not to follow illegal orders, Democratic Senator Adam Schiff and Federal Reserve officials Jerome Powell and Lisa Cook.

The case against James and one of two brought against Comey were thrown out by a federal judge. Bolton pleaded guilty and is scheduled to be sentenced this month. Grand juries and federal judges have stymied several other probes.

Omar has faced political insults from Trump, who has cast the Somali American community as a threat to Minnesota in a burst of anti-Somali and anti-Muslim rhetoric. Omar has called Trump’s focus on her an “unhealthy and creepy obsession.”

Civil rights advocates have criticized Trump’s rhetoric toward minorities and immigrants, including when he previously called Somalis “garbage.”

Trump in February said Omar and Democratic Rep. Rashida Tlaib, who also is Muslim, should be “institutionalized” and sent back to “where they came from.” Both lawmakers criticized Trump during his State of the Union address as he touted his administration’s immigration crackdown and enforcement actions.

Omar has said she and her family have faced death threats, which she attributes to “hateful political rhetoric,” especially from Trump.

Last month, a Minnesota man who squirted vinegar on Omar was sentenced to 14 months in prison after pleading guilty to assaulting a federal official. Anthony James Kazmierczak admitted to attacking Omar because he disagreed with her progressive views.

text:
Washington — The Supreme Court on Tuesday agreed to take up a dispute involving a government watchdog group's attempt to get information from the Department of Government Efficiency as part of a fight over whether the controversial cost-cutting entity is subject to public records law.

Arguments in the case, U.S. DOGE Service v. U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, will likely take place in early 2027, with a decision coming by that summer. The Trump administration has attempted to prevent the group, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, from getting information about DOGE, which spearheaded government-wide firings of federal workers and cancellations of government contracts.

The case arose out of a Freedom of Information Act request CREW filed in early 2025 for information about DOGE, including its organizational chart and financial disclosures.

But the Trump administration declined to process the request, arguing that DOGE is not subject to FOIA because it is housed within the Executive Office of the President and is a purely advisory entity. As a result, CREW sued and sought a court order declaring that DOGE is covered by FOIA and requiring the task force to respond to the records request.

A judge went on to allow the group to collect limited information about DOGE's structure and the scope of its authority, and to conduct a deposition with its administrator, Amy Gleason, to better address the question of whether it is an advisory panel that falls outside FOIA's scope or is an agency subject to the law.

The Trump administration attempted to stop the discovery process, and as part of that effort, went on to file an emergency appeal with the Supreme Court.

In a 6-3 decision, the Supreme Court set aside the lower court order that required DOGE to turn over information about its work. The high court took issue with some of the material DOGE had to provide to CREW, which "require[s] the Government to disclose the content of intra-Executive Branch USDS recommendations and whether those recommendations were followed."

"Separation of powers concerns counsel judicial deference and restraint in the context of discovery regarding internal executive branch communications," the Supreme Court said.

The high court sent the case back to the lower courts for more proceedings and ordered the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit to take "appropriate action to narrow" the district court's discovery order.

When the case returned to the lower courts, CREW withdrew its request for some categories of records and sought only information on DOGE's structure, its directives to cancel federal contracts and fire government workers, and examples of DOGE exercising substantial independent authority, like by gaining access to sensitive systems.

The D.C. Circuit then allowed that information-gathering to proceed, finding that CREW had narrowed its request for information in a way that was consistent with the Supreme Court's order.

The Trump administration appealed to the high court, arguing that if allowed, CREW would receive much of the information it sought in its FOIA requests before a court has said whether DOGE is even covered by the law.

"The decision below intrudes into the autonomy and confidentiality of presidential advisors and augurs time-consuming and burdensome discovery litigation, including through a deposition of USDS Administrator Amy Gleason," Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote in a filing. "Beyond this case, the court of appeals' FOIA ruling threatens to burden future presidential administrations with FOIA suits designed to leverage discovery against advisors in the Executive Office."

President Trump announced DOGE's creation soon after he began his second term as part of his plans to slash the size of the federal government. Led by billionaire Elon Musk and housed within the Executive Office of the President, the task force deployed team members to agencies across the executive branch. DOGE was behind efforts to shrink the federal workforce and cut contracts worth billions of dollars, as well as to shutter agencies like the U.S. Institute of Peace and U.S. Agency for International Development.

But the agency sparked concerns with its attempts to gain access to sensitive databases kept by the Internal Revenue Service, Social Security Administration and Office of Personnel Management.

Musk, who was working as a "special government employee," left DOGE in May 2025.

The Supreme Court on Tuesday added three new cases to its oral argument docket for the 2026-27 term, agreeing to decide, among other things, what kinds of orders trial courts can issue in disputes over access to government information and whether working as a cook in a camp run by violent separatists qualifies as providing “material support” for terrorism under federal immigration law.

President Donald Trump created the U.S. Department of Government Efficiency, also known as DOGE, in January 2025 to advance his agenda by “modernizing Federal technology and software to maximize governmental efficiency and productivity.” Although it is not a cabinet-level department, DOGE was widely involved in Trump’s efforts to reduce the size of the federal government.

The dispute now before the court, U.S. Doge Service v. U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, began after a government watchdog group, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, filed a request under the Freedom of Information Act for (among other things) communications between the DOGE administrator, Amy Gleason, and DOGE staff, as well as financial disclosures submitted by DOGE personnel.

CREW went to federal court in Washington last year, asking DOGE to disclose documents that it said it wanted before Congress passed a bill to fund the federal government.

CREW also sought to fast-track discovery – the process of exchanging information in litigation – to determine whether DOGE is a federal “agency” that must comply with FOIA. It asked for a list of current and former DOGE employees, a list of employees and positions for which DOGE had recommended termination, a list of government contracts and grants that DOGE had recommended be canceled, and the opportunity to depose Gleason.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper granted most of CREW’s discovery requests, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit turned down DOGE’s plea to pause that order.

U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer then came to the Supreme Court in May 2025, asking the justices to intervene. He told the justices that the discovery required under Cooper’s order “offends the separation of powers by compromising the ‘necessity’ for confidentiality that allows presidential advisors to provide ‘candid, objective’ advice and communication.”

In a two-page, unsigned order in early June 2025, the court – over the objections of Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan, and Ketanji Brown Jackson – sent the dispute back to the D.C. Circuit for another look. The majority wrote that the portions of Cooper’s discovery order that required the government to disclose the content of DOGE’s recommendations within the executive branch, as well as whether those recommendations were followed, were too broad. Moreover, it added, concerns about the separation of powers between the branches of government “counsel judicial deference and restraint in the context of discovery regarding internal Executive Branch communications.” The court put Cooper’s discovery orders on hold while the litigation continued.

When the case returned to the lower courts, CREW modified its discovery requests so that it no longer sought information about “recommendations” made by U.S. DOGE employees. The lower courts then declined to block CREW’s requests.

DOGE came to the Supreme Court in March, asking the justices to weigh in. Sauer told the court that the D.C. Circuit “has continued to approve intrusive discovery against a presidential advisory body without adequate consideration for the separation of powers, the FOIA statute, and” the Supreme Court’s order last year on the interim docket. Among other things, he argued, that order “required the courts below to reassess all remaining discovery—not just requests for USDS recommendations—with the ‘deference and restraint’ applicable to presidential advisors under Cheney v. U.S. District Court,” a 2004 case in which the justices held that when considering requests for information directed at the vice-president and other senior executive branch officials, “special considerations” should “control when the Executive Branch’s interests in maintaining the autonomy of its office and safeguarding the confidentiality of its communications are implicated.”

CREW urged the justices to deny review. It argued that in formulating the new discovery order, the D.C. Circuit had “followed this Court’s instructions” in its earlier ruling on the interim docket “to the letter.” Instead, it contended, the government was seeking “to transform this Court’s carefully crafted stay-stage order into a sweeping ruling that Cheney effectively forecloses discovery in this case. That is not what this Court said,” CREW insisted, “and, especially after remand, this case looks nothing like Cheney.”

On Tuesday, the court agreed to address the D.C. Circuit’s ruling.

The immigration case granted on Tuesday, Blanche v. Ozurumba, was also brought to the court by the Trump administration. In a petition for review filed in May, Sauer asked the justices to clarify what type of support an immigrant must be shown to have provided to a terrorist organization in order to be “removable and ineligible for various immigration benefits” under a federal immigration law that states that an individual who “affords material support” to such a group is “ineligible to be admitted to the United States.”

Blanche v. Ozurumba involves Izuchukwu Ozurumba, “a native and citizen of Nigeria,” who worked as a cook in a camp run by a separatist organization known as the “Unknown Gunmen” “for about six months” before escaping, according to the government’s petition. He made his way to Venezuela and then the United States, where he applied for asylum, but an immigration judge and then the Board of Immigration Appeals concluded that his work in the camp amounted to “material support” for terrorism and that he was, therefore, ineligible for asylum.

Ozurumba appealed his case to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit, which held that “the record does not support the conclusion that Ozurumba provided material support” to the Unknown Gunmen. “Cooking meals using food and supplies purchased by the organization may have ‘sustained’ the organization in the broadest possible sense—by converting raw groceries into meals they enjoyed—but provided nothing that the organization could use or readily divert to plan or carry out its terrorist activities,” concluded 4th Circuit Judge James Wynn in the majority opinion.

The Supreme Court will clarify what qualifies as "material support" of a terrorist organization such that an immigrant is ineligible for asylum and removable from the United States.

title: Supreme Court takes up DOGE documents fight and an asylum plea from a chef for terrorists
description:
The DOGE case raises fundamental questions about the power and transparency of an entity that slashed agencies with unusual speed last year.
The Trump administration appealed lower court orders requiring DOGE to disclose records, arguing that separation of powers concerns should bar such “wide-ranging and intrusive discovery” demands from federal courts.
Now, the Supreme Court will decide if the more pared down requests were proper.
The lower court ordered DOGE to provide all “directives” by its administrator to its employees, to disclose any plans to access classified information and a deposition by the head of DOGE, Amy Gleason.
The Supreme Court has increasingly made immigration a central theme of its new term.
text:
The Supreme Court agreed Tuesday to take up a pair of appeals from President Donald Trump’s administration, including a case about the Department of Government Efficiency, the government-cutting entity once run by Elon Musk, and a dispute about a Nigerian man who was denied asylum because he once cooked meals for members of a terrorist organization.

The two cases are a reflection of Trump’s return to power last year, both his crackdown on immigration and his moves to slash government spending.

The DOGE case raises fundamental questions about the power and transparency of an entity that slashed agencies with unusual speed last year. A left-leaning watchdog, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, sued to gain access to those documents under a federal transparency law, and lower federal courts have ordered DOGE to produce information to help decide whether the law applies.

The asylum case centers on a Nigerian national who served as a cook for a separatist group carrying out terrorist attacks, a dispute that the Trump administration says could affect thousands of immigration cases annually.

What was happening at DOGE?

The Trump administration appealed lower court orders requiring DOGE to disclose records, arguing that separation of powers concerns should bar such “wide-ranging and intrusive discovery” demands from federal courts. Those orders, the Justice Department told the Supreme Court, would “perversely give respondent much of the information that it sought in its” request for documents under the Freedom of Information Act “before any court has held that FOIA applies.”

While DOGE has slipped from public view, it had a significant impact on the federal government – carrying out Trump’s promise of limiting the federal government. Central to the case is whether DOGE was exercising power on its own, which might make it subject to open records requests, or whether it was merely acting as an advisory body to the president, in which case it would likely be shielded from those requests.

The Trump administration, which the president frequently claims is the most transparent in history, has aggressively fought the case, describing DOGE as a “presidential advisory body” within the White House that is tasked “with providing recommendations” rather than making decisions.

Over the dissent of the three liberal justices, the Supreme Court last year came down on the side of DOGE in an earlier stage of the case, requiring lower courts to narrow the scope of the material ordered in discovery. CREW withdrew its request for certain documents but lower courts allowed other requests to stand. Now, the Supreme Court will decide if the more pared down requests were proper.

The lower court ordered DOGE to provide all “directives” by its administrator to its employees, to disclose any plans to access classified information and a deposition by the head of DOGE, Amy Gleason.

Guns and butter

Izuchukwu Ozurumba, who entered the United States in 2023 and later claimed asylum, says he was forced to cook at a camp for the Unknown Gunmen in Nigeria until he escaped during a run for groceries and gas. An immigration judge denied his asylum claim under a federal law that bars sanctuary for any migrant who provided “material support” to a terrorist organization.

The Supreme Court has increasingly made immigration a central theme of its new term. It is already reviewing Trump’s push to deport migrants to countries they have no connection with and his administration’s mandatory detention policies.

“Providing meals to a terrorist organization’s members is no less a material form of support than providing gasoline for its vehicles,” US Solicitor General D. John Sauer, the Trump administration’s top appellate attorney, told the Supreme Court in its appeal.

Ozurumba was deported to Nigeria in 2025.

The Trump administration told the justices the particulars of Ozurumba’s case don’t matter. The law, it argued, “does not distinguish between guns and butter.”

But the Richmond-based 4th US Circuit Court of Appeals focused on the word “material” in the law, finding that Ozurumba’s six-month stint cooking meals for the separatist group didn’t meet that threshold. Ozurumba’s lawyers said their client didn’t realize what he was getting into when he sought the job and then was forced to continue to perform it against his will.

“Under the government’s reading, seemingly any interaction with a terrorist organization could be characterized as material support,” his attorneys said. A priest who hears confession to all comers, they argue, would be viewed as providing spiritual counsel. A doctor who treats a patient affiliated with a terrorist organization, they argue, could also be punished.

“Under such a test, ‘material’ loses all meaning – every conceivable form of support, no matter how attenuated, compelled, or incidental, would suffice,” they told the justices.

Decisions in both cases are expected by next summer.

text:
Immigration compliance has become a major focus of Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) inspections, and one in which it is “taking a harder line”, a Lewis Silkin webinar on the Irish Employment and Immigration Intersection (6 October) has heard.

Central Statistics Office figures indicate that, by the end of 2024, non-EEA nationals comprised an estimated 10% to 11% of Ireland’s workforce, with a substantially higher percentage in other sectors.

There are also proposed amendments to the employment-permits system, including to the 50:50 rule in the healthcare sector, to alleviate labour shortages.

Consequently, workplace matters increasingly require both employment and immigration-law expertise and this intersection is most frequently seen in WRC inspections.

Lewis Silkin senior associate Emma Quinn explained that inspections could be announced or unannounced, routine, prompted by a complaint or as part of a targeted sector-wide campaign.

They may also involve other agencies – including the gardaí, Revenue, and the Department of Social Protection.

Inspection targets

Food services, hospitality, and agriculture are “regular targets for WRC inspections” but large corporate multinationals have also been scrutinised.

Immigration formed a large part of a WRC inspection, Quinn said, adding “in some cases, inspectors will carry out a separate inspection to ensure right-to-work compliance”.

Lewis Silkin managing associate Declan Groarke said there had been a shift from historical sampling.

“It's becoming far more of a due-diligence exercise, and there's definitely been a change of approach,” he noted.

In addition to employment-law related documentation such as working-time records, employment contracts, records of annual leave and public holidays, and payroll records, employers are asked to provide all employees’ right-to-work status.

Where right-to-work is required, employers must provide details of stamps and permits and copies of these.

It can be time-consuming but, if immigration compliance isn’t in place, Groarke said, and there was doubt over an employee's status, staff would be sent home while investigations were conducted.

Operational repercussions

This can take months and have operational repercussions.

Emma Quinn drew attention to the WRC's 2025 annual report, which outlined that 60 out of 78 convictions were under the Employment Permits Act.

The three main sectors that received convictions were food services, hair and beauty, and wholesale/retail.

Declan Groarke said that food, retail, hospitality and leisure employers faced heightened risk because of higher numbers of non-EEA workers, the frequent absence of a HR function, tight margins, shift work, and reliance on Stamp 2 student permission-holders.

Stamp 2 holders may work up to 20 hours a week in term time and 40 hours during holiday periods, but Groarke flagged that the 20-hour limit was a cap, not an average, and holiday periods were standardised.

He added that employers could fail to understand that, although graduate level permissions allowed full-time work, they were time-limited, “So they can fall out of permission quite quickly”.

Groarke also warned that the ‘12-week concession’, which allows work to continue after a permission has expired once the renewal application has been lodged before expiry, does not apply in all circumstances.

Quinn noted that, even where inspectors found minor infractions, the WRC was “less willing to give an employer the benefit of the doubt, and they're moving more quickly to enforcement and prosecution”, backed by a rise in joint immigration operations with An Garda Síochána.

Employers found in contravention may be summonsed to the District Court and fined up to €4000, with scope in the act for fines up to €250,000.

However, Groarke said, “the real risk” of being found in contravention was “reputational damage” that “increases your risk rating within the WRC … and then all of a sudden you've more frequent inspections”.

Rigorous vetting

Quinn flagged that, while immigration law incentivised rigorous vetting, employment-law obligations remained.

“Employers really can't ask ‘are you Irish, where are you from, at an interview in place of a proper right to work check,” she said.

Quinn added: “And, if an employer was to take this approach, they would risk a race discrimination claim under the Employment Equality Acts”.

Similarly, a blanket policy of rejecting candidates requiring permission is most likely indirect discrimination on race grounds.

Role-specific restrictions may be justifiable where a role is ineligible for an employment permit.

Although the statutory defence requires an employer to show it took reasonable steps to carry out right-to-work checks, no official guidance exists on how to do this.

text:
Trump focused, however, on a favorite issue — immigration. Trump has long targeted Minnesota's large population of Somali immigrants and on Monday he linked that group to Haitians in Springfield, Ohio. During a presidential debate two years ago, Trump falsely accused the latter group of eating pets. Referencing those allegations Monday, Trump said "I was right" and boasted that Haitians were being driven out of the country by his administration's policies.

"If you want to stop Ohio from being plundered, ransacked and destroyed like Minnesota is being destroyed, we're going to stop it," Trump said. "Just like we did with Springfield, we're going to stop it, we're not going to let it happen."

Trump's remarks came on the same day Homeland Security agents searched the Washington home of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar, a Somali immigrant who represents a Minnesota district.

READ MORE: They lost their work permits and their legal status. Returning to Haiti is still 'unimaginable'

The president visited Youngstown less than a week after rallying in Dayton. The intense focus on Ohio, a state Trump won by 11 percentage points, shows the challenging environment Republicans are navigating in the midterms amid the Iran war and lingering inflation. In addition to the Senate contest, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy is locked in a close governor's race with Democrat Amy Acton.

The rally was also a reminder of the extent Trump is willing to go to boost his allies — he announced a new submarine component manufacturing center will be located in nearby Cleveland during the rally — and his persistent focus on Black immigrants.

Back in 2018, Trump privately complained about immigrants from countries like Haiti — using an expletive to describe them — and wondering why the United States couldn't get more migrants from places like Norway. The statement was condemned as racist and Trump denied making it at the time.

READ MORE: Ohio Democrats' path to governor's office runs through rural areas that have turned against party

But Trump admitted using the phrase last year, and his second administration has focused on restricting immigration and barring any refugees except white South Africans.

During the rally, he celebrated what he contended was an exodus of Haitians out of Springfield. The Trump administration ended a program that allowed more than 350,000 Haitians to stay in the country legally, which some of the roughly 15,000 Haitians who arrived in Springfield, population 60,000, in recent years.

"They're getting their town back," Trump said about the original residents of Springfield, as he also stood by his debunked statement at the 2024 presidential debate that the Haitians were eating local pets. That claim was based on a secondhand Facebook post whose author deleted it and apologized, saying she had no evidence it was true.

Trump devoted even more time to insulting immigrants from Somalia, where he claimed that people were "low IQ" and "don't have pants to wear."

READ MORE: Democrats see a chance to flip a seat as focus on abuse claims mounts against Ohio Rep. Max Miller

Trump's main goal was to boost Husted, who was appointed to replace Vice President JD Vance in the Senate in 2024 and faces a tough challenge from Brown, a longtime senator who lost his seat to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024.

The presidential visit came after mailers, sponsored by Enough Promises Ohio PAC, began arriving in voters' mailboxes in recent days. They promote independent candidate Greg Levy over Brown with messages such as "Join the Revolution" and "Send a Worker to the Senate." Levy describes himself as "Socialist running for the U.S. Senate to represent Ohio in 2026" on his X account.

Levy condemned the fliers for falsely impersonating his campaign and engaging in "dirty tricks" designed to mislead voters. He said he is considering legal action.

"This is a highly undemocratic practice and does a disservice to voters in Ohio and throughout the country," he wrote on X.

According to Federal Election Commission filings, Enough Promises Ohio was founded Sept. 29. It has not yet had to disclose its contributors, but additional federal filings lay out a trail of associations linked to Republicans.

Enough Promises paid the firm Seven Farms more than $397,000 on two dates last week for printing, postage and mail services either supporting Levy or opposing Brown. Seven Farms, also a new entity, lists as its address the same South Carolina business suite as the one used by Whistlestop Strategies LLC.

Whistlestop is a direct mail outfit operated by Big Dog Strategies LLC, the strategy firm that advises Trump's MAGA Inc. super PAC and that managed Moreno's successful campaign against Brown in 2024.

Enough Promises Ohio and Big Dog did not respond to requests for comment.

Associated Press writer Jill Colvin in New York contributed to this report.

text:
WASHINGTON – A Russian asylum seeker and six other people who were held in immigration detention and later released from custody have filed a class action lawsuit against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) over the agency’s routine failure to return personal property long after the owners exited ICE facilities.

Vladimir Izmailov, a plaintiff in the case from Russia who has a pending asylum claim, has been unable to get meaningful employment without his work authorization documents, which were seized when he was detained. ICE has not returned these documents – as well as other items, including Izmailov’s wedding band – for more than 5 months. Izmailov has been forced to borrow money to pay rent for himself, his wife and their two children as a result. He cannot drive and cannot afford to pay to replace either his documents or his wedding band.

“ICE refusing to return my belongings has made a horrible experience even worse,” said Vladimir Izmailov. “ICE detained me in terrible conditions, without proper nutrition and medical care for months. Now, I’m struggling to provide for my family because ICE still has my documents that show I am authorized to work. ICE even still has my wedding ring, which holds great sentimental value for me and cannot be replaced.”

Vladimir’s story is, unfortunately, not an isolated incident but an example of what amounts to an ongoing policy. ICE routinely fails to return property seized from people it detains and then releases. The agency has withheld government-issued identification documents, like driver’s licenses and passports; evidence of immigration status; employment authorization documents; Social Security cards; cell phones, cash, and other items. Without identification, employment authorization, or immigration documents, plaintiffs have lost jobs, risked re-arrest when leaving their homes, and suffered significant hardship for their families.

The plaintiffs are represented by the American Civil Liberties Union of the District of Columbia (ACLU of D.C.); the ACLU of Illinois; Democracy Defenders Fund; Willkie Farr & Gallagher LLP; and Platkin LLP.

The Constitution prohibits ICE from retaining property once its justification for holding it expires. In 2024, the federal appeals court in the District of Columbia ruled that the Fourth Amendment governed a similar practice by the Metropolitan Police Department, in a case litigated by the ACLU of D.C.

“The Fourth Amendment exists so that overzealous government agents cannot take and keep our property for no reason,” said Michael Perloff, senior staff attorney at the ACLU of D.C. “We cannot let ICE trample on this fundamental protection against abuse of power.”

The case, Gonzalez v. Department of Homeland Security, was filed in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia. The plaintiffs are asking the court to order ICE to return the items and to take the precautions necessary to ensure it returns property that it has no justification to retain.

“For nearly two years the Trump administration has unleashed federal officers to run roughshod over our neighbors and communities, and we have become quite familiar with their violent and dehumanizing tactics,” said Kevin Fee, legal director of the ACLU of Illinois. “This complaint shines a light on one important corner of the administration’s record of abuse – its agents are seizing people’s important property and simply failing to return it, even when people need it to fight for their rights or simply live their lives. This is not the way that government should act, and it evidences this administration’s callous disrespect for the communities it is supposed to represent and protect.”

"The Fourth Amendment’s protections against unreasonable seizures apply to all people in the United States, regardless of citizenship,” said Brian Ward, senior counsel at Democracy Defenders Fund. “No president or agency can strip away this fundamental right. DHS’ policy of separating people from their belongings and essential identity documents, leaving them without the property and documents they need to navigate their own lives, is cruel and unlawful, and has left many of our clients fearful to leave their homes."

“ICE does not get to release people from custody and then hold their freedom hostage by keeping the documents they need to live their lives,” said former Attorney General of New Jersey and partner at Platkin LLP, Matt Platkin. “Passports, work permits and birth certificates are not ICE’s to keep indefinitely. ICE is not above the law, and it must be held accountable when it exceeds its authority.”

“The legitimacy of government authority depends not only on the power it may exercise, but also on the fairness and humanity with which it exercises that power,” said Craig C. Martin, Chairman Americas at Willkie Farr & Gallagher. “Our Immigration laws and procedures, national security and human dignity need not be in conflict. As enforced here, they are; once the government's need for property expires, it has a basic obligation to return it.”
