title: Florida Rep. Salazar snags presidential endorsement — from Colombia
authors: Raquel Coronell Uribe | NBC News, Raquel Coronell Uribe, NBC News
description:
Rep. María Elvira Salazar, R-Fla., who faces a tightening race in her heavily Hispanic congressional district, picked up a presidential endorsement Monday — but not from the Oval Office occupant.
Colombia’s president, the Trump-allied Abelardo de la Espriella, called Salazar “Colombia’s best friend in U.S. Congress” in a Spanish-language video Salazar posted on X.
De la Espriella, a Colombian-American citizen who owns property in Salazar’s district, and his wife have donated nearly $90,000 to Salazar in the past.
Now, on the outs with Trump, Salazar is getting support from some right-wing stalwarts overseas.
The channel between de la Espriella and Congress goes both ways.
text:
Rep. María Elvira Salazar, R-Fla., who faces a tightening race in her heavily Hispanic congressional district, picked up a presidential endorsement Monday — but not from the Oval Office occupant.

Colombia’s president, the Trump-allied Abelardo de la Espriella, called Salazar “Colombia’s best friend in U.S. Congress” in a Spanish-language video Salazar posted on X.

De la Espriella, a Colombian-American citizen who owns property in Salazar’s district, and his wife have donated nearly $90,000 to Salazar in the past.

Salazar made waves last month when she broke with President Donald Trump over immigration, directly addressing him in an ad in which she said some of his immigration enforcement efforts had gone “too far.”

“Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy. The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today,” Salazar said.

She is one of several Republicans to have distanced themselves from Trump as the midterm elections approach.

In the days after the ad aired, Trump told reporters at the White House that “without me she wouldn’t have gotten elected,” adding that Salazar “got a little bit soft on the border” while saying he still supported her campaign.

Elections

Trump later attacked Salazar, using Truth Social posts to boost other users’ messages attacking her — including one calling for a new Republican to replace her, even though the election is only weeks away.

Now, on the outs with Trump, Salazar is getting support from some right-wing stalwarts overseas.

Last week, she posted a video endorsement from Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, who called her a “firm and loyal ally to the cause of Venezuelan freedom.”

Salazar is seeking re-election in a district where more than 74% of the population is Hispanic, according to census data. A significant part of the district has ties to Colombia and Venezuela.

Salazar has represented the district since 2021. It has swung dramatically among presidential candidates in recent elections. Trump won the district by 15 percentage points in 2024, while former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton won it by 20 points in 2016.

According to an NBC News poll, Latino voters nationwide are souring on Trump, dissatisfied over high prices and his approach to immigration enforcement.

Salazar is seeking to fend off Democrat Eliott Rodriguez, a former CBS News Miami anchor. The race, not originally expected to be competitive, has picked up steam in recent weeks.

Cook Political Report shifted the race toward Democrats in late September, moving it from “Likely Republican” to “Lean Republican.” The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, meanwhile, said last week that it was sending additional resources to the district in hope of flipping the seat, adding it to its “Red to Blue” program.

Reached for comment about the Latin American leaders’ endorsements of his opponent, Rodriguez turned the conversation to domestic issues, saying the district’s families are “struggling with skyrocketing housing, insurance, grocery and healthcare costs.”

“As much as my opponent would like to make this election about politics in Latin America, it’s really about the people of Florida’s 27th District,” Rodriguez said. “Those are the people I answer to, those are the problems I intend to solve, and those are the people I will represent in Congress.”

De la Espriella, who calls himself “the Tiger,” emerged as a flag-bearer of the Latin American right after his election in June. He got a boost after he received Trump’s endorsement shortly before his runoff against leftist Colombian Sen. Iván Cepeda, an ally of former Colombian President Gustavo Petro, who often found himself in Trump’s crosshairs.

The channel between de la Espriella and Congress goes both ways.

text:
NEW YORK, October 13, 2026 — A broad coalition of organizations representing religious, racial, ethnic, immigrant, and other communities targeted by hate is warning that recently released FBI hate crime data does not accurately capture the full scope of threats facing communities across the country.

In a joint statement released today during Hate Crimes Awareness Month and coinciding with the anniversaries of several devastating acts of hate and violence, the organizations urge policymakers to look beyond reported numbers and address the conditions that continue to put communities at risk. The statement was organized by the Jewish Council for Public Affairs (JCPA) and Asian Americans Advancing Justice (AAJC), and co-sponsored by UnidosUS, the National Urban League, the Muslim Public Affairs Council (MPAC), the Sikh Coalition, the Human Rights Campaign (HRC). In all, 35 organizations co-signed the statement.

As they write in the joint statement:

“In August, the FBI released its 2025 Hate Crimes statistics, which showed a decrease in the overall number of reported hate crimes. A decline from an historic peak, however, is not synonymous with safety. Instead of settling into complacency or believing the work is done, we, as organizations representing a range of religious, ethnic, and other vulnerable communities, are warning that the data released by the FBI is incomplete and fails to capture the real risks to our communities.

“While any reported decrease in threats is welcome, these numbers remain historically high, especially compared to pre-pandemic totals. And, because of a number of deliberate policy choices being made by the current administration—particularly the increase in aggressive immigration enforcement, dramatic funding cuts, and continued extremist rhetoric— we are concerned that the reporting is becoming less reliable even as threats are increasing.”

The groups point to three central concerns: 1) hate crime data remains incomplete; 2) some communities continue to experience rising threats; and 3) federal resources and programs designed to prevent and respond to hate are being reduced or redirected. Together, these trends make it harder to know whether reported declines reflect a genuine decrease in hate crimes — or a growing inability to identify and respond to them.

“We’ve long known that the FBI’s hate crimes data is woefully insufficient in capturing the reality of hate and extremism facing our communities — and now, as so many of us face rising threats, the federal government is cutting the very programs meant to keep us safe while advancing policies that undermine reporting and trust in law enforcement,” said Amy Spitalnick, CEO of the Jewish Council for Public Affairs (JCPA), which co-led the the statement. “We cannot mistake lower reported numbers for progress when communities continue to face threats and the resources needed to address them are being undermined. This broad coalition has come together to warn against complacency and to demand action to keep our communities safe.”

Thousands of law enforcement agencies did not report hate crime statistics to the FBI, while additional incidents may go unreported because victims are afraid to come forward or law enforcement does not classify or submit incidents as hate crimes. The organizations are particularly concerned that aggressive immigration enforcement is further eroding trust in law enforcement, making some people afraid to report crimes for fear of retaliation, deportation, or other consequences.

The statement also warns that political leaders and others have normalized conspiracy theories and hateful rhetoric once relegated to the fringes, putting all communities at risk.

“For Asian Americans, anti-immigrant rhetoric reinforces a harmful message that we are perpetual outsiders, regardless of how long we’ve been part of this country. But this issue extends far beyond any one community. The significance of this coalition is that organizations representing diverse communities are hearing the same concern: many people feel that the federal government is retreating from its responsibility to protect communities targeted by hate,” said Sim Singh Attariwala, Senior Director of AAJC’s Anti-Hate Program. “When the systems designed to prevent violence, enforce civil rights, and support victims are weakened, every community becomes more vulnerable.”

The organizations are calling on policymakers to restore funding for hate crime prevention and response programs, strengthen data collection and reporting, and ensure equitable access to security funding for vulnerable communities. Its recommendations also include ending immigration enforcement practices that undermine trust in law enforcement, investing in community-based prevention and conflict resolution, and confronting dehumanizing rhetoric, conspiracy theories, and online hate speech.

Spitalnick added: “When one community is targeted by hate, all of us are at risk. We have a responsibility to stand together, speak out against hate in all its forms, and ensure every community can live with dignity and safety.”

The coalition emphasizes that addressing hate requires more than tracking reported incidents. It requires rebuilding trust, supporting vulnerable communities, and sustaining the resources and partnerships needed to prevent violence and respond when it occurs.

Read the full statement and list of signatories HERE.

# # #

About JCPA: The Jewish Council for Public Affairs (JCPA) convenes and mobilizes partners and coalitions across communities to counter antisemitism and broader hate and extremism, protect democracy, and advance our shared values — recognizing that Jewish safety and inclusive democracy are inextricably linked. JCPA envisions a just and inclusive American democracy in which Jewish and all communities thrive in safety, dignity, and freedom.

About Asian Americans Advancing Justice: AAJC has a mission to advance the civil and human rights of Asian Americans and to build and promote a fair and equitable society for all.

About The Human Rights Campaign: The Human Rights Campaign (HRC) is the nation’s largest LGBTQ+ civil rights organization working to achieve equality for lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and queer (LGBTQ+) people, with 4 million members and supporters. The HRC Foundation (a 501(c)(3)) works to ensure LGBTQ+ people are safe, seen and supported where it matters most: at school, at work and in every community across the country. From the courtroom to the classroom, from Congress to corporate America, HRC and the HRC Foundation build power through partnerships, storytelling, and action—working to create a future rooted in equity, freedom and belonging for all LGBTQ+ people.

About MPAC: Founded in 1988, the Muslim Public Affairs Council (MPAC) is a national public affairs nonprofit working to promote and strengthen American pluralism by increasing understanding and improving policies that impact American Muslims. Over the past 38 years, MPAC has built a reputation of being a dynamic and trusted American Muslim voice for policymakers, opinion shapers, and community organizers across the country.

About The National Urban League: The National Urban League is a historic civil rights and urban advocacy organization with 90 affiliates serving 300 communities, providing direct services that impact and improve the lives of more than two million people nationwide.

About The Sikh Coalition: The Sikh Coalition is the largest Sikh civil rights organization in the United States. Through the community, courtrooms, classrooms, and halls of Congress, they have worked for 25 years to work to protect the constitutional right of Sikhs and others to practice their faith without fear.

About UnidosUS: UnidosUS is a nonprofit, nonpartisan organization that serves as the nation’s largest Hispanic civil rights and advocacy organization. Since 1968, we have built a stronger America by creating opportunities for Latinos and breaking down barriers to expand economic and social progress for all. UnidosUS partners with an Affiliate Network of nearly 300 community-based organizations across the United States and Puerto Rico. For more information on UnidosUS, visit www.unidosus.org or follow us on Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, X and Threads.

text:
The Department of Homeland Security issued a rule eliminating a grace period for immigrants whose work authorization expires while renewal applications are still pending.

The measure released Tuesday makes permanent an interim final rule DHS issued last year doing away with a 540-day automatic extension period adopted under the Biden administration. The agency said the change, which affects asylum seekers as well as spouses of H-1B specialty occupation workers, would allow for more frequent vetting of applicants.

The extension window was designed to ensure immigrant workers aren’t pushed out of jobs because of processing delays at US Citizenship and Immigration Services. The agency has added a number of hurdles, however, under the Trump administration for immigrants to keep or renew their employment authorization.

As of June 30, more than 432,000 work permit renewal applications were pending at USCIS for six months, including more than 91,000 for more than a year and a half. Foreign workers aren’t eligible to re-up the documents until 180 days before their expiration date.

A group of H-4 visa holders sued DHS in January, arguing the policy change violated the Administrative Procedure Act. A California judge last month enjoined the interim final rule for those plaintiffs, finding it didn’t follow procedural requirements or acknowledge the reliance interests of plaintiffs.

The final rule will take effect when it’s published in the Federal Register Oct. 14.

text:
FRESNO, Calif. (KFSN) -- ICE agents showed up at three Lennar job sites in Fresno and Madera counties over a two-day span last week, detaining workers at two locations and leaving without arrests at a third after a supervisor challenged agents' authority to enter the job site.

On Thursday, agents appeared at Lennar construction sites in west Fresno's Fanucchi Ranch development and the Riverstone development in Madera County. The following day, agents arrived at another Lennar site in the Tesoro Viejo development.

At Fanucchi Ranch, Andres Pacheco was detained as he arrived for work, according to his wife. She said Pacheco, who has lived in the United States for 23 years and is the father of three daughters, is being held at the Golden State Annex detention facility in McFarland.

"My whole life situation changed, especially for my girls. They are so attached to their daddy," she said.

At Riverstone, a worker who asked not to be identified said agents detained his father while the two were working together.

"I see my dad; he drops himself on the floor and I see all three ICE agents come get him," he said.

The son said his father had no criminal record and is also being held in McFarland.

At Tesoro Viejo, construction worker Nick Rodriguez recorded video as a site supervisor confronted ICE agents.

"Our homes are private property. You guys have to have a signed warrant to enter our homes," the supervisor says in the video.

Rodriguez said agents had been asking workers for visa paperwork before the superintendent intervened. Federal agents left without detaining anyone.

The interaction has drawn attention online because the supervisor challenged whether agents had the legal authority to enter the construction area without a signed warrant. Whether ICE can enter a construction site depends on whether the area is considered public or private.

Immigration agents generally may enter public areas of a workplace without a warrant, but access to nonpublic areas typically requires either consent or a judicial warrant signed by a judge. Administrative immigration warrants generally do not authorize entry into private areas.

Fresno City Councilmember Annalisa Perea, whose District 1 includes the Fanucchi Ranch area where Pacheco was detained, criticized the enforcement actions.

"It's heartbreaking. It's really heartbreaking to see families in real time being ripped apart," Perea said.

Madera County Supervisor Jordan Wamhoff, whose district includes the Riverstone development, urged residents not to interfere with federal operations.

"As a member of the law enforcement community, the safety of our neighbors and community will always be my number one priority," Wamhoff said in a statement. "I urge everyone not to jump to judgment from some of the videos circulating on social media. I would also urge residents not to intervene for the safety of others."

Madera County Supervisor Bobby Macaulay, whose district includes the Tesoro Viejo development, said he was concerned about the impact the enforcement activity has had on residents.

"I am sad to see so much fear and anxiety throughout the County," Macaulay said in a statement. "While I think most would agree violent criminals have no place here, we have to remove them in a way that is transparent and does not distress our communities."

Action News asked Lennar whether agents were granted access to the three sites, whether they had warrants, whether the detained workers were employed by Lennar or subcontractors and what requirements the company has for verifying workers are authorized to work in the United States.

The company did not respond before publication.

Action News also reached out to ICE regarding the recent enforcement activity. The agency said it could not discuss law enforcement operations and added that the Department of Homeland Security enforces the nation's laws every day.

HARRIS COUNTY, Texas (KTRK) -- The attorney for the man who was run over by an SUV driven by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents during a pursuit on Saturday claims her client has never met the alleged target in ICE's search.

ORIGINAL REPORT: Man hospitalized after ICE-driven vehicle strikes him during chase, HCSO says

Miguel Parra-Hernandez was injured around 7:30 a.m. on Saturday near Highway 6 North and Clay Road after he ran from an ICE-driven SUV that was pursuing another man, identified by ICE as Jose Mendoza-Cervantes.

Surveillance video from the scene shows a white pickup truck stopping along Clay Road, facing oncoming traffic. Two men exit the truck, with one running toward Highway 6, while the other, identified by ICE as Parra-Hernandez, runs through a shopping center parking lot before he was hit by ICE's SUV.

In an update on Monday, Parra-Hernandez's attorney Kim Bruno said that her client never met Mendoza-Cervantes. While Bruno said Mendoza-Cervantes was not the other person in the white pickup truck with Parra-Hernandez on Saturday, authorities have not released the identity or whereabouts of the other person who fled the scene.

Bruno, along with FIEL Houston spokesperson Cesar Espinosa, said that both of Parra-Hernandez's legs were injured, with one being broken in three places and requiring surgery.

Bruno and Espinosa also said that Parra-Hernandez is in ICE custody, claiming he is in the custody of the agents who ran him over. They also alleged that the agents prevented them from seeing Parra-Hernandez.

On Monday afternoon, Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare announced that his office has launched an independent investigation into the incident.

SEE ALSO: Man run over by ICE-driven SUV during pursuit recovering with both legs injured, family says

Over the weekend, ICE said agents targeted Mendoza-Cervantes because he had a final order of removal from a judge. The agency has not said whether it knew Parra-Hernandez's immigration status before the pursuit and collision.

Parra-Hernandez's niece, Natxielly Castañeda, said on Sunday that her uncle had been in the United States for more than 30 years and was working toward obtaining citizenship.

"Most Hispanic communities are here to work. We are here to work. We are here not to cause problems," she said.

text:
This article is part of Cafe, TPM’s home for opinion and news analysis.

Donald Trump’s ability to jail millions of people without even a bond hearing depends on what the Supreme Court thinks about one man’s case.

His name is Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha, he’s a Brazilian citizen, and he crossed the United States’ southern border without inspection over 20 years ago. Since then, he’s lived a model American life, becoming the owner-operator of a small construction business, a married father of two U.S. citizen children, and an asylum seeker with a work authorization and no criminal record.

Last September, he was arrested by immigration agents while driving to work in Norwood, Massachusetts.

For decades, if someone like Barbosa da Cunha wound up in ICE custody, he would have been afforded a bond hearing and been evaluated by an immigration judge on whether he was likely to attend future court dates, and whether his release would pose a risk to his community.

That changed in July 2025, when the Trump administration dramatically reinterpreted the law governing immigrant detention. ICE issued a memo saying that anyone who entered the country without inspection would be considered to be “seeking admission” to the U.S., and thus required to be jailed without bond for the duration of their immigration proceedings, even if they’d lived here without incident for years.

The administration’s brand-new interpretation of a 30-year-old law lumped people like Barbosa da Cunha in with recent arrivals at the border — and with suspected terrorists and people charged or convicted of certain crimes, who also face mandatory detention.

It also threw the federal court system into chaos. Without the option for a bond hearing in immigration court, people detained in ICE jails under the new policy have instead gone to federal civil court, filing habeas corpus petitions challenging their detentions by the tens of thousands; this year, those cases have so far amounted to a quarter of all civil suits filed in federal court, Reuters recently reported.

And judges have overwhelmingly ruled against the administration. Out of at least 24,100 federal court rulings concerning immigration detention, judges across the ideological spectrum have ruled against the Trump administration over 85% of the time, according to a running Politico tally. Two-thirds of those decisions against the administration concerned the new mandatory detention rule.

One of those cases was Barbosa da Cunha’s. After a district judge in Western New York ordered a bond hearing, Barbosa da Cunha was released last October.

The government appealed, and the case became one piece of one of the most epic “circuit splits” in American history. Every single appeals court in the country has weighed in on the administration’s mandatory detention rule this year except that of the District of Columbia, which doesn’t have an immigration jail of its own. Of the 11 numbered circuits, judges in nine have ruled against the Trump administration. Only the Fifth and Eighth circuits have ruled in Trump’s favor.

The Second Circuit affirmed the district court’s finding that the relevant mandatory-detention portion of the law did not apply to people “who were not apprehended at or near the border at the time of entry,” even if they had crossed the border illegally at one point. Instead, they were eligible for bond as they had been for decades, the court found.

Writing for the majority, Trump appointee Joseph F. Bianco called the mandatory detention policy the “broadest mass-detention-without-bond mandate in our nation’s history for millions of noncitizens.” Others have since written in even more dramatic terms, including by comparing the policy to Japanese internment during World War II and the 19th-century law requiring hard labor from Chinese immigrants found to be in the country illegally.

“Those shameful and abhorrent past detentions were limited in scope in comparison to the mandatory detention that the Government urges us today to find that Congress established thirty years ago in an ambiguously worded statutory provision,” Judge Nicole Berner, a Biden appointee, wrote for the majority in the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals last month. “We decline to do so.”

The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to examine the Second Circuit’s ruling in July, saying that after 30 years, it had “revisited the issue” of who was required to be detained under the Immigration and Nationality Act “and determined that its prior approach was inconsistent with the INA’s text.”

On Oct. 1, the court agreed to take up the case.

“This case is about an unprecedented detention policy that we’ve never seen in the American immigration system — a policy that would literally amount to the largest detention scheme in American history,” Michael Tan, deputy director of the ACLU’s immigrants’ rights project and counsel of record in Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, told TPM. “The stakes are enormously high — from a historical perspective, from a legal perspective, from a human perspective.”

6 Million Could Be Detained Without Bond

When Bill Clinton signed an overhaul of the INA into law in 1996, around 2 million people were believed to be living in the United States after having crossed the border without inspection. These days, that number is closer to 6 million, according to one estimate cited by attorneys challenging the administration policy.

And while it’s true that Trump has nowhere near the ICE detention space to jail millions of people all at once — at its peak in January, ICE was jailing about 73,000 people on any given day — the day-to-day detention numbers belie just how many people can churn through the detention system across several years, particularly with a motivated president.

Over 610,000 people were booked into ICE detention from the beginning of Trump’s second term through Aug. 6 of this year, according to a Marshall Project analysis of Deportation Data Project figures. And that number has likely increased significantly: August marked yet another ICE arrest record, with over 50,000 people cuffed in 31 days.

The administration has at times been explicit that it is using the miserable reality of ICE detention to encourage people to “self-deport.” Some data indicates this has been effective. “Among people who were detained at the start of their removal case, more than 10 times as many cases concluded with a voluntary departure decision in recent months than at the end of Biden’s term,” the Vera Institute of Justice found in May.

Rebecca Cassler, a senior litigation attorney with the American Immigration Council who recently argued against the administration’s mandatory detention policy before an en banc hearing held by the Fifth Circuit, said the pressure to self-deport in detention was “by design.”

“Putting someone in prison is inherently harmful to them — so people are giving up their cases,” she told TPM. “Civil detention is not supposed to be coercive. It’s not supposed to be a tool to get people not to assert their statutory and constitutional rights … but that’s certainly how it’s been used.”

Observers have expected the Supreme Court to weigh in for months. As things stand, a given ICE detainee’s right to a bond hearing depends on where they are jailed. The Fifth Circuit includes Texas and Louisiana, which together hold over a third of the nation’s ICE detainees, according to July data from the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, which collects and analyses government data. Immigration attorneys have complained for months that ICE has transferred detainees to those states to avoid releasing them.

“At a minimum, the transfers are faster,” Cassler said. “They are transferring people so they can’t file a habeas petition in the good jurisdiction.”

The Supreme Court’s move to take up this specific case provided some tangible good news for the respondents. Unlike another case concerning mandatory detention that the Trump administration had submitted to the Supreme Court, Barbosa da Cunha concerns only statutory interpretation — the letter of the law — and avoids constitutional due process questions, which so far haven’t produced a circuit split on their own.

Still, the Roberts Court has sided with the administration on immigration questions before, and there’s no sign it will stop now. And even an anti-Trump ruling on this question would leave other obstacles. Trump has politicized the immigration bench like never before in its history, and even before this administration, bond was regularly denied to detained migrants who were able to schedule hearings.

But advocates see the case as a key potential shift in the anti-immigrant tide.

“The Supreme Court rejecting the government’s argument here is just one step of many that would be needed to bring actual justice to this system,” Cassler said.

text:
Just after 10.30am on a recent weekday morning, a Bombardier CRJ200 Air Wisconsin aircraft landed at Youngstown-Warren regional airport.

Having made the 75-minute flight from Milwaukee, the 50-seater came to a halt and its twin engines fired down next to another Air Wisconsin plane and a larger Eastern Air Express Boeing 737, planes that flew in the evening before from Alexandria, Louisiana.

Together, the planes – which combined can handle about 300 passengers at a time – and this austere, quiet airport a few miles from the Ohio-Pennsylvania state line, represent the cornerstone of the Trump administration’s Great Lakes deportation campaign.

Last year, the facility, which handles no commercial flights, saw 398 “shuffle” – ICE-contracted flights between US airports – and direct deportation flights.

With about 300 flights from this and the neighboring Akron-Canton regional airport respectively recorded so far this year by ICE Flights Monitor, an advocacy group, these small, often empty airports have seen more enforcement flights between US cities than many bigger metro areas.

In fact, only seven other US airports this year have seen more deportation shuffle flights than the two combined.

Turning these small airports into a key cog of the Trump administration’s deportation campaign has angered many.

“We have to fight for the rights of others because if they’re going to come for them, you know who’s next; they could knock on our doors next,” said Erin Bracken-Sanchez, a military veteran and resident of Massillon, Ohio, who has come to the Youngstown-Warren airport to monitor the activities of the planes contracted by ICE.

“They’re [using these regional airports] to be more obscure, to be under the radar. Who’s here? No one’s here; no one knows.”

Away from towns and cities and largely out of the public’s eye, every day a network of contracted planes carries hundreds of immigrants caught up in Trump’s anti-immigration campaign between Wisconsin, Michigan, Ohio and Massachusetts.

The deportation shuffle flights in north-east Ohio’s airports typically take place in late morning, with immigrants held at jails across the region being bused to the airport and boarded on to planes that typically fly on to Alexandria, Louisiana, where ICE operates a swathe of detention facilities that have been pilloried for human rights abuses. From there, immigrants are flown overseas.

Sometimes, detention flights from north-east Ohio have taken immigrants directly to a tiny airport outside the Mexican town of Tapachula that is situated close to the border with Guatemala.

Now, flight safety among airlines contracted by the Trump administration has also come into focus.

On 28 September, a plane operated by Eastern Air Express, a Kansas City-headquartered company and one of ICE’s main contracting airlines, struck the left horizontal stabilizer of a parked aircraft belonging to the same company at the Akron-Canton regional airport.

“No injuries were reported, and other airfield operations were not impacted. [The airport’s] operations team responded immediately to the incident. Incident investigation is conducted by the Ohio state highway patrol,” said Lisa Dalpiaz, a representative for the Akron-Canton regional airport.

“One of the planes has left, and the other is undergoing maintenance at the FBO [fixed base operator].”

The incident has worried advocacy groups.

“We’ve been very concerned on the safety of detained passengers on charter flights and followed the incident in Ohio,” said Savi Arvey of ICE Flight Monitor.

A subsidiary of Eastern Air Holdings, Eastern Air Express has recently been in the spotlight for failing safety standards.

In July, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) proposed a $65,000 fine for Eastern Air Express for allowing 26 employees including pilots to “perform safety-sensitive functions when they were not subject to required random drug and alcohol testing”. A representative of the FAA said, “the process remains open.”

Emails sent by the Guardian to Eastern Air Express, which operates 19 aircraft, asking if the company plans to conduct its own investigation of the plane collision at Akron-Canton regional airport last month, were not responded to. Airlines are supposed to report incidents such as wing collisions to the National Transportation Safety Board but there is no record of the incident on the agency’s website.

A spokesperson for the NTSB said it “is not investigating that event” due to the absence of “substantial damage or serious injuries”. However, the agency did exactly that with regard to an incident involving a commercial airliner in San Francisco on 6 October.

The Department of Homeland Security and ICE didn’t directly respond to questions from the Guardian asking if the agencies plan to review their safety requirements for contracting airlines, considering the 28 September incident.

In January, Maura Healey, the Massachusetts governor, demanded Eastern Air Express and GlobalX, another airline contracted by the Trump administration to ferry immigrants to deportation sites, end those flights. But as recently as last week, an Air Wisconsin plane contracted by ICE that took off from Youngstown-Canton regional airport landed at Massachusetts’ Hanscom Field.

All the while, the ICE deportation flights have placed an additional cost burden on these small Ohio airports that have been struggling for years.

Since last February, these and dozens of other airports around the country used by ICE have found themselves out potentially millions of dollars in landing fees that airlines typically pay to airports they use.

“As of February 2026, landing fee waivers for Government operations were extended to cover contractors working on their behalf, so no landing fees are owed to the airport,” said Dalpiaz, of the Akron-Canton airport.

In August, the month for which the most recent data is available, Akron-Canton airport saw 34 ICE flights over 27 days, a rate that has been sustained since late April.

All this is happening at a time when these small regional airports are struggling with falling passenger numbers.

Back at Youngstown-Warren airport, pilots flying the Air Wisconsin plane that arrived from Milwaukee remained on the aircraft for several hours after landing. Nearby, ground crew set up a barrier under the left wing of the Eastern Air Express plane before walking off the tarmac and into the terminal.

For a moment, a man dressed in black appears on the roof of the terminal building to watch the Air Wisconsin plane taxi. Across four hours at the airport, no detainees are seen walking, though several of the plane’s window blinds are closed shut. Arvey said that last year, six deportation flights from Youngstown were flown directly to Honduras and Guatemala, with the most recent taking place in June 2026.

Bracken-Sanchez, who served in the US army in Kuwait in the 1990s and is a member of the Buckeye Veterans Coalition, said her motivation for monitoring the ICE flights is her family – two of her children are Hispanic.

While taking part in a protest outside the Akron-Canton airport recently, Bracken-Sanchez said she saw a bus belonging to the Butler county sheriff’s department in south-west Ohio, where dozens of Haitian nationals are being held, pass through on to the runway.

“I did not expect to go to the Akron-Canton airport, to the back gate where I used to go 27 years ago to the Ohio national guard, and watch them bring in buses of immigrants shackled to deport them out of the country,” she said.

“It doesn’t make sense to me in America, the country that I fought for.”

text:
Author: Dawn Ortiz-Legg

Date: 10/12/2026 11:12 AM

OFFICIAL STATEMENT FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE October 8, 2026

On October 8, 2026, our office was informed that the parent of a local middle school student was detained by federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents.

The circumstances surrounding this incident, along with reports of increased federal immigration enforcement activity, are deeply concerning. Currently, we do not have information regarding the specific circumstances or reasons for this individual's detention. This lack of transparency creates unnecessary fear and uncertainty for all our community, who may be left wondering whether they or their loved ones could face similar actions. When enforcement actions affect local families, the absence of clear information can have far-reaching consequences, especially for children who deserve to feel safe and secure in their communities.

Immigration enforcement is a federal responsibility, and our local governments have limited authority to intervene. However, that does not diminish our responsibility to the people we serve. California and San Luis Obispo County have established protections for immigrant communities, and we remain committed to upholding them, providing access to essential services, and advocating for transparency and accountability when federal enforcement actions affect our residents.

Members of the community may document any activity they directly witness when it is safe and appropriate. If you have information you would like to report directly to my office, you may email me at dortizlegg@co.slo.ca.us.

Families who may be impacted by immigration enforcement can also access the following resources and support:

SLO UndocuSupport – Immigrant Services Guide: https://www.sloundocusupport.org/immigrantservicesguide

Our community should not have to face uncertainty and fear alone. I will continue to advocate for the safety, dignity, and well-being of our families and children.

text:
Nayeli walked into court in Westminster on September 29 holding a slim green folder, ready to finally resolve the criminal charges that had been hanging over her for two months.

Her former boss had filed the charges over a $12.08 transaction that appeared on a company credit card after Nayeli quit her job at his Carroll County auto repair shop.

The money, which Nayeli says was charged to the card by accident because she didn’t realize it was still active in her McDonald’s app, was paid back almost immediately, according to documents reviewed by The Brew.

But her ex-boss, Rasheed Haroon, still wanted his 25-year-old former employee punished.

So he went to the police, who did not bring charges, and then filed theft charges against Nayeli himself using Maryland’s “ridiculously problematic” district court commissioner system.

As ordered, Nayeli went on that September morning to the Carroll County District Court to address the charges.

While she and her parents sat on a bench outside the courtroom before the hearing, four plainclothes law enforcement officers approached and said they needed to talk to Nayeli.

Two were wearing hoodies. They did not identify themselves, Nayeli said in an interview.

Believing these were local police officers who wanted to talk about her case, she walked away with them. But when they pulled her into a vestibule and began talking among themselves about how they should “do it here,” she realized they were Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers. They were about to arrest her.

She cried out for her mom, still sitting down the hall.

“This happened so quickly,” Nayeli’s mother, Sury, said in an interview. “They don’t identify, they don’t provide an arresting order. They only said, ‘ICE, she needs to go with me.’”

The Brew agreed not to use the family’s full names because they fear retaliation for talking to the media about their case. Their account has been verified using court records and videos of the arrest obtained by The Brew.

Nayeli’s mother and stepfather watched helplessly as the agents handcuffed their daughter and marched her to an ICE vehicle. Back inside the courthouse, Nayeli’s lawyer frantically informed the judge that her client had been taken by ICE from the hallway outside the courtroom.

“I don’t know what you want me to do about that,” Associate Judge Erin M. Danz responded, according to the official courtroom audio recording of the hearing. “It’s not my hallway,” the judge added.

The theft charges were nolle prossed, or dismissed, because Nayeli couldn’t appear at the hearing. A Carroll County prosecutor, Mitchell “Craig” Wolf, had already offered to “stet” the case, meaning it likely wouldn’t have been prosecuted anyway.

But two weeks later, Nayeli is still sitting in an ICE detention center in Virginia.

A “targeted operation”

Nayeli has a pending asylum case and had permission to stay in the U.S. while her case was being processed, according to court documents.

ICE appears to be using the Laken Riley Act to justify her detention.

The law, which mandated detention for immigrants accused of theft and other low-level crimes, passed Congress last year with the help of dozens of Democratic lawmakers who crossed party lines. They included Rep. April McClain Delaney, who represents Western Maryland and parts of Frederick and Montgomery counties. (She later disavowed her vote.)

“I’m trying to be as positive as I can,” Nayeli told The Brew from detention. “But I mean, of course, this is not my home.”

In an emailed statement, ICE described Nayeli as a “criminal illegal alien from Honduras,” who was arrested during a “targeted operation in Westminster, Maryland.”

ICE further said, “Her criminal history includes an arrest and charge from the Carroll County Sheriff’s Office for theft on July 27, 2026.”

That statement is not accurate.

Nayeli was served with a summons and was not arrested, has no prior criminal record, and was not charged by the Carroll County Sheriff’s Office. ICE did not respond to followup questions.

ICE called Nayeli a “criminal illegal alien,” although she had no prior criminal record and her theft case was not likely to be prosecuted.

ICE also defended its choice to make the arrest at a public courthouse.

“The ability of law enforcement to make arrests of criminal illegal aliens in courthouses is common sense,” the agency said.

“It conserves valuable law enforcement resources because they already know where a target will be.” the statement continued. “It is also safer for our officers and the community. These illegal aliens have gone through security and been screened to not have any weapons.”

Weak Maryland Laws

Democrats in Annapolis have made a lot of noise about protecting immigrants from the Trump administration’s radical mass deportation campaign, but the legislation they’ve passed has been largely toothless.

“Sensitive locations,” such as schools, churches and courthouses, were mostly shielded from civil immigration enforcement actions under the Biden administration.

The Trump administration revoked that policy, stoking fear in immigrant communities and prompting a response from Maryland state lawmakers.

The Maryland Values Act of 2025 did list courthouses as a “sensitive location” in need of greater protection from immigration enforcement, but did nothing to address ICE activity at courthouses.

This year state lawmakers passed another Maryland Values Act that required courthouses to “implement a policy which may consider” guidance issued by the Maryland Attorney General’s Office regarding ICE enforcement.

That guidance, recently updated, offers no information about ICE enforcement at courthouses. The guidance also acknowledges that the state has virtually no power to stop federal immigration enforcement.

It instead advises state employees not to allow ICE agents into nonpublic areas of sensitive locations without a warrant, offering extremely limited protection.

Democrats in Annapolis have made a lot of noise about protecting immigrants from Trump’s mass deportation campaign, but the legislation they’ve passed has been toothless.

Maryland’s district courts responded to the 2026 law by adding a single paragraph to their administrative regulations.

The paragraph advises that law enforcement officers intending to serve a warrant at a courthouse should present it to courthouse security and wait until court proceedings are finished before serving it. The regulation, which took effect October 1, says nothing about what to do if ICE officers don’t present a warrant.

The result of this mishmash of legislation and official guidance is widespread confusion in Maryland about where ICE can operate, and what protections are offered to immigrants under state law.

Nayeli’s lawyer, Kate DeNobile, believed that ICE enforcement was not permitted inside Maryland courthouses, only to learn that wasn’t true after her client was arrested.

She told The Brew that arrests like Nayeli’s will have a “chilling effect on the administration of justice and public safety generally.” Witnesses and victims of crime will fear coming to court if they are not protected from ICE enforcement there.

“People may not want to press criminal charges, they might not want to file for protective orders or otherwise report community safety concerns because they fear being picked up by immigration enforcement for doing so,” DeNobile said.

Nayeli’s Peace Order

Nayeli worked for Rasheed Haroon for about four years, cleaning cars and doing other odd jobs at his “A to Z Auto” repair shop near Sykesville. (She is authorized to work in the U.S., she and her mother said.)

Haroon let her use a company credit card to buy lunch and make other business purchases, according to his own statements in court papers. She considered him a nice man until he started making her uncomfortable.

Nayeli says that the 55-year-old business owner would say that he loved her like a daughter and kept asking for hugs at work. Nayeli eventually told him she didn’t want to hug. He asked her for a handshake instead, she recalled, and then held onto her hand so long that she had to tell him to stop.

In June, she decided to quit the job and texted Haroon to let him know she wouldn’t be coming in anymore.

According to a petition for a peace order that Nayeli filed against Haroon later that month, he repeatedly called and texted her to insist that they have a one-on-one meeting.

Three months before her arrest by ICE, Nayeli filed a peace order against Haroon saying his phone calls, texts and visits to her home were making her “increasingly uncomfortable.”

On one occasion, he showed up at Nayeli’s house uninvited and asked to use the bathroom. On another, according to Nayeli and her parents, he saw Nayeli driving, pulled a U-turn and tailgated her all the way to her parents’ house, where her stepfather had to intervene and tell Haroon that he could not force Nayeli to talk to him.

Nayeli said Haroon repeatedly dangled her last paycheck, which he had canceled so it couldn’t be cashed, to force her to talk with him. (The Brew reviewed a screenshot showing that a check for $1,650 had bounced.)

“I feel that I am being pressured to have a private conversation with him in order to resolve issues related to my pay, which has made me increasingly uncomfortable and concerned,” Nayeli wrote in her petition.

At a court hearing on the petition on June 22, Judge Danz said that there was not enough evidence to grant a final peace order, but she also warned Haroon to stay away from Nayeli.

“She doesn’t want to have contact with you,” Danz said, according to a courtroom audio recording of the hearing provided to The Brew by the district court. “If you continue to have contact, now that I have made that abundantly clear here in the courtroom, then you can come back and I will grant it at that point,” the judge added.

A week later, Nayeli bought a meal at McDonald’s for $12.08. She says she didn’t realize Haroon’s company card was still active in her McDonald’s app, which she had recently re-downloaded.

Haroon showed up at her mother’s work the next day to demand the money back. Nayeli’s mother, Sury, paid him immediately. The Brew reviewed a screenshot of the Zelle transaction.

“He told me, ‘I want to be nice with you and finish this nice, because for me, it’s easy to call ICE,’” Sury recalled.

Haroon has had his own financial troubles. In March, Judge Danz – the same judge who handled the peace order against Haroon and the charges against Nayeli – found that Haroon owed more than $20,000 in rent for the Woodbine Road property where his auto shop was then located.

That location is now listed online as permanently closed, and Haroon appears to have set up shop at a new address.

Court System Weaponized

Sury and her daughter both entered the U.S. in 2019 when Nayeli was 16 years old, according to court records.

They were released into the country while their removal cases were processed and applied for asylum. An immigration judge denied those applications in July 2025, but their case is still pending before the Board of Immigration Appeals.

After Sury paid him back, Haroon went to the police to try and get charges filed over the $12.08. The Carroll County Sheriff’s Office investigated and did not file charges, but told Haroon he could file charges himself, according to body-worn camera footage obtained by The Brew.

Haroon did just that on July 27.

District Court Commissioner Eric Miller signed off on two misdemeanors: theft of less than $100 and unauthorized use of a credit card.

The district court commissioner system that allows anyone to file criminal charges has been widely criticized as easy to abuse.

Court commissioners, who do not need to be lawyers to hold the job, don’t investigate whether the charges are true, relying on the statement of facts provided by the person requesting the charges. The system has led to the arrests of innocent people and rarely punishes people who file false charges.

Maryland lawmakers had the chance to reform the commissioner system during the last legislative session, but the bill failed at the last minute.

The district court commissioner system, which allows anyone to file criminal charges, has been widely criticized as easy to abuse.

Nayeli and her family say that her boss weaponized Maryland’s legal system to punish her over a $12.08 purchase. And while Nayeli normally would have been able to address the charges in court, her immigration status and ICE’s decision to arrest her before the hearing made that impossible.

“She went there and showed her face in court to defend herself against these bogus charges, and they snatched her away moments before she would have stepped into the courtroom and got this dismissed,” Nayeli’s stepfather Michael said.

Who Tipped off ICE?

Wondering who may have alerted ICE to the September hearing, The Brew reached out to Haroon and to Carroll County Assistant State’s Attorney Wolf.

In a brief phone exchange, Haroon said he was not responsible for Nayeli’s arrest by ICE. “She got arrested because she misused my card. Police told me to go file the charges.”

He did not answer followup questions, sent via email, including whether he contacted ICE ahead of the court date.

Wolf also did not directly answer the question of how ICE was alerted. “I can’t tell you why ICE does what it does,” he told The Brew.

Before the September 29 hearing, Wolf had offered via email to stet, or pause, Nayeli’s case as long as she agreed not to use Haroon’s credit card again and to undergo 10 hours of community service.

DeNobile, Nayeli’s lawyer, objected that 10 hours of community service seemed “excessive” for $12.08 that was returned to Haroon before the charges were filed.

Wolf disagreed. “Yes, it wasn’t a lot of money and she paid the money back quickly, but she used the company credit card – after she was let go,” he wrote to DeNobile.

Haroon also told Wolf that Nayeli had made more unauthorized purchases with another company card, according to another email. “I told him that it appears she will be deported, but that if he finds out that she is released, he should contact us/police to investigate the additional potential misuses of his card,” Wolf wrote to DeNobile after Nayeli’s ICE arrest on September 29.

“Needless to say, if she is released and if she did make additional unauthorized purchases, we will seek to reinstate the case and potentially add charges,” he continued.

Wolf, who is assigned to Carroll County’s Special Victims Unit focusing on domestic violence, according to his LinkedIn profile, did not respond to emailed questions from The Brew about whether his office contacted ICE ahead of Nayeli’s hearing.

Nor did he say whether he had considered the dynamics between Nayeli and her ex-boss before proceeding with the theft charges.

DeNobile had emailed Wolf to let him know that Nayeli was “terrified” to appear in court because of Haroon’s ICE threats.

“She is very scared he will call immigration on her and she will be arrested at the courthouse,” DeNobile wrote on September 4.

Stuck in Limbo

Nayeli is now stuck in limbo at the Caroline Detention Facility in Bowling Green, Virginia.

The food is terrible, she says, and there is no privacy to use the bathroom. The facility is full of people like her who have no criminal records, she adds.

Her fate is in the hands of Maryland’s chief federal judge, George L. Russell III, who is handling her pending petition for habeas corpus.

She hopes to get home to her little dog, Nico, and her new job at a car dealership. She had been saving money to study business at a community college.

She said she is especially frustrated that she never got to defend herself against the theft charge.

“They didn’t give me the chance to go fight in court. Anyone can just put charges against someone in an immigration process, and they can just arrest them without proving that they’re guilty or not.”

text:
Unreported in FBI Hate Crimes Data: Immigrant Purges Leave Communities At Risk

In August, the FBI released its 2025 Hate Crimes statistics, which showed a decrease in the overall number of reported hate crimes. A decline from an historic peak, however, is not synonymous with safety. Instead of settling into complacency or believing the work is done, we, as organizations representing a range of religious, ethnic, and other vulnerable communities, are warning that the data released by the FBI is incomplete and fails to capture the real risks to our communities.

While any reported decrease in threats is welcome, these numbers remain historically high, especially compared to pre-pandemic totals. And, because of a number of deliberate policy choices being made by the current administration — particularly the increase in aggressive immigration enforcement, dramatic funding cuts, and continued extremist rhetoric — we are concerned that the reporting is becoming less reliable even as threats are increasing.

The true picture of hate crimes in America is hidden by this report in a number of ways:

1. Unreliable Data

We know that the data in this report is historically unreliable. Even according to the FBI’s own 2025 data, thousands of law enforcement agencies, serving populations that total approximately 17 million people, refused to report any hate crimes statistics at all.

Among the cities that did report hate crimes, we know that many additional crimes and incidents may yet be unreported because the police who responded did not classify them as hate crimes or chose not to share accurate data with the FBI. Grants and other programs that were created to help prevent hate crimes and report incidents have been abruptly terminated by the Trump Administration and Department of Justice, despite bipartisan support for such measures.

We also know that still other crimes were not reported at all by communities due to even greater mistrust and lack of confidence in law enforcement. The influx of violent, masked, and poorly trained immigration enforcement agents into our communities has created fear and confusion about the role and reliability of law enforcement more broadly. Community members are afraid to report crimes because they are afraid of retaliation, deportation (despite traditionally being eligible for a U-Visa as a victim or witness), or otherwise exposing their community to the public safety risk of violent and oppressive immigration enforcement.

2. Increasing Threats

Despite persistent underreporting, hate and violence continue to rise. While some communities did see a decrease, Sikh, Hindu, and Buddhist communities have documented increases in hate crimes, and the prevalence of anti-immigrant, Islamophobic anti-Arab, anti-Hispanic and Latino, anti-Black, anti-LGBTQ+, and antisemitic rhetoric and action are still creating new threats daily. Moreover, political leaders have normalized conspiracy theories and hateful rhetoric that were once relegated to the fringe, leaving all communities at risk. Hate speech online, which is known to lead to violence, is spreading unchecked. This includes large and growing platforms such as social media, video games, and streaming that shape the minds of so many.

From targeting houses of worship and congregants under the guise of protesting political differences, to the use of bigoted conspiracy theories like the debunked “Great Replacement” theory, to justify dehumanizing policies, extremism is on the rise — and without a reliable hate crimes report and comprehensive prevention programs, we will not be able to understand and respond to the reality of hate impacting all our communities.

3. Less Security

At a time of growing threats to communities, the Department of Justice’s Civil Rights Division has not only failed to prioritize our protection but has also ceased meaningful engagement with many of the organizations that represent those most frequently targeted by hate. In neglecting its core mission, the Division has redirected its resources toward interpretations of civil rights law that legitimize and risk emboldening actors who traffic in hate, exclusion, and intolerance. And in some cases, like of white supremacist violence or the numerous Black bodies found hanging from trees across the country, necessary hate crimes investigations have not even been initiated, while others have been granted pardons. The FBI has similarly pulled back from engagement with civil rights and community partners that have long served as trusted intermediaries for reporting hate crimes, identifying patterns of violence, and raising community concerns. At the same time, the Administration and the partisan majority in the 119th Congress have targeted leading anti-hate organizations, including groups that have historically monitored extremist activity and supported vulnerable communities.

At the same time, policies aimed at maximizing deportations have exacerbated these problems and left our communities at risk, as Department of Justice staff and FBI agents have been reassigned to focus on immigration enforcement. Finally, many programs that have helped communities build resilience to hate crimes have been completely cut and abandoned. In 2025, the DOJ moved to rescind or terminate $46 million in grant funding intended for hate crime prevention and response initiatives. Other programs, like the Nonprofit Security Grant Program, have been laden with mismanagement as well as new terms and conditions based on politics, not security, that make these grants less accessible to many of the communities that feel the greatest threat. As a result, communities facing rising threats are being left more vulnerable by the very institutions charged with protecting them. The erosion of education, federal partnerships, prevention programs, and civil rights enforcement has not merely reduced support, it has compounded the risks facing communities already targeted by hate and violence.

Recommendations

The FBI’s statistics do not exist in a vacuum. They are being released at a moment when community trust is being undermined by immigration enforcement policies, bigotry and violence as responses to political differences are being mainstreamed, anti-hate organizations are being targeted and sidelined, federal resources are being shifted away from preventing and responding to hate crimes, and critical programs that help vulnerable communities protect themselves are being curtailed.

Taken together, these actions weaken our nation’s ability to monitor hate, support victims, prevent violence, and keep communities safe. Policymakers should not mistake lower reported numbers for evidence of progress when many of the very mechanisms designed to confront hate are themselves being dismantled.

If we want to see a true decrease in hate crimes, we must:

It is a date keeping US healthcare providers up at night: 1 January 2027.

As the midterm elections loom, everyone from hospital leaders and to patient advocates are focused on the New Year, when Republicans scheduled the most controversial elements of their healthcare reform law to go into effect.

Millions of Medicaid beneficiaries will be required, though a maze of government paperwork, to show they’re working 80 hours per month. And that’s just the marquee change.

“The costs to the family – and society as a whole – cannot be overstated,” said the American Academy of Pediatrics president, Dr Andrew Racine.

HR 1, also known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” and signed into law by Donald Trump on 4 July 2025, cut roughly $1tn in federal spending from the healthcare industry – the biggest clawback of federal health spending ever. Paired with Republicans’ refusal to extend subsidies for plans in Obamacare marketplaces, the cuts are expected to result in about 17 million newly uninsured individuals through 2034.

Although the US has one of the most widely privatized healthcare systems in the world, nearly half of all health spending is paid for by government – whether federal, state or local, according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid (CMS). Nearly 40% of US health spending in 2024 was from just two programs: Medicare and Medicaid, the public health insurance programs for the aging and low-income. To put the scale of the $1tn cut into context, Medicaid spent $937bn in 2024, according to the CMS.

As a result, advocates, researchers, hospital leaders and doctors are all expecting more medical debt, more delayed care and more people losing coverage for which they technically qualify.

“There couldn’t be a clearer link,” said Dr Luke Messac, an emergency physician at Mass General Brigham and a historian who has written about medical debt. “We saw that when Medicaid eligibility was expanded the flow of medical debt rapidly declined and sustained that decline.

“The easiest way to reverse that trend – to make medical debt more of a problem – is to yank people off Medicaid and leave them uninsured and unprotected.”

There is a manic quality to Donald Trump’s desperate dash to do something, anything, ahead of November’s midterm elections to convince beleaguered Americans that he can make the pressures his policies have imposed on their livelihoods go away.

The US president offered to lower barriers against beef imports to limit surging meat prices, only to consider backtracking under pressure from the cow lobby. In the face of such setbacks, maybe Trump felt he had to demonstrate he still can get something done. title: PolitiFact FL: Angie Nixon said Trump has deported 'over 13,000' Cubans. That's mostly true
description:
As she courted South Florida voters, Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Angie Nixon said Cubans had been a target of the Trump administration’s deportation efforts.
The Trump administration is seeking to deport immigrants, including Cubans, during his second term as he continues to push his mass deportation promise.
PolitiFact asked the Department of Homeland Security how many Cubans it has deported during Trump’s second term, but it did not say.
Part of the number tracks back to third-country deportation agreements the Trump administration has signed with over 35 countries.
Our ruling Nixon said Trump has deported “over 13,000 Cubans since he has been in office, his first term and his second term.” Trump deported about 3,400 Cubans during his first term, government data shows.
text:
WLRN has partnered with PolitiFact to fact-check Florida politicians. The Pulitzer Prize-winning team seeks to present the true facts, unaffected by agenda or biases.

As she courted South Florida voters, Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Angie Nixon said Cubans had been a target of the Trump administration’s deportation efforts. Cuban-Americans largely supported Trump in the 2024 presidential election.

“Donald Trump is the deporter in chief and we have witnessed him deporting over 13,000 Cubans since he has been in office, his first term and his second term,” Nixon told Jim DeFede, host of CBS News Miami’s “Facing South Florida” Oct. 4.

Nixon, a state House member, is running to unseat Republican Sen. Ashley Moody, who was appointed to fill the seat Marco Rubio vacated when he became secretary of state.

The Trump administration is seeking to deport immigrants, including Cubans, during his second term as he continues to push his mass deportation promise.

During Trump’s first term, the government deported about 3,400 Cubans, according to Office of Homeland Security Statistics data. PolitiFact asked the Department of Homeland Security how many Cubans it has deported during Trump’s second term, but it did not say. Neither DHS nor Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s websites report the data.

But Human Rights Watch, an international nongovernmental organization that tracks and investigates human rights abuses, provided data that shows Nixon’s figure is close. As of Aug. 5, the U.S. has deported about 8,500 Cubans during Trump’s second term, the group’s senior adviser Brian Root said. It’s possible more Cubans have been deported since August.

The organization based its figure on ICE data released in response to a Freedom of Information Act request made by the UCLA Center for Immigration Law and Policy’s Deportation Data Project.

We reached out to Nixon’s campaign for comment, but we didn’t receive a response.

Human Rights Watch estimates of Cubans deported to Mexico

In May, Human Rights Watch reported that from Jan. 20, 2025, to March 9, 2026, U.S. authorities deported more than 18,000 people to countries they aren’t from; nearly 13,000 were sent to Mexico. Of the 13,000, about 4,400 were Cubans.

The report says many of the Cubans Human Rights Watch interviewed were 60 years old and older who had lived in the U.S. for decades, mainly in Florida. Some had arrived during the 1980 Mariel boatlift or in the 1990s, fleeing the Cuban government or for economic reasons.

Part of the number tracks back to third-country deportation agreements the Trump administration has signed with over 35 countries.

The U.S. government has also sent Cubans to Liberia, Equatorial Guinea, Guyana and Eswatini.

Why are more Cubans being deported?

Historically, Cubans haven’t been a primary target of U.S. deportation policy.

The Trump administration ended a Biden administration parole program that let Cubans and other immigrants vetted by the U.S. government enter the country if they were sponsored by someone living in the U.S. As the program ended, so did immigrants’ parole-based employment authorizations, leading the administration to deport some of them.

The Cuban government generally has refused to accept deportees who previously committed crimes in Cuba or in the U.S., said Michael J. Bustamante, associate professor of history and the Emilio Bacardí Moreau Chair in Cuban and Cuban-American studies at the University of Miami. He said this group of people has been in limbo, and the Trump administration has particularly targeted them for deportation to countries they aren’t from.

“It wasn’t a protection on paper. In theory, they always had pending orders of deportation, but there was kind of an inertia there,” Bustamante said. “We’re talking people who’ve been in the country for 30-plus years or 40-plus years who never thought that they would be sent anywhere. And this administration is finding ways to ship them out of the country.”

Even though deportations of Cubans aren’t new, what’s different is the Trump administration’s pace in arresting and deporting them, said Guadalupe Correa-Cabrera, an immigration studies expert at George Mason University. She said people with pending cases and at immigration check-ins have been arrested. The end of parole and the deportations to other countries such as Mexico has also changed things for Cubans.

Our ruling

Nixon said Trump has deported “over 13,000 Cubans since he has been in office, his first term and his second term.”

Trump deported about 3,400 Cubans during his first term, government data shows. DHS did not confirm to PolitiFact how many Cubans have been deported during Trump’s second term. But Human Rights Watch estimated about 8,500 Cubans have been deported. That brings the figure close to 12,000, based on the best estimates up to Aug. 5. It’s possible more have been deported since then.

The statement is accurate but needs clarification or additional information. We rate it Mostly True.

text:
NEW YORK – A federal judge ruled on Friday that the Justice Department’s push to obtain state voter rolls and check them against a federal immigration database to demand that states remove voters it deemed ineligible was unlawful.

U.S. District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan’s decision marked the latest setback for President Donald Trump’s push to expand federal control over election administration ahead of the November 3 midterms, with his Republican Party battling to hold majorities in both houses of Congress.

In a 78-page decision siding with a challenge to the Justice Department’s practice brought by watchdog group Common Cause, Sooknanan wrote that the Justice Department had downplayed the risk that its practice would wrongfully disenfranchise eligible citizens despite evidence that the immigration database, known as SAVE, could be inaccurate.

“The challenged policy represents the federal government’s attempt to decide who gets to vote. But Congress has left that authority where our Constitution has always placed it: with the states,” wrote Sooknanan, who is based in Washington and was appointed by Democratic President Joe Biden.

Supreme Court paused previous ruling

Ming Cheung, a lawyer with the American Civil Liberties Union who represented the plaintiffs, said in a statement, “Today’s ruling makes clear that the administration cannot use the federal government to disrupt elections.”

The Justice Department is reviewing the decision, a spokesperson said.

In a separate case, Sooknanan blocked the Trump administration in June from using an expanded version of the SAVE database to check the accuracy of voter rolls. The Supreme Court temporarily paused that decision last month.

Federal election law prohibits the systematic review of voter rolls in the 90 days before any federal election, potentially blunting the impact of both Sooknanan’s decision and the Supreme Court’s pause of her previous order on the upcoming midterms.

Latest defeat for Justice Department

Trump, who falsely claims his loss in the 2020 presidential election was due to voter fraud, ordered the Justice Department last year to crack down on voting by ineligible people, despite multiple state audits and independent studies showing such voter fraud is rare.

The Justice Department then demanded that nearly all 50 states hand over their complete, unredacted voter rolls, including sensitive information such as voters’ Social Security numbers or dates of birth.

Eighteen mostly Republican-led states complied. After receiving the voter data, the Justice Department ran it through SAVE and alerted states to voters found to be non-citizens so the states could remove them.

Sooknanan said the Trump administration’s expansion of SAVE meant it now contained citizenship data from the Social Security Administration, which could be outdated, meaning many immigrants who had since been naturalized as citizens would still be flagged as noncitizens.

The Justice Department sued 30 Democratic-led and Republican states that refused to hand over their unredacted voter rolls, as well as Washington, D.C. It has lost 26 of those cases so far, without winning one.

Reporting by Luc Cohen in New York; editing by Andrea Ricci and Rod Nickel.
