text:
Brian Snyder | Reuters

Congressional Democrats and civil rights groups are concerned about a proposed Trump administration change to the U.S. census that would exclude noncitizens without permanent resident status, altering congressional representation and potentially how federal funding is distributed.

Opponents warn the rule, which was posted in September, could have negative effects, potentially shifting congressional power to parts of the country where fewer immigrants live and underfunding education, healthcare, food assistance and emergency management programs. The public can comment on the rule until Nov. 2, the day before Election Day.

″The greatest likelihood is that this is going to end up in litigation,” said Meeta Anand, senior director of census and data equity at the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights. “I’m under no delusion that we will see everything remedied because I do know that it’s been a project of the administration to exclude noncitizens from the count.”

The proposed census change is the latest volley in the Trump administration’s push to reduce illegal immigration. If certain categories of immigrants living in the U.S. are not counted, areas where they are concentrated could get less federal money. The rule’s supporters say counting all immigrants living legally in the U.S. encourages illegal immigration.

The rule would exclude from the census millions of noncitizens without a green card, including people in the country on student visas, people with temporary protected status, refugees and asylum seekers. It would also bar the collection of demographic information on race and ethnicity from the census’s short-form questionnaire. That information can be used for civil rights enforcement and to assess compliance with federal laws that bar racial discrimination.

The White House referred CNBC to the Commerce Department, which oversees the census, when asked for comment on the proposed rule. The Commerce Department and the Census Bureau did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

Critics argue the proposal flies in the face of the 14th Amendment, which states, in part, that “representatives shall be apportioned among the several States according to their respective numbers, counting the whole number of persons in each State.”

“This rule is yet another attack on democracy by Donald Trump,” Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said in a statement after the rule was announced last month. “An accurate census count is at the very foundation of ensuring equal representation across our country and delivering federal funds where they’re needed most. The Census is enshrined in our Constitution and not up for political debate.”

Census has counted noncitizens since U.S. founding

Proponents, including some congressional Republicans who have introduced legislation to end the counting of noncitizens, argue the census practice of counting all U.S. residents — which dates back to the nation’s founding — encourages illegal immigration and makes some voters more powerful than others.

“Republicans have long warned that Democrats’ intentional illegal invasion and sanctuary policies are rooted in a desire to boost blue states’ power,” Rep. Andrew Clyde, R-Ga., said in a statement in September announcing legislation that would call for reapportioning congressional seats before the 2028 election while excluding noncitizens and adding a citizenship question the 2030 census. The proposal has 42 Republican co-sponsors.

Normally, seats are reapportioned every 10 years using new census data.

“Amid high stakes and slim margins, Congress must act before the 2028 elections to ensure only American citizens decide how congressional maps are drawn and who resides in the White House,” Clyde added.

Sen. Bill Hagerty, R-Tenn., introduced similar legislation last year that would require the Census Bureau to include a citizenship status question on any future census, arguing noncitizens heavily skew the congressional map.

“While people continue to flee Democrat-run cities, desperate Democrats have back-filled the mass exodus with illegal immigrants so that they do not lose their seats in Congress or their electoral votes, hence artificially boosting their political power and in turn diluting the power of other Americans’ votes,” Hagerty said in a statement.

Next U.S. census is in 2030

The census changes are not final, but any change the administration implements would be difficult to undo before the 2030 census.

The administration in its proposal states that “the Census Bureau is considering how best to distinguish between foreign citizens in the United States who are counted for apportionment” and suggests it would use administrative records to check the legal status of those counted. The proposal also says that the Census Bureau could add an immigration status question to the census’ short-form questionnaire.

The first, Anand said, would likely have the effect of suppressing response rates and contribute to an inaccurate count. The second would likely lead to errors and the wrongful discounting of people in the country with legal status.

A New York Times analysis of the proposal found that it would result in lost House seats in several states, including places that generally favor Republicans. Florida, Rhode Island and Texas would all stand to lose a seat, according to the Times, while Minnesota, Ohio and Oregon could each add a representative to their congressional delegations.

But beyond apportioning congressional seats, the rule could reduce funding for federal programs aimed at low-income populations, such as Medicaid, the Children’s Health Insurance Program, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and Head Start, said Julie Morita, president and CEO of the Joyce Foundation, a nonpartisan philanthropy that supports racial equity and economic mobility in the Great Lakes region. She noted these programs amount to “trillions of dollars.”

“An inaccurate count risks a decade of consequences,” Rep. Grace Meng, D-N.Y., said in a statement in September. “Census data help determine representation in Congress, electoral districts, and the allocation of federal resources for health care, education, infrastructure, and other essential services.”

Trump has tried to exclude noncitizens before

In the waning days of his first term, Trump attempted to exclude undocumented immigrants from congressional apportionment, though the change wasn’t implemented. In August 2025, Trump announced in a TruthSocial post that he’d instructed the Department of Commerce to “begin work on a new and highly accurate CENSUS.”

“People who are in our Country illegally WILL NOT BE COUNTED IN THE CENSUS,” Trump posted.

The Commerce Department has authority over the count, but must present to Congress any changes in subjects and the types of information to be compiled at least three years before the next Census Day, which would set an April 1, 2027, deadline. The department is also required to report to Congress the questions that will be included in the census at least two years before Census Day.

Congress does have the authority to overrule proposed changes with legislation. But unless Democrats win a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate, overruling the Trump administration is unlikely.

A Democratic president who wins election in 2028 could also introduce a new rule to cancel out Trump’s exclusion of certain immigrants, but the rule-making process is time-consuming and cumbersome, and there would be little time.

“Planning for the census takes lots of time, effort, research, operational changes, programming of computers, developing code,” Anand said.

description:

text:
Immigrants have increasingly lost asylum claims since President Donald Trump returned to office, and are more likely to lose if their case is before one of his administration’s newest immigration judges.

Immigration judges installed on a permanent basis since Trump returned to office have denied 49% of asylum applications that went before them from October 2025 through August 2026, compared to 41% among previously appointed judges who have remained on the bench over the same period, according to a Bloomberg Law analysis.

That difference encompasses tens of thousands of the more than 313,000 asylum petitions resolved since the second Trump administration began appointing new judges last October.

The findings reveal how the new recruits, nearly half of whom bring military backgrounds and largely lack immigration experience, have helped reshape the immigration courts as an extension of the White House’s deportation agenda.

Alongside the high denial rate, the overall asylum grant rate has reached a record low of 3%, down from 17% in the first month of Trump’s second term. For new appointees, the rate was even lower at 2% of asylum applications approved. The remaining applications were either abandoned, paused, or withdrawn.

The low asylum approval rate comes as the more than 700 judges currently serving at the Justice Department’s immigration courts are pressured to deny asylum in most cases and quickly adjudicate the roughly 3 million cases in the backlog.

“Speed seems to be the goal in managing these dockets rather than compassion or fairness,” immigration lawyer Kimberly Fasking said.

The administration has added nearly 400 temporary and permanent judges since last October. The new hires have replaced roughly 200 judges who have left or were fired by the administration, many of whom had previous careers defending immigrants in court.

The new judges are also issuing more removal orders — at a 79% rate among the Trump administration’s permanent appointees through late July, compared to roughly 74% among judges appointed before January 2025.

This has left immigration lawyers questioning the fairness of proceedings, especially as more migrants are ordered to appear at new makeshift immigration courts run by Department of Homeland Security personnel.

A DOJ spokesperson said in an emailed statement that the department “continues to bring on talented legal professionals who are committed to protecting national security and public safety.”

“Reducing the immigration court backlog remains one of the highest priorities for this administration” after the “Biden Administration allowed millions of unvetted migrants into our communities and intentionally turned a blind eye to hundreds of thousands of unaccompanied alien children in need of care,” the spokesperson said.

The Bloomberg Law analysis is based on government data compiled by California-based nonprofit Mobile Pathways. The analysis focused on ruling data as of Sept. 23 for judges appointed through July 29. Limited data is available for the judges who joined in August and September.

Rapid Asylum Denials

Fasking, who represents migrants in Georgia and Louisiana, experienced the impacts of the administration’s agenda last November when she went to Louisiana’s LaSalle Immigration Court for her first appearance before one of the newly appointed immigration judges.

She was ready to argue for asylum for a young adult who entered the US as an unaccompanied child and faced threats from gang members in his home country in Central America. The judge hearing the case instead denied the asylum application without an evidentiary hearing.

Orders dismissing asylum applications without a hearing, known as pretermission, have become the new normal for Fasking and other immigration lawyers going before the Trump-era recruits.

“A lot of these judges are very quickly ordering individuals removed, pretermitting applications because they’re following the guidance that’s being provided to them,” said Amiena Khan, a former assistant chief immigration judge in New York who was fired last year.

Under a September 2025 policy memo, judges are expected to complete most removal cases for non-detained migrants within a year of a notice to appear. For detained migrants, the expectation is 60 days.

On top of that, judges must comply with precedential decisions from DOJ’s Board of Immigration Appeals, the highest administrative body interpreting immigration law. One of the board’s recent decisions held that a judge may pretermit an asylum application without first receiving a motion from DHS.

But those supportive of the administration’s changes say the asylum denials and increase in removal orders are necessary to respond to the influx in immigration under Joe Biden’s administration.

“Most of those people had no basis for applying for admission to the United States,” said Matt O’Brien, deputy executive director of the Federation for American Immigration Reform, which advocates for restrictive immigration policies.

Ordering Removal

As judges are pressured to quickly adjudicate cases, the overall removal rate has continued to increase across the board well into the second year of Trump second term — to 82% in August alone. The highest removal rate during Trump’s first term — nearly 78% — was in February 2020, according to data compiled by Mobile Pathways.

Some of the new judges with the highest removal rates are assigned to the Federal Plaza Immigration Court in Manhattan, which has received the most new appointees of any court in the past year, with at least 28 temporary and permanent judges installed, according to Bloomberg Law’s analysis.

On average, permanent judges across the immigration courts are issuing orders of removal at a higher rate, nearly 80%, than the judges who have been installed to serve six-month stints on the bench, roughly 62%.

The variation could be due, at least in part, to permanent judges being placed more frequently on the detained docket, in which higher removal rates are more typical due to the limited relief options for detained people, said Anam Petit, a former immigration judge in Annandale, Va., who was fired last year.

At least 13 judges initially installed to serve temporarily have since been appointed permanent judges. At the same time, at least two Trump appointees have been elevated to supervisory roles.

Experience Divide

Many of the judges who have quickly taken on the responsibility of deciding migrants’ fate have little to no prior experience in immigration law.

At least 180 temporary and permanent judges hired by the administration are current or former members of the military’s judge advocate general corps, or have served other legal or active duty roles in the armed forces. Around 120 judges have prior immigration experience, with the majority serving in prior roles as lawyers for DHS, including with ICE and Customs and Border Protection.

While the backgrounds alone don’t guarantee a bias, DOJ’s hiring is “sending a clear signal that they don’t want anyone who represented immigrants previously,” said Petit, who now appears before the Annandale court as a partner with immigration law firm Murray Osorio PLLC.

DOJ has dropped previous hiring standards for immigration judges, including seven years of relevant post-bar legal experience. In online job postings, EOIR requires that potential new hires have a law degree, be an active bar member, and have “qualifying post-licensure litigation or adjudication experience.”

At least 11 permanent immigration judges appointed by the second Trump administration have already left.

text:
The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child (CRC) recently delivered a landmark decision in a case involving immigration detention of children. In Jas.K.B. and Others v the Czech Republic (communication No. 193/2022), the Committee found that the State party had violated the rights of two sisters under articles 3 and 37(a) and (b) of the Convention on the Rights of the Child, guaranteeing the child best interests principle and their freedom from torture or other ill-treatment and from arbitrary detention, respectively. The Committee’s decision reaffirms the obligations of States towards migrant children. The ICJ, the AIRE Centre, the Dutch Council for Refugees and the European Council on Refugees and Exiles (ECRE) had intervened in the case by filing a legal brief with the Committee.

The case concerns the immigration detention of an 11-year-old girl from Afghanistan together with her older sister and parents in the Czech Republic, pending transfer to Austria under the EU Dublin III Regulation. No detention order was issued against the younger girl, but she was placed with her family in a closed detention centre and subjected to the same restrictions as adults held there.

The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child reiterated that “detention of a child because of their or their parents’ migration status constitutes a violation of children’s rights and is contrary to the principle of the best interests of the child given the harm inherent in any deprivation of liberty and the negative impact that immigration detention can have on children’s physical and mental health and on their development.” (para 9.3).

The Committee also clearly held that “in the context of immigration, the possibility of deprivation of liberty as a measure of last resort is not applicable, and that such deprivation of liberty is generally disproportionate and therefore arbitrary within the meaning of article 37 (b) of the Convention.” (para 9.3)

Recalling joint general comment No. 4 of the Committee on Migrant Workers and No. 23 of the Committee on the Rights of the Child (2017), the Committee reiterated that “children should never be detained for reasons related to their or their parents’ migration status and States should expeditiously and completely cease or eradicate the immigration detention of children,” and that “any kind of child immigration detention should be forbidden by law and such prohibition should be fully implemented in practice.” (para 9.3)

“This is a landmark case on immigration detention of children by the UN CRC, confirming that the possibility of detention as a measure of last resort does not apply to children in the context of migration control. The Committee set out this position in its Joint General Comment No 4 and 23 (together with the Migrant Workers Committee). It has now also clearly reaffirmed and applied these standards in this case, finding that the detention of children with their parents for 34 days, in a facility the authorities presented as adapted to families, was incompatible with the prohibition of torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment” said Karolína Babická, ICJ Europe and Central Asia Programme Senior Legal Adviser.

“States can no longer use the “family unity” as a reason to detain children with their parents. On the contrary – they have the obligation not to detain the child and keep the family together, using real alternatives to detention,” she added.

The Committee also notes in its decision, that the assessment conducted by the domestic authorities focused primarily on the preservation of family unity and the alleged suitability of detention conditions. However, the Committee recalled that, where the best interests of the child require maintaining family unity, this does not justify the detention of the child but rather requires the adoption of non-custodial solutions applicable to the family as a whole. (para 9.4). The Committee also found that the authorities had assessed the best interests of the child only to a limited extent, without addressing the harm inherent in detention giving meaningful consideration to non-custodial measures that could also have preserved family unity or showing how the children’s interests had been weighed against other considerations, as article 3 requires (para. 9.5).

In their intervention, submitted on 5 October 2023 after the Committee granted leave to intervene, the ICJ, the AIRE Centre, the Dutch Council for Refugees and ECRE argued that international law prohibits immigration detention of children, including when they are accompanied by their families, that the possibility of detention as a measure of last resort under article 37(b) does not apply in the context of migration, that family unity requires non-custodial solutions for the whole family rather than detention, and that age assessment must be guided by the presumption of minority and the benefit of the doubt (paras 6.2-6.5).

text:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

October 13, 2026

Contact: press@civilrights.org

WASHINGTON — Today the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights released its 2026 Congressional Voting Record — a review of the 119th Congress’ votes on civil rights issues. The Voting Record, which The Leadership Conference has released since 1969, showed this congress was one of the most harmful to our rights in the 76-year history of the organization, especially for people of color, immigrants, religious minorities, and the LGBTQ+ community.

“From the day its members were sworn in last year, a majority of the 119th Congress abdicated their responsibilities as an independent branch of government. They turned a blind eye to their constituents’ needs and demands, as well as this administration’s abuses of power, violations of civil and human rights, corruption and cruelty. Too many served corrupt overreach and the interests of billionaires over those of working people,” said Maya Wiley, president and CEO of The Leadership Conference. “This congress began with H.R. 1, the president’s ‘Big Ugly Bill,’ which slashed health care and food assistance in favor of violating the due process and civil rights of immigrants and putting taxpayers’ money in the pockets of billionaires through tax breaks. It presided over some of the longest government shutdowns in history, resulting in months of lost wages for workers. Too many elected leaders failed to intervene when the administration ignored acts of prior congresses and dismantled critical work in the Department of Education, the U.S. Agency for International Development, and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, among others. Elon Musk’s DOGE decimated our government and violated our privacy rights simultaneously.

“This congress will leave a permanent stain on our constitutional history and require us to fight for a Third Reconstruction of our democracy. The Leadership Conference was created to usher in the Second Reconstruction that fought for and won critical civil rights laws and government programs to create equal opportunity and protect everyone’s rights and freedoms. The 119th Congress has not stood by the advances of the First Reconstruction which ended slavery and enshrined fundamental rights through an amended Constitution this administration aggressively seeks to unravel. This onslaught of efforts to undermine voting rights and threaten the very existence of civil rights advocacy and free speech is outrageous because it is not unprecedented. This congress has chosen the dark past over the responsibility to brighten our shared future. Americans are demanding bold change for a future that is diverse and where rights and freedoms are protected for a third time. We know because we asked them. They want health care over ICE, voting rights protected, a Supreme Court with term limits, and an economy that works for everyone. We’re committed to building what the 119th Congress attacked: an America as good as its ideals.”

The Voting Record examined 24 House and 23 Senate votes taken across both sessions of the 119th Congress from January 2025 through September 2026. It addresses civil rights issues including voting rights, immigration, economic justice, health care, key judicial and executive branch nominations, LGBTQ+ equity, and more. Overall, 158 House members and 44 senators (including several members who did not serve out an entire term) supported our positions on more than 90 percent of the votes included in the Voting Record.

The Leadership Conference also recently released its fifth annual Civil Rights Monitor, showing broad support among voters across race, ethnicity, and party for civil rights priorities, including secure voting rights, a Supreme Court with term-limits, and an economy that works for everyone. Specifically, 54% of voters back the idea of a systemic, constitutional, and cultural overhaul to secure a robust multiracial democracy, with 32% strongly supporting it. The Civil Rights Monitor shows a record of American values and attitudes on human rights. This is a national survey of 1,000 likely voters, conducted by phone using professional interviewers from August 23 to September 6, 2026.

The Leadership Conference’s 2026 Congressional Voting Record is available online here.

The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights is a coalition charged by its diverse membership of more than 240 national organizations to promote and protect the rights of all persons in the United States. The Leadership Conference works toward an America as good as its ideals. For more information on The Leadership Conference and its member organizations, visit www.civilrights.org.

text:
Coalition calls for upcoming FIFA presidential election to centre human rights

The 2026 Men’s World Cup exposed a failure of FIFA’s leadership to implement its own human rights policies, with the pursuit of record revenues prioritised over fairness and equality, the Sport & Rights Alliance and Football Supporters Europe said in a joint report released today. The 50-page report, “Profit Over People: The 2026 FIFA Men’s World Cup,” documents a tournament marked by a climate of fear given the backdrop of mass immigration detentions and deportations; discriminatory visa bans; cost and accessibility barriers for fans, players and journalists; unclear safeguarding and eligibility standards; and lack of effective access to remedy.

“The 2026 World Cup exposed how the priorities and direction set by FIFA’s leadership put profit over people,” said Andrea Florence, Executive Director of the Sport & Rights Alliance. “For everyone touched by the tournament, access and participation were limited by economic status, nationality, immigration status, disability, gender identity and sexual orientation or political circumstance. Not only did FIFA fail to use its leverage to uphold human rights obligations, it chose to lift up a government that is actively violating human rights by awarding an unvetted ‘FIFA Peace Prize’ to U.S. President Donald Trump.”

As a 48-nation, 104-match tournament hosted for the first time in three countries – Canada, Mexico, and the United States – the 2026 Men’s World Cup was the biggest mega sporting event in history, and one that, as FIFA promised would be a tournament where everyone “feels safe, included and free to exercise their rights.” The tournament was the first World Cup to be hosted under FIFA’s recognition and adoption of international business and human rights obligations, through its 2017 Human Rights Policy, integration of human rights criteria in the bidding process, and a dedicated “FWC26 Human Rights Framework” for 16 local host committees. Yet due to rising concerns about potential human rights abuses at the tournament, over 65,000 people joined Amnesty International’s call for FIFA and host nations to address risks and guarantee a World Cup for everyone.

ICE raids surged, protests were blocked and discriminatory visa policies kept many fans from enjoying what was billed as ‘the most inclusive World Cup ever’.

Frank Conde Tangberg, Policy Advisor at Amnesty International

“The unity and joy we saw on the pitch and in the stands were a world away from the fear and division beyond the stadiums. ICE raids surged, protests were blocked and discriminatory visa policies kept many fans from enjoying what was billed as ‘the most inclusive World Cup ever’,” said Frank Conde Tangberg, Policy Advisor at Amnesty International. “Many of these violations stemmed from repressive and abusive government policies, but FIFA failed to use its leverage to protect fans and local communities. It spent its political capital on maximising revenue rather than standing up for human rights.”

The report details how excessive ticket pricing, coupled with expensive visa requirements and a lack of affordable inter-city transport, as well as U.S. travel restrictions on over 39 nations, disproportionately excluded fans with disabilities, with limited incomes and/or from the Global South. Participating teams and officials faced severe disruptions: members of the Iranian national team had U.S. visas delayed or denied, and for two U.S. matches the team had to enter and depart the country on the same day – while Somali referee Omar Artan, despite having a valid visa, was denied entry at Miami International Airport following an 11-hour interrogation. These and other barriers unfolded alongside aggressive U.S. immigration enforcement, with, as Human Rights Watch documented, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) conducting over 167,000 arrests in and around 11 World Cup host cities leading up to the tournament. Although reporting of ICE detentions inside World Cup venues was limited, enforcement surged during the tournament, including over five days in late June when approximately 10,000 people were arrested.

“Supporters were treated as objects to be exploited rather than the heart of the game,” said Ronan Evain, Executive Director of Football Supporters Europe. “When ticket prices are at the highest in World Cup history, legal accessibility requirements for fans with disabilities are ignored, and dedicated supporters face discriminatory visa rejections or militarized border enforcement, you no longer have a global celebration – just an exclusive, sanitized spectacle meant only for the elite.”

The report also documents other human rights abuses in Mexico, where police confronted planned protests with tear gas and detained two journalists. In Canada, preparations were marked by street sweeps displacing unhoused residents in host cities – and immigration authorities rejected more World Cup visa applications, which came mostly from Global South applicants, than they approved. Within FIFA’s direct control, questions remain about whether FIFA failed to enforce its own in-competition policy explicitly requiring athletes to declare they have never been investigated for a sexual or other violent offence, given that at least eight players facing pending sexual assault cases or allegations competed in the 2026 World Cup. Independent journalism was also severely constrained by FIFA’s opaque media accreditation processes, U.S. visa barriers, and a lack of regular press conferences with top leadership.

“In recent years, the U.S. – the country hosting the majority of World Cup matches – fell from 45th to 64th in our Press Freedom Index, and journalists have faced violence, detention, and deportation,” said Clayton Weimers, Executive Director of Reporters Without Borders (RSF) USA. “Yet FIFA’s lack of clarity on media accreditation, coordination with visa processes, and blasé attitude toward media briefings underscored FIFA’s failures to uphold human rights. On top of this, FIFA’s continued lack of advertising for its grievance mechanism for journalists, players, fans, workers and community members means we don’t know the true extent of the harm.”

FIFA is in clear need of systemic governance reform that embeds human rights and good governance into leadership and decision-making structures, provides an independent system of checks and balances, and ensures meaningful accountability when its commitments are not met.

text:
New York City has found itself mired in the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown after officials said federal agents shot a driver while his 5-year-old was in the back seat.

The Department of Homeland Security and city officials remain at odds over immigration agents’ tactics that led to them opening fire on 28-year-old Oscar Belgal. Federal officials accuse Belgal of trying to drive his Honda CRV into agents in the city’s Marble Hill neighborhood in the Bronx during a targeted enforcement operation.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin told CNN’s Jake Tapper that Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents acted appropriately, in part because New York refuses to honor the agency’s requests to detain undocumented people accused of crimes. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said there is no active warrant for Belgal’s arrest, and plainclothes ICE officers’ actions like those during Thursday’s daylight shooting on a busy street make New Yorkers less safe.

With this latest shooting, New York City finds itself in a familiar place as other American cities, such as Minneapolis, Houston and Chicago, that have seen ICE operations result in federal agents shooting people, often while in vehicles.

Some surveillance and police body camera footage has been released by the New York City Police Department, and Mullin says he expects video from ICE officers’ body cameras to be released.

As the shooting remains under investigation, here’s what to know.

What we know about Oscar Belgal

Belgal, a Dominican national who officials say entered the U.S. on an unknown date, has ties to the Trinitarios gang, according to DHS.

Mullin said he was part of an investigation into a shooting of a Customs and Border Protection officer last year and had previously fled from officers in September.

Belgal was arrested for robbery in 2023. He ultimately pleaded guilty to fourth-degree grand larceny and received five years of probation, according to New York court records.

He was also arrested last year on drug charges and has pleaded not guilty, court records show.

DHS has said Belgal had an immigration detainer, which allows ICE to take custody of immigrants in criminal custody, but Belgal was released after that earlier arrest.

Mamdani told MS NOW on Sunday there is no active warrant for Belgal’s arrest.

Now that Belgal’s in custody, ICE plans to quickly remove him from the country, according to Marcos Charles, executive associate director of the agency.

Belgal’s attorneys filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus in federal court Friday, arguing he was arrested “without a valid warrant and without any consideration of his individual circumstances.”

U.S. District Judge J. Paul Oetken then ordered Belgal to remain in the country for now.

In an update about his condition on Sunday, Belgal’s lawyers said he is in solitary confinement. With the bullet still lodged in his neck, the left side of his face is numb and he has difficulty hearing out of his left ear, according to a joint statement from the Legal Aid Society and Make the Road New York, two nonprofit advocacy organizations representing Belgal. He also has a shoulder wound from shattered glass during the shooting.

He urgently needs surgery but has yet to receive it, the statement said.

NYC, Trump’s DHS starkly divided on immigration enforcement

The shooting of Belgal highlights stark divides between deep-blue New York City and the Trump administration, even as Mamdani and President Donald Trump have formed an unlikely cordial relationship.

Mamdani has repeatedly called on ICE to be dismantled, calling the agency “rotten to its core.”

“Today’s shooting is only further devastating confirmation of what we have long known, which is that ICE operates with impunity, that they sow chaos and terror across our country, that they have killed far more of our neighbors than they could ever have claimed to save,” he said. “We will not normalize ICE’s viciousness. We will not accept its cruelty.”

New York lawmakers also expressed outrage at ICE opening fire on a car with a child inside.

“No child should ever have to experience the terror of gunfire, let alone wonder if they’ll make it home alive,” Gov. Kathy Hochul said in a statement after the shooting. “As a mother and grandmother, I cannot imagine how frightening those moments must have been.”

Citing Belgal’s criminal history, Mullin has called him the “worst of the worst” and said he intentionally put his child at risk. Mullin blamed New York’s so-called sanctuary policies that limit local officials from cooperating with federal immigration enforcement.

“We asked the city to give them to us, and they released them back on the streets,” Mullin told CNN. “If anybody should be in outrage, it should be the public to the sanctuary states and the sanctuary politicians that continue to release these murderers and thugs back on the streets and put the American people in danger.”

What videos do and don’t show

The New York City Police Department has released surveillance footage of the incident, as well as video from police officers’ body-worn cameras when they responded to 911 calls after the shooting.

Surveillance footage released by the NYPD appears to show plainclothes ICE officers approach Belgal’s parked vehicle with their guns drawn. As he tries to move the car forward, an agent starts to punch the driver’s side window of the car, video shows.

The surveillance video then changes to another angle, which appears to show the aftermath of the shots being fired offscreen, as bystanders are seen ducking. Soon thereafter, an agent wearing plainclothes is seen holding a child, presumably Belgal’s 5-year-old, who was in the back seat of the vehicle at the time of the shooting.

Officers’ body cameras showed tense scenes of a man who appeared to be an ICE agent, wearing a construction vest holding up a rifle. Nearby, bystanders were yelling while a handcuffed man sat on the street receiving treatment to his neck.

While witnesses told NYPD that a 5-year-old had been in the car, a law enforcement source said the child wasn’t on scene when police arrived. Police went on a frantic hunt to find the child, resulting in detectives going door-to-door on the street, reviewing video footage and contacting Belgal’s family. It wasn’t until about 7 p.m. that police found the child, who wasn’t injured, with an aunt at a Yonkers beauty salon, the source said.

What isn’t directly shown on publicly released videos is the moment the shots were fired, prompting many to call on ICE to release footage from the agents’ body cameras. Mullin said Sunday he was sure footage would be released, though he didn’t provide a timeline. FBI and Homeland Security Investigations, which is part of ICE, are handling the investigation, Mullin said.

Bronx District Attorney Darcel Clark said her office would also investigate the shooting, which was supported by New York Attorney General Letitia James.

Meanwhile, Mamdani said the city would be doing its own full investigation of the entire 24-hour period. He said this included the actual shooting, but also the NYPD response and ensuing protests outside a nearby hospital where Belgal was transported after being shot.

In the aftermath of Thursday’s shooting, NYPD clashed with demonstrators protesting ICE. During the scuffle, Mamdani ally Darializa Avila Chevalier, a democratic socialist and frontrunner to be the next congressperson representing the area where the incident took place, was knocked to the ground by NYPD. Mamdani said it was unacceptable to throw any New Yorker to the ground, regardless of whether she’s going to be in Congress.

title: Architecture of containment: How the EU Pact entrenches harms in Bosnia detention centre
description:
Inside Lukavica detention centre Located on the edge of East Sarajevo, the facility is deliberately isolated - removed from everyday life, transport links and public view.
Even those granted access are constrained: Collective Aid notes that observers are not allowed to take photographs, leaving almost no independent oversight.
The EU Pact and the intensification of containment The EU Pact on Migration and Asylum came into effect on 12 June 2026, and human rights NGOs have already raised serious concerns.
As Human Rights Watch has documented, serious human rights violations exist in every country on the EU's ‘safe’ list – Bosnia included.
Ultimately, documenting and challenging externalisation, human rights abuses and unlawful detention remains the only path to accountability.
text:
Guest post by Georgia Wells. Georgia is a remote research officer at Collective Aid, currently undertaking fieldwork in Bosnia and Herzegovina for her MSc thesis at SOAS, investigating deaths and disappearences of people on the move at the Croatia-Bosnia border.

"You don't feel like you are a human there… This place is worse than prison… I want you to help people inside. This is why I tell you."

This testimony was recorded by Collective Aid, an NGO supporting people on the move in Europe, from a person who was detained in Lukavica, Bosnia's only official immigration detention centre. Between 2018 and 2024, 4,631 people were detained there, including 115 children and 263 women. Official narratives describe the facility as legally compliant, with adequate healthcare and free legal aid. But Collective Aid's 2026 investigative report tells a different story. Despite 17 years of documented human rights violations, conditions have not improved.

Lukavica is not an isolated failure, but one node in a much larger system of detention and removal across the Global North. Its existence stems not only from Bosnia's domestic legal framework, but from international pressure and the EU's broader push to manage migration beyond its own borders.

Inside Lukavica detention centre

Located on the edge of East Sarajevo, the facility is deliberately isolated - removed from everyday life, transport links and public view. This isolation is reinforced by invisibility, since only three photographs of Lukavica exist publicly, and all depict its remote, carceral character. Even those granted access are constrained: Collective Aid notes that observers are not allowed to take photographs, leaving almost no independent oversight.

With so little public information on Lukavica, no single source can support a claim about the system as a whole; this is exactly how the facility operates with such impunity. Collective Aid’s Total Incident Ecology (TIE) methodology challenges this by cross-referencing different sources to turn fragmented, low-visibility data into verified, pattern-based findings. While a single testimony from a detainee can be dismissed, the same account corroborated across multiple independent sources is much harder to deny.

Why do so many people end up at Lukavica?

Bosnia's legal framework for immigration detention casts a wide net. The 2015 Law on Aliens allows detention on four broad, overlapping grounds: being considered a threat to public order or national security; being subject to a bilateral readmission agreement, most commonly with Croatia; having received an expulsion order; or failing to establish identity within six hours of arrival at a border crossing.

The 2025 Border Control Law goes even further, treating irregular migration as equivalent to a serious crime. It makes the act of crossing the border without documentation sufficient grounds for detention, with little scrutiny of individual circumstances or protection needs.

Alarmingly, children are detained under the same legal framework, with no additional safeguards. As one lawyer told researchers, “there is no procedure for age assessment.”

The human cost

The Global Detention Project rated Lukavica "deficient or at risk" consistently across 2019, 2024 and 2025, condemning the ongoing inadequate conditions and systemic human rights concerns in Lukavica. Since 2009, Human Rights Watch and the UN Special Rapporteur documented the same failures: no meaningful legal aid access, inhumane conditions, detention of minors, and a severe lack of accountability. Earlier this year, the Council of Europe's Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT) urged Bosnian authorities to enforce a zero-tolerance policy against abuse in detention. This demand followed an official investigation which uncovered widespread physical beatings of detainees and severe ill-treatment of a foreign national with a serious mental health condition while in solitary confinement at Lukavica.

As reported by Collective Aid, detainees described the food inside as inedible and water access as restricted. Accounts also detail detainees going months without outdoor access despite domestic regulations requiring two hours per day. One detainee reported being administered tranquilisers to suppress rebellion. Vasa Prava, the only NGO permitted inside, has had its capacity severely cut following UNHCR funding reductions.

Who is accountable for inhumane conditions in Lukavica?

Lukavica operates in a shrinking civic space. According to Vasa Prava, the Service for Foreign Affairs (SFA) and other authorities can "get away with anything" due to the lack of monitoring and oversight.

The management of the facility further fragments accountability. Responsibility for detention diffuses across a web of institutional actors, including the police, Service for Foreigner Affairs (SFA), the Ministry of Security and IOM. Each holds only a portion of responsibility, leaving each with room to deflect accountability to another agency.

The opacity of IOM and EU involvement in Bosnia's migration governance is particularly important to highlight. While the IOM publicly presents its work in Bosnia through the language of humanitarian assistance and "migration management", Collective Aid’s report found that IOM representatives admitted to having 24/7 access to Lukavica and contributed to its EU-funded expansion, despite initially claiming limited involvement in detention. Between 2018 and 2021, IOM spent over a million euros in EU funds on private security contracts across Bosnia's reception centres. Crucially, systemic guard violence is widely documented in these facilities, leading to the death of a migrant at an IOM-run centre in 2020.

Lukavica was built with €1.2 million in EU funding, and its ongoing expansion is EU-financed too. This is part of a longer pattern: EU support to Bosnia has gone mainly towards border control and detention since 2015, rather than reception or integration. This shift is reinforced by a 60% increase in EU funding to the Western Balkans, specifically targeting border security, management, and deportations. With EU accession conditionality treating migration securitisation as a benchmark for membership, detention at Lukavica is not a governance failure to be corrected – it is a performance indicator being rewarded.

The EU Pact and the intensification of containment

The EU Pact on Migration and Asylum came into effect on 12 June 2026, and human rights NGOs have already raised serious concerns. Framed as ‘set of rules for managing migration’, the Pact’s operational effect is to intensify and systematise what has been happening in Bosnia for over a decade: more detention and less accountability.

Three mechanisms point to a significant expansion of detention after the pact takes effect. First, the European Commission’s Provisional Political Agreement on Safe Third Countries automatically grants Bosnia safe third country status, meaning asylum claims can be declared inadmissible on grounds of transit alone, regardless of any meaningful connection to the country. As Human Rights Watch has documented, serious human rights violations exist in every country on the EU's ‘safe’ list – Bosnia included.

Second, the Pact's border procedure allows detention for up to 12 weeks during asylum examination, extendable to 18 months where removal has no viable legal route. This will extend detention for people from countries with no readmission agreement with Bosnia, such as Afghanistan, Algeria, Pakistan and Syria.

Third, the EU and UK have both proposed return hubs in the Western Balkans, positioning Bosnia alongside Serbia and Albania as holding sites for people rejected elsewhere in Europe. Collective Aid's reporting on UK externalisation in the Balkans shows a convergent agenda: Brussels and Westminster pursuing parallel strategies to offshore responsibility onto a country with 17 years of documented detention failure.

Bosnia's value to the EU lies in compliance, not rights protection – so there is little incentive for authorities to challenge what happens inside detention or Temporary Reception Centres. As Collective Aid warns, many Balkan countries like Bosnia face EU pressure to expand detention and restrict asylum access, overlooking the human cost so long as it keeps them useful within the EU's wider migration strategy. Therefore, externalisation policies not only intensify, but politically entrench the harms that already exist in countries like Bosnia.

‘The walls are literally being raised higher’

As the Mixed Migration Centre's recent analysis makes clear, the Pact's restrictive policies have little effect on whether people move, but significantly increase the risks they face along the way. For example, over half of smugglers surveyed reported raising their fees in response to new controls; 40% reported higher profits.

Lukavica has already received new procurement notices for reconstruction and expanded surveillance. With the walls of Lukavica literally being raised higher, so will the walls to accountability. Rather than treating the Western Balkans as a “warehouse” for people Europe does not want, the EU and UK could invest in functioning asylum systems and alternatives to detention.

Collective Aid urges that Bosnia, the EU and IOM abandon their securitised model of impunity in favour of rights-based transparency, halting Lukavica's expansion before more harm is done. Ultimately, documenting and challenging externalisation, human rights abuses and unlawful detention remains the only path to accountability.

text:
In Mira Mesa on Monday morning, one person was apparently apprehended by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on his way to work.

Community activist Arturo Gonzalez received a desperate message from the man’s family, who were looking for him and his truck. Gonzalez was driving near City Heights and College Grove area, monitoring ICE activities, when he got the message.

“Let me know the description of the truck and his usual route to work,” Gonzalez said, using voice-to-text to respond.

It was 10 o’clock, and he had been driving around for the past three hours.

“This morning, we had a family reach out that they were about to leave for work, and they said that there were cars parked outside of their apartment complex,” Gonzalez said. “So we got there and immediately confirmed that those vehicles were, in fact, ICE.”

He then alerted his social media network to ICE’s presence. He also used a megaphone to alert residents in the apartment complex that ICE was there. He said agents left without detaining anyone.

He’s been doing this for nearly two years since the Trump administration began cracking down on immigrants and deporting them. Lately, though, he’s seen an uptick in enforcement activities.

“This is unlike what we've seen all year long,” Gonzalez said. “What's happening right now in the last week and a half is a complete, big, immense surge — the biggest surge I have ever seen since I started doing this work.”

According to the Washington Examiner, the administration is launching a 45-day enforcement surge, starting in San Diego. Quoting sources, the newspaper said agents were instructed to go after anybody, regardless of criminal history.

“(It’s) very unfortunate that it is happening at this time,” said Ian Seruelo, an immigration attorney at PAG-ASA Law Clinic, serving the Filipino and Asian community. Pag-asa means hope in Tagalog.

He’s been getting a lot of calls lately from family members of detainees.

“They are calling because their family members have been arrested,” Seruelo said. “So that climate of fear has really intensified.”

ICE agents are also changing their tactics. Gonzalez said they were seen wearing orange safety vests at construction sites to blend in.

“I’ve seen them try to use vehicles that look less obvious,” he said. All this to create a climate of fear among the immigrant community.

“People are scared to take their kids to school,” Gonzalez said. “People are at the grocery store, and once they hear us screaming that ICE is here, they don't even want to leave that grocery store.”

Because of the crackdown, Seruelo advised vulnerable people to carry what’s known as the “red card” with them everywhere they go. It helps immigrants inform ICE agents that the cardholder is aware of their rights, regardless of their status.

“The right to remain silent, the right not to answer any questions from ICE,” he said. “The right not to provide any kind of documents from ICE, the right to have an attorney.”

People who are stopped by ICE can show the card to agents to exercise their legal rights, Seruelo said.

Both noted the timing of the enforcement surge being so close to the midterm elections. They think it’s a fear tactic to keep immigrants from voting.

“I think this administration has been known to use all tools available to them to threaten, to intimidate people of color, especially from voting,” Seruelo said.

“I think it's definitely a tactic that they're using to scare people and to get people to not go out and vote,” Gonzalez said. “It's also because they know that once we get out there and vote, that we're going to do what we can (to) elect officials (who) are going to start implementing things to stop ICE from what they're doing. And they're scared of that.”

description:

At the same time, Republican senator Roger Marshall – who had once vehemently backed Trump’s immigration agenda – started to grow uneasy in a tightening re-election race, and softened his hardline rhetoric.

text:
If there is one campaign promise that Donald Trump has kept, it is his pledge to deliver “mass deportations”.

Two years later, voters are living uneasily with the consequences.

Trump himself has called the midterm elections this November – which will decide which party controls each house of Congress – a referendum on his presidency. In many ways, they will also serve as a referendum of his hardline anti-immigration policies, and the multitudinous ways they have reshaped Americans’ daily lives.

In Florida, restaurant and hotel owners have said that ICE’s presence is frightening away both workers and customers, and Republican congresswoman María Elvira Salazar, who is running for re-election, aired a Spanish-language ad breaking with the president, saying his immigration crackdown had “betrayed” Hispanic voters in her district.

In Maine, the fatal ICE shooting of a 25-year-old asylum seeker has cast a pall over the campaign to re-elect Republican senator Susan Collins, who supported Trump’s plans to supercharge immigration enforcement.

In Kansas, cattle ranchers said ICE operations were having “a massive chilling effect on the legal, documented, skilled workers that put beef on the table” and warned that meat prices would spike as a result. At the same time, Republican senator Roger Marshall – who had once vehemently backed Trump’s immigration agenda – started to grow uneasy in a tightening re-election race, and softened his hardline rhetoric.

And in Texas, which has seen a slew of violent ICE arrests including a fatal shooting in July and a non-fatal shooting in September, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico appears to be gaining momentum against the state’s Trump-backed attorney general Ken Paxton, with a message that Trump’s ICE has gone too far.

Several national polls have shown voters’ growing distaste for the Trump administration’s militarized immigration enforcement operations. A Reuters/Ipsos poll released on 21 September found that only 36% of voters approved of Trump’s handling of immigration. According to Pew research, half of Americans see the administration’s immigration tactics as too aggressive.

In Texas, a recent poll by the New York Times and Siena University found voters there evenly split on which Senate candidate they trusted more to handle immigration – a striking shift in a state that hasn’t elected a Democratic senator in almost 40 years.

And while Latino voters, who swung toward Trump in 2024, still rank the economy as a top issue, a strong majority are viscerally opposed to the president’s immigration agenda. An October NBC News/Telemundo poll of registered Latino voters found that two-thirds believe his enforcement policies have gone “too far”. The issue is deeply felt, with more than one in four saying they know someone who had been deported or detained by ICE since Trump’s second term began, and 17% saying that they or someone close to them had considered not voting in person this year because of concerns about ICE.

After the killing of two US citizens during immigration raids in Minneapolis sparked massive public backlash, the Trump administration signalled it would take a softer approach, and the new homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, said his goal would be to keep ICE out of the news headlines.

But immigration agents are still shooting people. And with enforcement operations across the US gaining momentum, and immigration arrests at a record high, voters are continuing to see a supercharged ICE at work.

“It does cause quite a disruption in the community,” Scott Fischer, the Republican chair in Ford county, Kansas, told Politico. “We don’t want our community disrupted.”

‘It’s an issue across the economy’

Perhaps even more pertinently, voters – and the politicians vying for their support – are coming to the realization that even if immigration itself doesn’t rank in surveys as a top issue, Trump’s immigration policies have affected every other issue that matters to them.

“Even if this isn’t a top concern for voters casting their ballots, it is a part of a general perception that the president’s policies have gone too far, and that they’re affecting people who are not immigrants,” said Matthew Grossman, a political scientist and professor of public policy at Michigan State University.

Take, for instance, the cost of living – a consistently top-ranking issue for voters in midterm polls. Trump’s immigration raids, and his policies stripping legal work permits from thousands of workers, are causing disruptions not just in the cattle industry, but also across agriculture, food service, hospitality and construction.

“So many industry segments are reliant on immigrants, so it’s an issue across the economy,” said Matt Teagarden, CEO of the Kansas Livestock Association. Dairy producers and ranchers have long lobbied the government to create more legal pathways for the immigrant workers who staff their enterprises. But now, the US cattle herd has shrunk to its lowest numbers in 75 years – and ranchers are struggling to keep up with consumer demand, Teagarden said, adding: “But they are not able to expand without the workforce.”

Meanwhile, about two-thirds of farm workers are non-citizen immigrants. As the administration targets these workers, food producers could struggle to keep up operations, and prices are expected to increase steeply, according to a study by the thinktank Fwd.us.

Many of the staff at chef Carlos Raba’s restaurant Clavel in Baltimore are Salvadorians who have lived and worked in the US for years while holding temporary protected status (TPS). Trump has already revoked TPS for thousands of Haitians and Syrians, and if the administration also revokes TPS protections for Salvadorians – as it is imminently expected to do – Raba could lose 80% of his staff, he said at a congressional hearing. “We could not operate the way that we operate today if they are all gone,” he said.

“I think about the cooks, dishwashers, farmers, bakers, entrepreneurs that I work with,” he said. “They are my co-workers, my friends and my community.”

The owner of a burger restaurant not far from Trump’s Mar-a-Lago golf course said the president’s policies and immigration raids had affected not only workers but also customers, who are scared to come out and eat due to the constant presence of ICE officers.”Our sales have dropped 70%. We spend hours empty,” said Katia Rios of Pipo Burgers.

The same applies for healthcare, a top issue especially for rural voters, according to a KFF-AP poll. According to the Association of American Medical Colleges, a non-profit organization representing physicians in North America, nearly one in four doctors in the US was trained abroad – and these immigrant physicians have been key to addressing medical staff shortages especially in rural areas, where few American doctors want to move.

Senior living and eldercare facilities – which are also heavily staffed with immigrant caregivers – have also been left in the lurch. Of the 330,000 Haitian TPS holders who suddenly lost their legal status this summer, about 13,000 work daily as nursing assistants, caring for 65,000 patients, according to the Boston Globe.

Even voters who aren’t cattle ranchers or restaurateurs, who might not clearly see the impacts of immigration policies on their economic reality, are nonetheless feeling the effects, said Grossman, of Michigan State University.

“Regardless of whether people connect the dots between the president’s policies and outcomes, if those policies have real effects, then that’s another channel by which people tend to move against the party in power,” he said.

Lauren Gambino contributed reporting

text:
HOUSTON — A man who was injured when an ICE officer’s car ran over him has had surgery on his leg but needs additional procedures to reconstruct the leg and other parts of his body, an advocate for the man said Monday.

Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, had leg and hip injuries and a shattered ankle after the officer’s vehicle struck him during a pursuit Saturday, said Cesar Espinosa, a co-founder and the executive director of FIEL, who was speaking on Parra’s behalf. Parra cannot put weight on his leg for six weeks and must wait for swelling to reduce before doctors can perform additional surgery, he said at a news conference Monday.

Espinosa said Parra — who had gotten out of a vehicle and was on foot — was hit “in a violent and brutal fashion.”

ICE has said it attempted a vehicle stop and the people in the car ran away. The officers tried to apprehend the fleeing men, and “Miguel Parra Hernandez ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck,” it said.

It has said Parra was not the target of the attempted stop.

Espinosa said Parra told him that he fled because it was unclear there were officials in the vehicles, which he said were unmarked, did not use sirens and had dark, tinted windows.

Video obtained by NBC affiliate KPRC of Houston shows a white truck headed in the opposite direction of traffic on a busy roadway. The video shows a vehicle jumping a yellow median and heading in the direction that Parra is running.

It then appears to show the vehicle, which is not marked, swerving left toward Parra’s path, in front of a truck stopped in the shopping center. The parked truck leaves, and a man can be seen on the pavement behind the ICE vehicle, the video shows.

The Department of Homeland Security and ICE did not respond to a request for further comment.

Parra was at a Houston area hospital Monday morning when his attorney and Espinosa visited him, Espinosa said. But they had only 10 or 15 minutes before ICE officers came in and began recording their conversation and forced them out, Parra’s attorney Kim Bruno said.

“To add insult to injury, Mr. Miguel is in the custody of the ICE agents who ran him down,” Espinosa said. “This is so disheartening and so angering that Miguel has to face the people that brutally attacked them every single day, 24 hours a day.”

Parra has lived in the U.S. for 34 years, having arrived at age 14, and he has no criminal record, Bruno told NBC News. DHS said he was in the country without legal permission.

Bruno said he has never had encounters with immigration authorities. He and the man with him in the car do stucco work, she said.

Neither Parra nor the other man in the car was the target of ICE in Saturday’s traffic stop, Bruno and Espinosa said.

ICE identified the man it was targeting as Jose Mendoza Cervantes, who it said is not legally in the country and had been removed twice and entered the U.S. illegally five times. It said that Mendoza Cervantes had been arrested multiple times for drunken driving and once for unlawful possession of a firearm and that he had an active removal order.

Bruno and Espinosa countered that neither Parra nor the man in the car with him, whom he had picked up for work, knew Mendoza Cervantes.

The Civil Rights Division of the Harris County District Attorney’s Office sent investigators to the intersection where Parra was hit, said Damali Keith, a spokesman for the district attorney’s office.

The Harris County Sheriff’s Office has said it is leading the investigation of what it described Saturday as an “auto-ped” incident, with help from the Harris County District Attorney’s Office.

Parra was struck less than two weeks after the Trump administration issued guidance setting tighter rules for vehicle stops.

The guidance says only agents who have completed specific training should make vehicle stops. The memo also says that vehicles used for traffic stops must have lights and sirens and that all officers on the scenes of vehicle stops must wear and activate their body cameras.

text:
In his first televised interview since a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent shot Oscar Bergal in New York City last week, Mayor Zohran Mamdani told MS NOW’s Jacob Soboroff that during a nearly two-hour phone call with President Donald Trump and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, he demanded the agency cease its operations in the city. Mamdani said ICE’s actions were “making a mockery of what law and order is supposed to be” and leaving residents in a “state of terror.”

Bergal, a 28-year-old Dominican national — whose last name has also been reported as “Belgal” — was shot in the neck while sitting in a car with his 5-year-old son during an attempted arrest Thursday afternoon in Marble Hill, a neighborhood in northern Manhattan. Federal officials have defended the operation, citing Bergal’s criminal history and alleged gang affiliations.

According to Mamdani, Thursday’s shooting was yet another example of ICE’s disregard of protocol. “What they have shown, time and again, is that they view the law as a suggestion,” he said. “There is a reason why the NYPD would not be shooting at a moving vehicle. There is a reason why law enforcement agents are supposed to wear identifiable information and uniforms.”

Mamdani said bystanders witnessed a scene that looked more like a mass shooting than a law enforcement operation. “We’re talking about people carrying their shopping bags, walking by a bodega, thinking they’re on their way home, then they hear shots ring out. And they don’t even know whether this is from someone who is supposed to be a law enforcement agent or just someone who is terrorizing the city,” he said. “And when it comes to ICE, there is no difference between those two things.”

Asked whether the city would pursue criminal charges against the agent who fired, Mamdani told Soboroff that local authorities were investigating. “Right now, this case is with District Attorney Clark in the Bronx, and I am fully confident in the district attorney,” he said.

Mamdani also discussed his nearly two-hour call with Trump and Mullin shortly after the shooting, during which he said he pressed the administration to end its immigration operations in New York City.

“I’ve said directly to the president, I’ve said directly to the secretary, as someone who cares about public safety, who cares about law and order, I am demanding that ICE cease their operations in our city immediately,” he said. “Because these operations make New Yorkers less safe. They leave New Yorkers in a state of terror, and that is something that should be opposed by all of us.”

More articles

Mamdani said he told Trump that public safety was one of his “top priorities” and argued that ICE’s presence undermined that goal. “It is from that concern that I believe that ICE should not be in this city at all,” the mayor said. “ICE should, frankly, not even be an agency that exists, because what we see from their actions is an agency that terrorizes, one that creates a sense of fear, as opposed to any idea of safety.”

Soboroff asked if, given that the mayor has met and spoken by phone with the president on several occasions since he returned to the White House, Mamdani believed his “cordial“ relationship with Trump had helped the city. Mamdani pointed to the release of a New York City college student from ICE detention after an earlier meeting but acknowledged that his negotiations after the shooting of Bergal had not produced the outcome he wanted.

“Those two hours over the course of Thursday evening, those negotiations, they were ultimately unsuccessful,” Mamdani said. “However, I would be betraying my duty as the mayor of our city if I did not try at every single juncture with every single person to keep this city safe, and that is something that I will always continue to do.”

“A willingness to negotiate should never be understood as a willingness to surrender our principles,” he said.

You can watch Soboroff’s full interview with Mamdani in the clip at the top of the page.

title: Rep. Omar accuses Trump of political intimidation after agents search her home - PBS
description:
Geoff Bennett: Federal agents searched the Washington, D.C., home of Minnesota Democratic Congresswoman Ilhan Omar early this morning.
Devlin Barrett, The New York Times: So, Geoff, the Trump administration has been signaling just such a move for months now.
Geoff Bennett: And, of course, we're talking about federal agents searching the home of a sitting member of Congress.
Geoff Bennett: What would legal experts look for to distinguish a legitimate criminal investigation from one driven by political motivations?
Geoff Bennett: Devlin Barrett of The New York Times and the author of the book "The Department of Revenge: How Trump Took Control of American Justice."
text:
Geoff Bennett:

Federal agents searched the Washington, D.C., home of Minnesota Democratic Congresswoman Ilhan Omar early this morning. The reason for the search has not been made public. Agents with Homeland Security Investigations, the investigative arm of ICE, were seen carrying boxes from the home into an unmarked car.

Omar accused the Trump administration of political intimidation, writing on social media -- quote -- "Make no mistake, this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement."

For more, we're joined now by Devlin Barrett, Justice Department reporter for The New York Times and author of the book "The Department of Revenge: How Trump Took Control of American Justice."

Devlin, always great to have you with us.

So the DOJ says this search is part of an ongoing criminal investigation. What have you learned about what prompted it and what investigators are looking for?

Devlin Barrett, The New York Times:

So, Geoff, the Trump administration has been signaling just such a move for months now. If you go back to the spring, J.D. Vance, the vice president, said that Ilhan Omar -- quote -- "definitely committed immigration fraud."

And DHS officials have since said they're investigating. So this move isn't much of a surprise, but I think it does speak to the way that law enforcement actions keep happening at the at the impetus and prodding of the White House.

And what's at issue here, according to our sources, is all the paperwork in the congresswoman's family that led them to becoming U.S. citizens. That's paperwork that her father filled out, paperwork that was done later. And what they're investigating is false statements on immigration documents potentially and various types of fraud and conspiracy.

Geoff Bennett:

A federal judge had to approve this search warrant, so what does that suggest about the evidence investigators presented? Would it have been the sort of documents that you're talking about?

Devlin Barrett:

Right.

So they have to show probable cause to believe that evidence of this crime or possible crimes existed at her house. And probable cause is not the same thing as the amount of evidence it takes a jury to convict. We are told by sources that prosecutors first applied for this search warrant more than a week ago.

And that led to a back-and-forth with a federal judge over whether they had shown enough of a legal argument for why they needed to do this and whether they had considered the issues related to the constitutional protections that are specific to a lawmaker.

Geoff Bennett:

And, of course, we're talking about federal agents searching the home of a sitting member of Congress. How extraordinary is that? What safeguards are supposed to govern an investigation this sensitive?

Devlin Barrett:

Well, the federal government does investigate lawmakers all the time. That's not particularly unusual.

What's so unusual here is that they're doing it 22 days before an election, because the Justice Department has for many years followed something called a 60-day rule, which is basically meant to go quiet, make the Justice Department go quiet about things exactly like searches of lawmakers' homes and businesses, because they don't want to be seen as trying to influence the election.

Here, what you see is a very publicly observable, overt act of investigation that past administrations would have done everything they could to try to avoid doing just before an election.

Geoff Bennett:

What would legal experts look for to distinguish a legitimate criminal investigation from one driven by political motivations?

Devlin Barrett:

Well, it's things like, what is the basis of the evidence that leads you to probable cause?

Obviously, a judge has determined that there is some probable cause here. And -- but, at the same time, we also know that there was the judge didn't immediately accept that application, that there was some back-and-forth before they got to this point.

I think one of the ways in which the Trump administration sort of creates its own headaches and its own problems when it comes to criminal investigations is, remember how this process began. It began with the vice president of the United States publicly declaring her to be guilty.

And there's obviously a long history of the president himself, Donald Trump, accusing Ilhan Omar of various things. So the challenge that will -- that the government will have to overcome if it proceeds to try to charge her is overcoming questions or skepticism about, what was the motivation behind this investigation?

Geoff Bennett:

And when you say if the government proceeds, what would come next in this investigation?

Devlin Barrett:

Well, if they decide they have enough evidence that they can get an indictment, then they would present their evidence to a grand jury.

What's going to happen now is, after -- now that there's been a search and we have seen agents taking away boxes of evidence, they're going to have to sort through everything they have taken. And there may be some fights, legal fights, to come over what of that evidence that is seized is properly part of the investigation.

And so we don't know if there's going to be a legal fight over that. I wouldn't be surprised if there is. But the next prosecutorial step, assuming that they know what evidence they have and they believe it would survive a vote in a grand jury, would be to present the evidence to a grand jury.

Geoff Bennett:

Devlin Barrett of The New York Times and the author of the book "The Department of Revenge: How Trump Took Control of American Justice."

Devlin, always a pleasure to speak with you. Thanks.

Devlin Barrett:

Thanks, Geoff.
